concepts.title: Thermodynamics
concepts.content: Thermodynamics studies the energetics of chemical reactions. Gibbs free energy is defined by AG = AH - TAS, where H is enthalpy, S is entropy (a measure of disorder), and T is temperature. The sign of AG, taken from the point of view of the system, determines favorability: a reaction is spontaneous (exergonic) when AG < 0 and nonspontaneous (endergonic) when AG > 0. Reactions with a negative AH are exothermic and release heat, while those with a positive AH are endothermic and absorb heat. When AG = 0 the reaction is at equilibrium, the point where the forward and reverse rates are equal and net concentrations stay constant; adding or removing a reactant or product shifts the reaction to re-establish equilibrium (Le Chatelier's principle).

problems.prompt: Assuming a constant temperature appropriate to the reaction, which of the following would indicate that a chemical reaction is NOT spontaneous? (Recall AG = AH - TAS.)
choices: A reaction with a large positive AH and a large positive AS
A reaction with a large positive AH and a large negative AS
A reaction with a small negative AH and a large positive AS
A reaction with a small positive AH and a large positive AS

problems.prompt: In a study of mRNA folding, researchers discovered that the decrease in free energy due to folding was heavily impacted by nucleotide sequence. What is most likely to be true regarding mRNA folding?
choices: mRNA folding results in an increase in AS of the transcript.
Folded mRNA exists in greater quantities than the unfolded transcript at equilibrium.
Folded mRNA exhibits a greater degree of rotational freedom.
The intra-molecular nucleotide interactions alone dictate the energetics of mRNA folding.

problems.prompt: In the endoplasmic reticulum, viral protein p21 forms a dimer stabilized by disulfide bonds. Which of the following is most likely true if the formation of the p21 dimer is an exothermic process?
choices: The formation of a p21 dimer is spontaneous at all temperatures.
The formation of a p21 dimer is nonspontaneous at all temperatures.
The formation of a p21 dimer is spontaneous only at low temperatures.
The formation of a p21 dimer is spontaneous only at high temperatures.

concepts.title: Thermodynamics vs. Reaction Rates
concepts.content: The term spontaneous (AG < 0) means a reaction can proceed without an added input of energy, but it says nothing about how fast the reaction occurs; many reactions with a negative AG proceed at negligible rates. Thermodynamics describes only where a system starts and finishes, not the path traveled to get there. Because AG depends only on the nature of the reactants and products, it is independent of the reaction pathway and of the reaction rate. As a result, the free energy change for oxidizing sugar is the same whether the sugar burns in a furnace or is broken down in the human body.

concepts.title: Kinetics and Activation Energy
concepts.content: Chemical kinetics is the study of reaction rates. Even thermodynamically favorable reactions can proceed slowly because reaching the unstable transient intermediate (the transition state) requires an input of energy called the activation energy (Ea); this barrier, not AG, determines how fast a reaction proceeds. A catalyst speeds a reaction by lowering Ea and stabilizing the transition state without changing AG, and it is not consumed but regenerated with each cycle. Enzymes are biological catalysts that lower the activation energy, so they have a kinetic role rather than a thermodynamic one, altering how quickly equilibrium is reached but not the equilibrium concentrations of product.

problems.prompt: Which of the following is a true statement regarding catalysts?
choices: Catalysts increase the energy of activation for a reaction, thus reducing AG.
Catalysts are always specific and reduce the energy of activation for a reaction.
AG is unaffected by a catalyst; however, the energy of activation is increased, thereby increasing the rate of the reaction.
AG remains unaffected by a catalyst, while the energy of activation is reduced.

problems.prompt: Patients on the anticoagulant warfarin are monitored to keep the drug in its therapeutic range. In patients with supratherapeutic (very high) levels, elimination of warfarin displays zero-order kinetics. Which of the following would be true regarding these patients?
choices: The patients would have a decreased risk of bleeding relative to patients in the therapeutic range.
Patients would show increased elimination of warfarin with higher serum concentrations of the drug.
Elimination rates would be increased by concurrent treatment with injections of vitamin K.
The half-life of drug elimination would be dependent on the initial medication concentration.

concepts.title: Oxidation and Reduction
concepts.content: The production and use of cellular energy come down to a series of oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions, where oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain of electrons. Oxidation can be recognized as a gain of oxygen atoms, a loss of hydrogen atoms, or a loss of electrons, and reduction is the exact opposite. Whenever one species is oxidized, another must be reduced, so the two always occur together as a redox pair. Organisms store chemical energy in reduced molecules such as carbohydrates and fats and then oxidize them to CO2 while capturing energy as ATP; in glucose oxidation (C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O) the sugar's carbons are oxidized and oxygen is reduced to water. Catabolism (breakdown) is generally oxidative, whereas anabolism (building up), such as fatty acid synthesis, is generally reductive.

problems.prompt: In an oxidation-reduction reaction:
choices: the molecule being oxidized loses electrons and the molecule being reduced is known as the oxidizing agent.
the molecule being oxidized gains electrons and the molecule being reduced is known as the oxidizing agent.
the molecule being reduced loses electrons and is known as the oxidizing agent.
the molecule being oxidized loses electrons and is known as the oxidizing agent.

problems.prompt: In tumor lysis syndrome, xanthine is converted to uric acid by the reaction xanthine + O2 + H2O -> uric acid + H2O2. Which of the following best characterizes this reaction?
choices: Carbon serves as an oxidizing agent.
Oxygen serves as a reducing agent.
There is an increase in the oxidation state of carbon.
There is a decrease in the oxidation state of carbon.

problems.prompt: Most disulfide bond formation occurs in the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and not in the cytoplasm. Which of the following statements best describes these environments?
choices: Both the ER lumen and the cytoplasm are reducing environments.
Both the ER lumen and the cytoplasm are oxidizing environments.
The ER lumen is an oxidizing environment, while the cytoplasm is a reducing environment.
The ER lumen is a reducing environment, while the cytoplasm is an oxidizing environment.

problems.prompt: To track p16 dimerization, HeLa cells infected with vaccinia virus were pulse-labeled with 35S-methionine, and p16 was immunoprecipitated and separated by gel electrophoresis under nonreducing (no DTT) and reducing (with the reducing agent DTT) conditions; the autoradiography results are shown. The results indicate that:
choices: p16 dimerization was prevented by DTT because it prevents the formation of, or breaks, disulfide bonds.
the additional band at 240 minutes in the absence of DTT must be due to dimerization with a different protein.
the absence of reducing conditions prevented the dimerization of p16.
because the band indicating dimerization is less than 30 kDa, no conclusion can be made about the effect of DTT on dimerization.

concepts.title: Proteins as Enzymes
concepts.content: Enzymes are biological catalysts that greatly increase reaction rate by lowering the activation energy without altering the AG between reactants and products, giving them a kinetic rather than a thermodynamic role. A reaction that would take a hundred years to reach equilibrium without an enzyme may occur in just seconds with one. Enzymes are commonly classified by the type of reaction they catalyze, for example isomerases, ligases, lyases, kinases, oxidoreductases, polymerases, phosphatases, phosphorylases, and proteases. However, an enzyme cannot control the direction in which a reaction proceeds, and enzymes within a given class are often seen to function in reverse.

problems.prompt: Protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) is the enzyme that catalyzes the formation of disulfide bonds in the ER. When viral p16 monomers are combined with PDI in vitro, p16 dimers form. Which of the following is true once the solution has reached equilibrium?
choices: The rate of p16 dimer formation is the same as the rate of p16 dimer dissociation.
Removal of PDI from solution will decrease the amount of p16 dimers in solution.
Addition of more PDI will increase the amount of p16 dimers in solution.
p16 monomers have ceased to associate together to form p16 dimers.

concepts.title: ATP as an Energy Source: Reaction Coupling
concepts.content: Many essential cellular reactions are thermodynamically unfavorable (AG > 0), such as the biosynthesis of DNA and protein, yet they proceed by reaction coupling, in which a highly favorable reaction is used to drive an unfavorable one because free energy changes are additive. The cell's usual energy source is the hydrolysis of a phosphate group from ATP, which releases about -12 kcal/mol and is therefore very favorable. Coupling an unfavorable reaction to ATP hydrolysis, for example by transferring a phosphate group to a substrate or by driving a conformational change in a protein, can make the summed AG negative and thus spontaneous. The underlying rule never changes: the overall AG of a single reaction or of a linked series of reactions must be negative for it to occur spontaneously.

concepts.title: Enzyme Structure and Function
concepts.content: Most enzymes are proteins that must fold into a specific three-dimensional shape, usually globular, to form the active site, the region directly involved in catalysis; the reactants are called substrates. The lock-and-key model treats the substrate and active site as perfectly complementary, whereas the more widely accepted induced-fit model holds that substrate binding induces a conformational change in the enzyme; in either model, catalysis works by stabilizing the transition state and thereby lowering the activation energy. Active sites are highly specific, including stereospecificity, and amino acids far apart in the primary sequence can fold together to form a single active site. Because active-site structure is critical, both temperature and pH strongly affect activity, and sufficiently large deviations can denature the protein or change the charge of ionizable R groups. Many enzymes also require cofactors (metal ions or small molecules); an organic cofactor is called a coenzyme, and many dietary vitamins serve as cofactor precursors.

problems.prompt: Glucokinase is composed of a single polypeptide subunit. Researchers find that the glucose- and ATP-binding sites within its active site are significantly further apart than expected given the size of the product glucose-6-phosphate. Which of the following best explains this observation?
choices: Binding of the substrates results in a change in the tertiary structure of the enzyme.
A shift in the quaternary structure of the peptide brings the two groups in apposition to one another.
Hydrogen bonding between the peptide and substrate stabilize the transition state.
ATP is serving as an allosteric inhibitor and not a substrate.

concepts.title: Regulation of Enzyme Activity
concepts.content: Metabolic enzymes are tightly regulated rather than continually active, through several mechanisms. Covalent modification, most commonly the reversible phosphorylation of serine, threonine, or tyrosine residues by protein kinases (and reversal by phosphatases), can either activate or inactivate an enzyme. Proteolytic cleavage converts inactive zymogens into active enzymes, and association with regulatory subunits or other polypeptides can switch activity on or off. In allosteric regulation, small molecules bind reversibly and noncovalently at sites distinct from the active site, changing the enzyme's conformation to increase or decrease catalysis. A common pattern is feedback inhibition, in which a pathway's end product shuts off an enzyme catalyzing an early committed step, while feedforward stimulation activates an enzyme in response to its substrate.

problems.prompt: Hexokinase I/A is found in many tissues, whereas glucokinase (hexokinase IV/D) is expressed mainly in the liver and pancreatic B-cells. Glucose-6-phosphate acts as an allosteric inhibitor of hexokinase I/A but not of glucokinase. The most likely reason for this difference is to:
choices: decrease competition for the active site in glucokinase.
allow for continued glycogen production in hepatocytes at high substrate concentrations.
shunt glucose through the Krebs cycle by inhibition of hexokinase I/A.

concepts.title: Basic Enzyme Kinetics
concepts.content: Enzyme kinetics measures the reaction rate (velocity V), the amount of product formed per unit time, as a function of substrate concentration [S] at a fixed enzyme concentration. At low [S] the rate is roughly proportional to [S], but as more active sites become occupied the V vs. [S] curve flattens, and once every active site is continuously occupied the enzyme is saturated and the rate reaches its maximum, Vmax. The Michaelis constant Km is the substrate concentration at which the reaction rate is half of Vmax. Km is unique to each enzyme-substrate pair and reflects affinity: a low Km means little substrate is needed to reach half-maximal rate, indicating that the enzyme has a high affinity for that substrate.

problems.prompt: Hexokinase I/A exhibits a low Km, while glucokinase displays a high Km (Km is the substrate concentration required to reach half-maximal velocity). Which of the following best characterizes the differences between hexokinase I/A and glucokinase?
choices: Hexokinase I/A has a greater affinity for glucose and can function at lower substrate concentrations than glucokinase.
Hexokinase I/A has a greater affinity for glucose and requires higher substrate concentrations than glucokinase.
Glucokinase has a greater affinity for glucose and can function at lower substrate concentrations than hexokinase I/A.
Glucokinase has a greater affinity for glucose and requires higher substrate concentrations than hexokinase I/A.

problems.prompt: In pancreatic B-cells, glucokinase works together with GLUT2 (a glucose transporter that facilitates glucose uptake from the blood) to serve as a glucose sensor that triggers insulin release. What would be the most likely abnormality noted in a patient with a loss-of-function mutation in the GLUT2 gene?
choices: Increase in apparent Km of glucokinase
Decrease in apparent Km of glucokinase

problems.prompt: Researchers made missense mutations in human B-cell glucokinase and measured its kinetics. Native B-cell glucokinase: Vmax = 100 units/mg, Km(glucose) = 8 mM. Mutant 1 (G175R): Vmax = 51, Km(glucose) = 39. Mutant 2 (T228M): Vmax = 0.4, Km(glucose) = 10. Mutant 3 (E279Q): Vmax = 55, Km(glucose) = 41. Mutant 4 (E300Q): Vmax = 100, Km(glucose) = 20. Of the mutants evaluated, which is most likely to demonstrate activity most similar to endogenous glucokinase?

concepts.title: Cooperativity
concepts.content: Some multi-subunit enzymes do not follow simple saturation kinetics because the binding of substrate to one subunit modulates the affinity of the other subunits, a property called cooperativity. In positive cooperativity, binding at one subunit increases the affinity of the others, shifting the complex from a low-affinity tense state to a high-affinity relaxed state (negative cooperativity is the opposite). Cooperative binding produces a sigmoidal rate-versus-[S] curve rather than a hyperbolic one, and cooperative proteins must have more than one active site, usually as a multisubunit quaternary complex. Cooperativity is a special kind of allosteric interaction, but the binding takes place at the active site rather than at a separate regulatory site; hemoglobin's cooperative, sigmoidal O2 binding is a classic example, even though hemoglobin is a carrier rather than an enzyme.

concepts.title: Inhibition of Enzyme Activity
concepts.content: Enzyme inhibitors reduce activity by several distinct mechanisms. Competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate and compete for the active site, so their effect can be overcome by adding more substrate; Vmax is unchanged but the apparent Km increases. Noncompetitive inhibitors bind an allosteric site and cannot be displaced by substrate, lowering Vmax while typically leaving Km unchanged. Uncompetitive inhibitors bind only the enzyme-substrate complex, decreasing Vmax and, by sequestering that complex, increasing the apparent affinity of the enzyme for substrate (decreasing Km). Mixed-type inhibitors bind either the free enzyme or the enzyme-substrate complex and always decrease Vmax, with the apparent Km rising or falling depending on which form the inhibitor prefers.

problems.prompt: Metoprolol, a competitive antagonist (inhibitor) of B-adrenergic receptors, is a commonly prescribed medication that decreases heart rate and blood pressure. Which of the following is most likely true?
choices: Metoprolol principally affects the parasympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system.
The quantity of norepinephrine in the synaptic cleft directly affects the degree of inhibition.
Metoprolol binds to an allosteric site on the receptor.
Kd (a measure of a receptor's affinity for its ligand) will be unaffected by metoprolol.

problems.prompt: All of the following are true of uncompetitive inhibition EXCEPT:
choices: the inhibitor binds to the active site.
inhibition results in an increase in apparent affinity of the enzyme for the substrate.

problems.prompt: Thymidylate synthetase converts dUMP to dTMP. Kinetic data were collected using substrate alone and with each of two compounds, DHV52 and HKA10. Reaction rate (pmol/min) at each substrate concentration (nmol) for control / +DHV52 / +HKA10 was: [S]=5: 12 / 9 / 16; [S]=10: 24 / 18 / 24; [S]=15: 33 / 23 / 28; [S]=20: 39 / 27 / 30; [S]=25: 42 / 30 / 31; [S]=30: 44 / 32 / 32; [S]=35: 44 / 32 / 32. Which of the following is true?
choices: Both DHV52 and HKA10 have a similar mechanism of inhibition and both bind an allosteric site on the thymidylate synthetase peptide chain.

DHV52 binds an allosteric site of the enzyme, effectively decreasing the maximum reaction rate; in contrast, HKA10 binds the enzyme-substrate complex, decreasing enzymatic activity, maximum reaction rate, and apparent Km.
DHV52 is an uncompetitive inhibitor that binds the enzyme and enzyme-substrate complex with similar affinity, while HKA10 is a noncompetitive inhibitor.
HKA10 is likely a noncompetitive inhibitor that binds the active site, while DHV52 is either an uncompetitive or mixed inhibitor.

concepts.title: Lineweaver-Burk Plot
concepts.content: The Lineweaver-Burk plot linearizes enzyme kinetics as a double-reciprocal graph of 1/V against 1/[S], following 1/V = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax, which has the form y = mx + b. The slope equals Km/Vmax, the y-intercept equals 1/Vmax, and the x-intercept equals -1/Km. Because both axes are reciprocals, increasing [S] moves the point left along the x-axis and increasing V moves it down the y-axis. The plot makes different inhibition types easy to distinguish by how the intercepts shift; for example, an uncompetitive inhibitor decreases both Km and Vmax, giving a line parallel to that of the uninhibited enzyme.

problems.prompt: An enzyme's kinetics are measured with and without an inhibitor and plotted on a Lineweaver-Burk (double-reciprocal) graph. The inhibitor's line shares only the x-intercept with the baseline (uninhibited) line. What can be concluded about the apparent affinity of the enzyme for its substrate when this inhibitor is present? (On a Lineweaver-Burk plot the x-intercept equals -1/Km.)
choices: The apparent affinity has decreased along with an increase in Vmax.
The apparent affinity remains unchanged in the presence of the inhibitor.
The apparent affinity has decreased based on the change in Km.
The apparent affinity could increase or decrease, based on the concentration of the enzyme.

problems.prompt: Kinetic data indicate that the inhibitor DHV52 lowers the enzyme's Vmax while leaving its Km unchanged (i.e., it is a noncompetitive inhibitor). In the Lineweaver-Burk plots shown, the solid line is the uninhibited enzyme and the dashed line is with DHV52. Which plot correctly represents DHV52?

concepts.title: Amino Acid Structure and Nomenclature
concepts.content: The generic amino acid is built on a central tetrahedral alpha-carbon bonded to four groups: an amino group (-NH2), a carboxyl group (-COOH), a hydrogen, and a variable side chain (R-group). All twenty amino acids share this same nitrogen-carbon-carbon backbone, so it is only the side chain that distinguishes one amino acid from another and gives it its physical and chemical properties. Because the alpha-carbon bears four different substituents in every amino acid except glycine (whose R-group is just H), it is a stereocenter, making all amino acids except glycine chiral. Each amino acid also has a standard three-letter and one-letter abbreviation that are useful to know for the MCAT.

problems.prompt: A passage on intestinal amino acid transport notes that the System B transporter moves glutamine and alanine, the System B3 transporter moves glycine, and the inhibitor MeAIB (a-(methylamino)isobutyric acid) has no chiral center. Based on this, which statement is true?
choices: All amino acid system complexes transport chiral amino acids.
System B complexes transport chiral amino acids.
System B3 complexes transport chiral amino acids.

concepts.title: Classification of Amino Acids
concepts.content: Amino acids are grouped by their side chains into four broad categories: acidic, basic, nonpolar (hydrophobic), and polar. Aspartic acid and glutamic acid have carboxylic-acid side chains (pKa about 4) and are anionic (aspartate, glutamate) at physiological pH, whereas lysine, arginine, and histidine are basic; Lys and Arg are cationic at physiological pH, but histidine's side-chain pKa near 6.5 lets it act as either a proton donor or acceptor. Nonpolar amino acids (e.g., glycine, alanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, and the aromatics phenylalanine and tryptophan) have aliphatic or aromatic side chains and pack into the water-excluded interior of folded proteins, with larger groups giving a stronger hydrophobic effect. Polar amino acids (serine, threonine, tyrosine, asparagine, glutamine) form hydrogen bonds with water without acting as acids or bases, and the hydroxyls of Ser, Thr, and Tyr are common sites for regulatory phosphorylation by kinases. Cysteine and methionine carry sulfur, and proline is unique in that its side chain loops back to its own amino nitrogen to form a rigid ring.

problems.prompt: What best characterizes the active site of an enzyme designed to catalyze a reaction with a positively charged transition state?
choices: Hydrophobic amino acids to stabilize the transition state with weak interactions
Acidic amino acids to stabilize the transition state with electrostatic interactions
Basic amino acids to stabilize the transition state with electrostatic interactions
Large variability in the active site within a species

problems.prompt: Posttranslational modification converts translated proteins into mature products through folding, cleavage, addition of functional groups, and other processes. Which of the following examples of posttranslational modification generally requires the consumption of ATP?
A protein's transmembrane region includes the primary sequence Leu-Leu-Ile-Val-Leu-Asp-Leu. Which amino acid, if deleted, would likely cause the biggest change to the functionality of the protein?

Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) is a serine protease. A variant with a missense mutation at position 117 (normally asparagine, N) in the active protease domain still retains enzymatic activity. Which substitution is most likely?

In humans, leucine and lysine are exclusively ketogenic while the other 18 amino acids are glucogenic or both. PEPCK catalyzes the first step of gluconeogenesis. During fasting, which amino acid's carbon skeleton would NOT rely on PEPCK to generate cellular energy?

Phosphomimetic substitutions replace a phosphorylatable residue with one that mimics the structure and charge of the phosphorylated form. Protein kinase B (PKB) is normally phosphorylated on serine 473. Which statement is most likely true?
choices: A point mutation at residue 473 of PKB (S to D) would be phosphomimetic.
A nonsense mutation at residue T19 of MLC or S473 of PKB will closely match the outcome of a phosphomimetic at the same site.
Changing residue 19 of MLC to amino acid A instead of T will have the same effect as a phosphomimetic.
None of the above statements is likely true.

problems.prompt: Integrin-linked kinase (ILK) is a serine/threonine kinase that phosphorylates myosin light chain (MLC) at threonine 19 and protein kinase B (PKB) at serine 473. Which option shows the MLC and PKB substrate residues, respectively, in their correct forms after the ILK-catalyzed reaction? (Choose the structure.)

The amino acid transport A system absorbs many neutral amino acids and is blocked by the small molecule MeAIB; this inhibition can be overcome when local amino acid concentrations are high. Which statement, paired with the amino acid whose import is affected, is most likely true? (Choose the option.)

In a transport study, brush border membrane vesicles (BBMVs, intestinal) and hepatic plasma membrane vesicles (HPMVs, liver) were mixed with radiolabeled substrates; label inside a vesicle lumen indicates transport occurred. The measured substrates were glucose, alanine (A), leucine (L), glutamine (Q), arginine (R), and valine (V). In the high-dose group, intestinal (BBMV) arginine transport was elevated while liver (HPMV) glutamine transport was unchanged. Which observation matches the high-dose data?
choices: [3H]-glutamic acid is found in BBMV lumens.

concepts.title: Amino Acid Reactivity
concepts.content: Because each amino acid contains an acidic carboxylic-acid group and a basic amino group, amino acids are amphoteric, meaning the same molecule can act as either an acid or a base depending on the surrounding pH. This dual acid/base character underlies how amino acids gain or lose protons and carry different net charges as the pH is changed. The detailed acid/base mechanisms are treated together with the rest of carbonyl and amine chemistry in the organic chemistry material.

concepts.title: The Peptide Bond
concepts.content: A peptide bond is the amide linkage formed between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the alpha-amino group of the next, with the loss of a water molecule; repeating this links residues into a polypeptide. The N-C-C backbone runs from a free amino terminus, written first by convention, to a carboxyl terminus made last, and each unit in the chain is called a residue. Peptide-bond formation is thermodynamically unfavorable, so cells spend stored energy to drive it; once formed, the bond is kinetically stable because its hydrolysis has a high activation energy. Cleavage of peptide bonds by another protein is called proteolysis, carried out by proteases such as trypsin (which cuts on the carboxyl side of basic residues) and chymotrypsin (which cuts adjacent to large hydrophobic residues).

problems.prompt: Proopiomelanocortin (POMC) is 241 amino acids long and is synthesized from pre-POMC, which is 285 amino acids long. POMC is then cleaved to give rise to multiple peptide hormones (e.g., melanocyte-stimulating hormone, ACTH, and beta-endorphin). This means that POMC:
choices: is generated via proteolytic cleavage of a precursor molecule and contains 240 peptide bonds.
is hydrophilic in nature and must start with a sulfur-containing amino acid.
costs the cell approximately 950 high-energy bonds to synthesize.
is a protein with at least quaternary structure.

problems.prompt: In a transport study, patients were treated with a synthetic peptide hormone that is 191 residues long and made by the adenohypophysis (anterior pituitary). In intestinal brush border vesicles measured in a sodium buffer, the high-dose group showed increased transport of glutamine (Q) and arginine (R) but no change in alanine (A). The results support which conclusion?
choices: Insulin at a high dose increases intestinal absorption of glutamine and arginine.
Growth hormone at a high dose enhances the activity of system B amino acid transporter complexes.
Insulin at a high dose enhances the activity of system B and system Y amino acid transporter complexes.
Growth hormone at a high dose increases intestinal absorption of glutamine and arginine.

concepts.title: The Disulfide Bond
concepts.content: The thiol (-SH) side chain of one cysteine can be oxidized together with that of another cysteine to form a covalent sulfur-sulfur bond called a disulfide bond, and the paired residue is then called cystine. The two cysteines may lie in the same chain or in different polypeptide chains, and the bridge helps stabilize higher-order (tertiary and quaternary) protein structure. Because forming the bond removes hydrogen atoms, disulfide formation is an oxidation, so disulfide bridges form under oxidizing conditions. The reducing interior of cells keeps most cytoplasmic cysteines reduced, so disulfide bridges are found mainly in extracellular proteins such as antibodies and insulin.

concepts.title: Primary (1°) Structure: The Amino Acid Sequence
concepts.content: Primary structure is the linear order of amino acid residues in a polypeptide, i.e., its sequence, and it is set by the peptide bonds that covalently join one residue to the next. From this sequence a protein folds into a unique three-dimensional shape through four hierarchical levels of structure, and a protein that is folded incorrectly, or denatured, is nonfunctional. Denaturation is the disruption of a protein's shape without breaking peptide bonds, so primary structure is preserved; it can be caused by urea (which breaks hydrogen bonds), by extremes of pH or temperature, and by changes in salt concentration.

concepts.title: Secondary (2°) Structure: Hydrogen Bonds Between Backbone Groups
concepts.content: Secondary structure is the local folding of the backbone into regular motifs stabilized by hydrogen bonds between backbone N-H and C=O groups, the two most common being the alpha-helix and the beta-pleated sheet. The alpha-helix is a right-handed coil with about 3.6 residues per turn, in which each backbone carbonyl oxygen hydrogen-bonds to an amide proton roughly four residues away; because these motifs satisfy the polar backbone with internal hydrogen bonds, alpha-helices make good hydrophobic transmembrane segments. Proline is a helix breaker: forming a peptide bond to proline removes its only backbone N-H, and its rigid ring kinks the chain, so proline is essentially never found within an alpha-helix. In a beta-pleated sheet the backbone is extended rather than coiled, with hydrogen bonds between strands that may be far apart in the sequence or on separate chains, arranged either parallel or antiparallel.

problems.prompt: Which of the following amino acids would be LEAST helpful in the formation of an alpha-helix?

The protein presenilin 1 requires cyclophilin B to fold properly. A missense mutation P246L (a proline replaced by leucine at position 246) alters the recognition site for cyclophilin B, giving a dysfunctional protein. Which of the following structures would you most expect to be disturbed in the mutant presenilin 1?

concepts.title: Tertiary (3°) Structure: Hydrophobic/Hydrophilic Interactions
concepts.content: Tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional shape a single polypeptide adopts through interactions among side chains that may be far apart in the sequence, including van der Waals contacts between nonpolar groups, hydrogen bonds between polar groups, disulfide bonds between cysteines, and electrostatic interactions between acidic and basic side chains. The main driving force is the hydrophobic effect: nonpolar R-groups fold into the protein's interior away from water while hydrophilic R-groups face the aqueous surface. Under the right conditions a polypeptide folds spontaneously into its lowest-energy, functional conformation, as shown by Anfinsen's classic ribonuclease experiments, and this correct folding is what lets the protein do its job, such as forming a working enzyme active site or transporter.

problems.prompt: Researchers hypothesized that integrin-linked kinase (ILK) phosphorylates GSK3. In Western blots, phospho-GSK3 rose with growth-factor treatment in both JV32 cells (which express ILK) and NA13 cells (which lack ILK); the blots did not measure total GSK3. Is the hypothesis supported by these data?
choices: Yes; in both JV32 and NA13, phospho-GSK3 levels increased with growth factor treatment, while DK5 cells had low phospho-GSK3.
No; if ILK is the only protein phosphorylating GSK3, phospho-GSK3 should increase in JV32 cells with growth factor but should not increase in NA13 cells.
No; there is no way to determine the effect of ILK on GSK3 phosphorylation, since the researchers did not show whether the total amount of GSK3 changed with growth factor treatment.
No; the researchers cannot determine the effect of ILK on GSK3 without knowing how phospho-GSK3 changes in DK5 cells after growth factor treatment.

problems.prompt: A collaborating lab reports that in sympathetic neurons ILK phosphorylates GSK3, decreasing GSK3 activity and thereby promoting dendrite initiation and growth. Which findings would support this conclusion? I. Pharmacologically inhibiting ILK activity in cultured sympathetic neurons reduces dendrite formation. II. Expressing a dominant negative GSK3 allele causes robust dendrite initiation. III. Genetic knockdown of GSK3 promotes dendrite initiation even when ILK is simultaneously inhibited.

In the ILK Western blot experiment, blots were quantified and normalized to a housekeeping protein (beta-actin), and protease inhibitors were included in every lysis buffer. Based on this, which statement is true?
choices: Total MLC levels also increase with exposure to growth factor in DK5 cells.
S473 is phosphorylated by ILK only in kidney proximal tubule epithelial cells.
Each lane of the Western blot contained the same amount of beta-actin, indicating equal amounts of each lysate were used.
The variation in the total MLC blot could be due to protein degradation of some lysate samples but not others.

problems.prompt: Both enterocytes (intestinal cells) and hepatocytes (liver cells) express a Na+/H+ antiporter and ion-dependent transporters. Amino acid transport was high in sodium-rich buffers but much lower in a potassium-rich buffer. Which of the following is true of both enterocyte and hepatocyte amino acid transporter complexes?
choices: High dose groups show elevated transport of nonpolar neutral amino acids.
Amino acid transport is coupled to sodium ion transport.
System Y amino acid transporters are sensitive to hormone treatment.
Glucose transport is high in the presence of sodium but not potassium.

concepts.title: Quaternary (4°) Structure: Various Bonds Between Separate Chains
concepts.content: Quaternary structure describes how two or more separate polypeptide subunits assemble into a single multisubunit protein complex. It is stabilized by the same forces that hold tertiary structure together (van der Waals forces, hydrogen bonds, disulfide bonds, and electrostatic interactions) but never by the peptide bond, which instead defines each subunit's primary sequence. Interactions between subunits are often central to function and regulation, as in the cooperative, allosteric binding of oxygen by the four subunits of hemoglobin.

problems.prompt: During glycolysis, the production of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (an early intermediate) can increase pyruvate production by stimulating pyruvate kinase, the last enzyme of the pathway. This type of enzymatic regulation is an example of:

concepts.title: Monosaccharides and Disaccharides
concepts.content: A monosaccharide, or simple sugar, is a single carbohydrate unit with the general formula (CH2O)n; glucose, fructose, and ribose are common metabolically important examples. Two monosaccharides join through a glycosidic linkage, a covalent bond formed in an enzyme-catalyzed dehydration reaction, to make a disaccharide (a few units form an oligosaccharide and many form a polysaccharide). A glycosidic bond is named by the carbons it connects and by whether the anomeric configuration is alpha or beta; for example, lactose is a galactose-beta-1,4-glucose linkage while sucrose is a glucose-alpha-1,2-fructose linkage. Common MCAT disaccharides include sucrose (Glc-a-1,2-Fru), lactose (Gal-b-1,4-Glc), maltose (Glc-a-1,4-Glc), and cellobiose (Glc-b-1,4-Glc).

concepts.title: Polysaccharides
concepts.content: Polysaccharides are large polymers of monosaccharides that serve important biological roles. Glycogen is the energy-storage carbohydrate of animals, made of thousands of glucose units joined by alpha-1,4 linkages with alpha-1,6 branches; starch is essentially the same molecule (with slightly different branching) used for storage in plants. Cellulose is a polymer of cellobiose whose beta-glycosidic bonds let it adopt a long, straight, fibrous shape, and it makes up wood and cotton. Hydrolysis of polysaccharides into monosaccharides is thermodynamically favored but requires specific enzymes named for the sugar they cleave, such as maltase; mammals generally cannot break the beta-glycosidic bonds of cellulose, and humans digest lactose only because they make the enzyme lactase.

concepts.title: Introduction to Cellular Respiration
concepts.content: When glucose is oxidized to release energy, very little ATP is made directly; instead the oxidation is coupled to reduction of the high-energy electron carriers NAD+ and FAD, forming NADH and FADH2. Glucose is oxidized to CO2 and ATP in a four-stage process: glycolysis, the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC), the Krebs cycle, and electron transport/oxidative phosphorylation. Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules without using oxygen, while the PDC and Krebs cycle occur in the mitochondrial matrix. Although the PDC and Krebs cycle can proceed only when oxygen is available, they do not use it directly; oxygen is consumed only in the fourth stage, where the reduced carriers are reoxidized and the energy released is used to make ATP.

problems.prompt: What is the most likely value for the equilibrium constant for the combustion of glucose?
choices: Unable to determine from the information provided

problems.prompt: Consider these two reactions and their standard free energy changes. Reaction 1: Glucose-6-phosphate -> Glucose + Inorganic Phosphate, delta-G = -13.9 kJ/mol. Reaction 2: ADP + Inorganic Phosphate -> ATP, delta-G = +30.5 kJ/mol. Which of the following reactions results in the largest liberation of free energy?
choices: Glucose-6-phosphate + ATP -> Glucose + 2 Inorganic Phosphate + ADP

problems.prompt: Which of the following is produced by all the cellular respiration pathways (glycolysis, the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, and the Krebs cycle), but NOT by the electron transport chain?

concepts.title: Glycolysis
concepts.content: Glycolysis is the universal first step of glucose metabolism, present in all cells, and it splits one glucose into two pyruvate molecules in the cytoplasm without requiring oxygen. The net yield per glucose is 2 ATP (formed from ADP + Pi) and 2 NADH (formed from NAD+), although 2 ATP must first be invested to phosphorylate glucose to glucose-6-phosphate and then fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. Hexokinase catalyzes the first step and is feedback-inhibited by its product, glucose-6-phosphate. Phosphofructokinase (PFK) catalyzes the committed step, the essentially irreversible conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, and it is the key regulatory valve of the pathway, allosterically inhibited by high ATP.

problems.prompt: If a yeast culture is treated with 2-deoxyglucose (an inhibitor of glycolysis), which of the following is the most likely result?

concepts.title: Fermentation
concepts.content: Under aerobic conditions the pyruvate from glycolysis is fully oxidized in the PDC and Krebs cycle, and the resulting NADH and FADH2 are reoxidized by the electron transport chain, where oxygen is the final electron acceptor. Under anaerobic conditions the electron transport chain cannot run, so the cell's limited NAD+ is quickly converted to NADH, which would halt glycolysis because glycolysis requires NAD+. Fermentation regenerates NAD+ by using pyruvate as the acceptor of the high-energy electrons carried by NADH, allowing glycolysis to continue without oxygen. Examples include the reduction of pyruvate to ethanol by yeast and to lactate in human muscle cells; the ethanol or lactate accumulates and becomes toxic at high concentrations.

problems.prompt: A patient presenting to the emergency room with shortness of breath and a headache is diagnosed with acute carbon monoxide poisoning. What best describes glucose metabolism in this patient's cells?
choices: Increased activity of the electron transport chain

concepts.title: The Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex
concepts.content: The pyruvate produced by glycolysis is transported into the mitochondrial matrix, where it is oxidatively decarboxylated by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) rather than entering the Krebs cycle directly. In this reaction pyruvate, a 3-carbon molecule, loses one carbon as CO2 and is oxidized to a 2-carbon acetyl unit while NAD+ is reduced to NADH. The acetyl group is attached to coenzyme A (CoA-SH) through a high-energy thioester bond, forming acetyl-CoA, which readily transfers the acetyl fragment into the Krebs cycle for further oxidation. Regulation of the PDC is crucial; a low energy charge, such as a high level of AMP, stimulates it and speeds the entry of pyruvate into the Krebs cycle.

concepts.title: The Krebs Cycle
concepts.content: The Krebs cycle, also called the citric acid cycle or the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, takes the 2-carbon acetyl unit from acetyl-CoA, condenses it with 4-carbon oxaloacetate to form citrate, and then releases two CO2 molecules while regenerating oxaloacetate so the cycle can continue. Each turn stores reducing power along with a high-energy phosphate, so per glucose (two turns) the cycle yields 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, and 2 GTP. The GTP is made by substrate-level phosphorylation and can transfer its high-energy phosphate to ADP to form ATP. Most of the captured energy is held in the NADH and FADH2, which go on to drive ATP production in electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation.

problems.prompt: During the Krebs cycle, one mole of glucose will result in the generation of how many ATP equivalents via substrate-level phosphorylation?

concepts.title: Compartmentalization of Glucose Catabolism in Eukaryotes: The Mitochondria
concepts.content: To understand oxidative phosphorylation you must know the structure of the mitochondrion, which has two lipid-bilayer membranes. The outer membrane is smooth and studded with large pores formed by porin proteins, while the inner membrane is impermeable even to small ions like H+ and is densely folded into cristae. The innermost space enclosed by the inner membrane is the matrix, and the intermembrane space between the two membranes is continuous with the cytoplasm through the outer-membrane pores. The enzymes of the Krebs cycle and the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex sit in the matrix, whereas the electron transport chain and ATP synthase are bound to the inner membrane. Because glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm, the electrons of its NADH must be shuttled into the mitochondrion to reach the electron transport chain, while the NADH and FADH2 made in the matrix are already correctly positioned.

concepts.title: Electron Transport and Oxidative Phosphorylation
concepts.content: Oxidative phosphorylation couples the oxidation of NADH and FADH2 by the electron transport chain, a set of carriers embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane, to the phosphorylation of ADP into ATP. As electrons pass down the chain, three large membrane complexes pump protons out of the matrix into the intermembrane space, building a proton gradient, and oxygen is reduced to water as the final electron acceptor. The protons flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase, and the energy of this flow drives ATP synthesis. Because NADH enters at the first complex (NADH dehydrogenase) it yields about 2.5 ATP, whereas FADH2 enters later at ubiquinone and yields about 1.5 ATP, giving a theoretical total of roughly 30 to 32 ATP per glucose.

problems.prompt: In a newly discovered fungus, an unknown protein is isolated that has a localization sequence directing it to the inner mitochondrial membrane. When this gene is knocked out, the cell appears to be capable of metabolizing FADH2; however, products of fermentation rapidly begin to accumulate. What is the most likely identity of this protein?

concepts.title: Gluconeogenesis
concepts.content: Gluconeogenesis makes glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors such as lactate, pyruvate, Krebs cycle intermediates, and the carbon skeletons of most amino acids, occurring mainly in the liver (and to a lesser extent the kidneys) when dietary glucose and glycogen stores are depleted. It is essentially glycolysis run in reverse, using many of the same enzymes, but the three irreversible glycolytic steps (catalyzed by hexokinase, phosphofructokinase, and pyruvate kinase) must be bypassed by different enzymes. Pyruvate carboxylase first adds CO2 to pyruvate to form oxaloacetate, and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK) then decarboxylates and phosphorylates it to phosphoenolpyruvate; further along, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase remove the phosphates. Dephosphorylation of glucose-6-phosphate is required to release free glucose from liver cells into the blood, and note that acetyl-CoA cannot be converted into glucose.

problems.prompt: In a study of the invertebrate Caenorhabditis elegans, glycolysis was inhibited by RNAi against phosphofructokinase (pfk) and pyruvate kinase (pyk-2), and gluconeogenesis was inhibited by RNAi against fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (fbp-1) and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (pck-2). Median lifespan was measured as percent survival over a 40-day period, shown in Figure 2 for each RNAi treatment versus empty vector control. According to the data in Figure 2, which of the following is most accurate?
choices: Glycolytic inhibition and gluconeogenic stimulation increase median lifespan.
Glycolytic inhibition increases median lifespan while gluconeogenic inhibition decreases median lifespan.
Glycolytic stimulation and gluconeogenic inhibition increase median lifespan.
Glycolytic inhibition decreases median lifespan while gluconeogenic inhibition increases median lifespan.

problems.prompt: In a study of Caenorhabditis elegans, glycolysis was inhibited by RNAi against phosphofructokinase (pfk) and pyruvate kinase (pyk-2), and gluconeogenesis was inhibited by RNAi against fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (fbp-1) and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (pck-2). Locomotory capacity was measured as the number of head thrashes in a 30-second period at 10 and 15 days of life (Figure 1); age-1(RNAi) is a positive control known to extend locomotory ability. Based on Figure 1, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
choices: Inhibition of glycolysis increased the locomotory capacity of C. elegans at both 10 and 15 days.
age-1(RNAi) increased locomotory capacity of C. elegans at 15 days but not at 10 days.
Inhibition of gluconeogenesis decreased the locomotory capacity of C. elegans at both 10 and 15 days.
General locomotory capacity of C. elegans decreased from 10 to 15 days.

problems.prompt: In a study, PCK-2 is identified as phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK), a gluconeogenic enzyme. Which of the following is true regarding the effect of PCK-2 in humans?

In a C. elegans study, dietary restriction increases levels of DAF-16, a transcription factor that promotes longevity, and increased DAF-16 leads to increased levels of the gluconeogenic enzyme PCK-2. Investigators next measured the transcriptional activity of DAF-16 by quantifying SOD-4::GFP, a direct transcriptional target of DAF-16. Based on information in the passage, what result might investigators expect?
choices: Increased levels of SOD-4::GFP correspond to increased gluconeogenic activity.
Increased levels of SOD-4::GFP correspond to decreased fatty acid catabolism.
Increased levels of SOD-4::GFP correspond to increased blood glucose.
Increased levels of SOD-4::GFP correspond to increased glycolytic activity.

problems.prompt: In a C. elegans study, inhibiting glycolysis (via pfk and pyk-2 RNAi) increased both locomotory capacity and lifespan, whereas inhibiting gluconeogenesis (via fbp-1 and pck-2 RNAi) decreased both. Dietary restriction is known to decrease glycolytic activity and increase gluconeogenic activity. Based on this, dietary restriction could:
choices: decrease gluconeogenic activity, decrease locomotory capacity, and decrease longevity.
decrease glycolytic activity, decrease locomotory capacity, and decrease longevity.
increase gluconeogenic activity, increase locomotory capacity, and increase longevity.
increase glycolytic activity, increase locomotory capacity, and increase longevity.

concepts.title: Regulation of Glycolysis and Gluconeogenesis
concepts.content: Because glycolysis and gluconeogenesis serve opposing roles, they must be regulated reciprocally to avoid futile cycling, in which the same molecule activates one pathway's enzyme while inhibiting the other's. The two key regulated enzymes are phosphofructokinase (PFK) for glycolysis and fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase for gluconeogenesis; for example, in an energy-starved state high AMP activates PFK and inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase. Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate exerts similar reciprocal control, stimulating PFK and inhibiting fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, and its level is set hormonally: insulin (released when blood glucose is high) raises it to favor glycolysis, while glucagon (released when blood glucose is low) lowers it to favor gluconeogenesis. In general, enzymes catalyzing irreversible steps are the sites of regulation, rising levels of a pathway's intermediates tend to slow it, and cellular respiration is stimulated by energy deficits and inhibited by energy surpluses.

problems.prompt: A side effect of an investigational medication causes fatty acid beta-oxidation to be favored in cells exposed to the drug. What aspect of metabolism is most likely to be directly impacted in treated cells?
choices: Stimulation of phosphofructokinase, inhibition of PEP carboxykinase
Stimulation of glycogen phosphorylase, inhibition of phosphoglucomutase
Stimulation of ATP synthase, inhibition of hexokinase
Stimulation of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, inhibition of phosphofructokinase

problems.prompt: In a study, subjects consumed preload meals sweetened with aspartame, stevia, or sucrose, and their post-prandial plasma glucose (Figure 2) and plasma insulin (Figure 3) were measured over time. The insulinogenic index is defined as the change in insulin divided by the change in glucose (delta insulin / delta glucose) at 30 to 60 minutes post-load. Based on Figures 2 and 3, which conclusion about the insulinogenic index between 30 and 60 minutes after lunch is the most likely?
choices: Aspartame has a higher insulinogenic index than sucrose.
Stevia has a lower insulinogenic index than sucrose.
Aspartame has a lower insulinogenic index than sucrose.
Stevia has a higher insulinogenic index than sucrose.

problems.prompt: In a study comparing preload meals sweetened with aspartame, stevia, or sucrose, stevia consistently produced the lowest post-prandial blood glucose and insulin levels, and the artificial sweeteners lowered total caloric intake for the same level of satiety and satisfaction. Assuming these results can be externally validated in participants' dietary routines at home, which of the following outcomes would be most likely over the long term?
choices: Supplementation with aspartame would decrease incidence of type 2 diabetes mellitus.
Supplementation with stevia would decrease incidence of type 2 diabetes mellitus.
Supplementation with stevia would increase incidence of obesity.

problems.prompt: Which of the following statements best describes the mechanism by which insulin decreases blood glucose levels?
choices: Insulin binds directly to individual molecules of glucose in the bloodstream, facilitating uptake.
Insulin passes easily through the lipophilic cell membrane and travels to the nucleus, where it upregulates the synthesis of glucose transporter proteins.
Insulin binds to the extracellular portion of the insulin receptor, triggering an intracellular cascade that increases expression of glucose transporters on the cell surface.
Insulin binds to a receptor in the brain, leading to increased autonomic nervous system activity and, thus, cellular respiration.

concepts.title: Glycogen Metabolism
concepts.content: Glycogen is a branched glucose polymer stored in liver and muscle and is the main form of carbohydrate storage in animals. Glycogenesis begins with glucose-6-phosphate, which phosphoglucomutase reversibly isomerizes to glucose-1-phosphate; this is activated with UTP to form UDP-glucose, which glycogen synthase then adds to the growing polymer. Glycogenolysis removes glucose units from the polymer as glucose-1-phosphate, which is converted to glucose-6-phosphate and can reenter glycolysis. Insulin stimulates glycogenesis when blood glucose is high, while glucagon triggers glycogenolysis when blood glucose is low; the liver has glucose-6-phosphatase to release free glucose into the blood, but skeletal muscle lacks this enzyme, so its glucose stays phosphorylated and trapped for local use.

problems.prompt: Glucagon has what impact on glucose metabolism?
choices: Increased glucose uptake from the bloodstream

problems.prompt: In an experiment, hexokinase is exposed to an inhibitor such that feedback inhibition on the enzyme no longer occurs. Which reaction is most likely to be favored in this situation?
choices: Conversion of glucose-6-phosphate to glucose-1-phosphate by phosphoglucomutase
Conversion of glucose-6-phosphate to glucose by hexokinase
Conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate by pyruvate carboxylase
Conversion of glycogen to glucose-1-phosphate by glycogen phosphorylase

problems.prompt: The rate of which of the following biochemical processes would increase with increasing insulin secretion?

concepts.title: Pentose Phosphate Pathway
concepts.content: The pentose phosphate pathway (also called the hexose monophosphate shunt) diverts glucose-6-phosphate out of glycolysis to make NADPH, ribose-5-phosphate, and glycolytic intermediates. It consists of an irreversible oxidative phase that generates NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate, followed by a reversible non-oxidative phase that produces the glycolytic intermediates. NADPH serves as a reducing agent for anabolic processes such as fatty acid synthesis and helps neutralize reactive oxygen species, while ribose-5-phosphate is used to build nucleotides. The cytoplasmic pathway is controlled at its first enzyme, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PDH), which is feedback-inhibited by its product NADPH; G6PDH deficiency is a common inherited disorder that limits red blood cells' ability to eliminate reactive oxygen species.

problems.prompt: What cellular need provides the most consistent reason to stimulate the pentose phosphate pathway?
choices: Production of nucleotides to be used in mismatch repair
Increased demand for glycolytic intermediates during times of stress
Exposure to reactive oxygen species as part of cellular respiration

concepts.title: Introduction to Lipids
concepts.content: Lipids are oily or fatty substances whose defining property is hydrophobicity, since their carbon-carbon and carbon-hydrogen bonds are nonpolar and do not dissolve in water. They fill three main physiological roles: triacylglycerols store energy in adipose cells, phospholipids form the barrier of cell membranes, and cholesterol is the building block for steroid hormones. Fatty acids are long, unsubstituted alkane chains ending in a carboxylic acid, typically 14 to 18 carbons long and usually even-numbered because they are built two carbons at a time from acetate. A saturated fatty acid has no carbon-carbon double bonds and thus the maximum number of hydrogens, whereas an unsaturated fatty acid has one or more double bonds that are almost always cis (Z). When placed in water, free fatty acids cluster into a micelle in which the hydrophobic tails hide in the center and the polar carboxyl heads face the water, a process driven by the hydrophobic interaction.

concepts.title: Triacylglycerols
concepts.content: The storage form of fatty acids is fat, technically a triacylglycerol (triglyceride), which consists of three fatty acids esterified to the three hydroxyl groups of glycerol, a three-carbon triol. Storing fatty acids as relatively inert fat is necessary because free fatty acids are reactive chemicals. Triacylglycerols undergo the reactions typical of esters, including base-catalyzed hydrolysis; saponification is the base-catalyzed hydrolysis of triglycerides into glycerol and fatty acid salts (soaps), which are amphipathic sodium salts of fatty acids. Lipases are the enzymes that hydrolyze fats. Fats are more efficient energy-storage molecules than carbohydrates for two reasons: their hydrophobicity lets them pack together tightly without carrying water of solvation, and because they are more reduced they store more energy per carbon.

problems.prompt: What are the components of lipids that are stored in the body as a potential source of energy?
choices: Glycerol backbone, three fatty acid chains, required to have equivalent R groups
Glycerol backbone, two fatty acid chains, four isoprene units
Glycerol backbone, three fatty acid chains, possibly equivalent R groups
Glycerol backbone, two fatty acid chains, one phosphate group

problems.prompt: During sphingomyelin synthesis, diacylglycerol is produced as a side-product, and the enzyme diglyceride acyltransferase can convert diacylglycerol (a glycerol bearing two fatty acids) into triacylglycerol by attaching a third fatty acid. The reaction catalyzed by diglyceride acyltransferase involves the formation of:

concepts.title: Phospholipids and Lipid Bilayer Membranes
concepts.content: Membrane lipids are phospholipids, derived from diacylglycerol phosphate, whose phosphate group often carries a larger polar molecule such as choline, ethanolamine, or inositol. Like fatty acids, phospholipids minimize contact with water, but they do so by forming a lipid bilayer that is driven by hydrophobic interactions and then stabilized by van der Waals forces between the long tails. Three structural factors set membrane fluidity: the degree of saturation, the length of the fatty acid tails, and the amount of cholesterol. Unsaturation (cis double bonds) and shorter tails both increase fluidity by disrupting the orderly packing of the tails. Cholesterol keeps fluidity at an optimum, acting as a membrane antifreeze that raises fluidity at low temperatures but reduces it at high temperatures.

problems.prompt: Phospholipids are the main structural component of biological membranes. In cerebral ischemia (insufficient blood flow to the brain), phospholipases can be activated, changing membrane phospholipid composition. Mass spectrometry (MALDI-IMS) of phospholipids from normal versus ischemic brain tissue produced spectra with the same set of peaks (same m/z values) but with different peak heights (intensities). Which of the following describes how neuronal cell membranes change in response to ischemia?
choices: Cells express a different set of phospholipids.
Cells express the same phospholipids at the same relative proportions.
Cells express the same phospholipids but in different relative proportions.
Cells express phospholipids along the length of the long axon process.

problems.prompt: Cerebral ischemia is a condition of insufficient blood flow to the brain, so affected cells receive little oxygen; it can also activate phospholipases that change membrane phospholipid composition. Which of the following is LEAST likely to be an effect of ischemic injury?
choices: Upregulation of citrate synthase and isocitrate dehydrogenase

problems.prompt: In phospholipid synthesis, glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase reduces DHAP (a glycolytic intermediate) to glycerol-3-phosphate, and glycerol-3-phosphate O-acyltransferase then adds an acyl group to glycerol-3-phosphate to form lysophosphatidic acid (which is later converted to phosphatidic acid). What would be the effect of a hyper-activating mutation in glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and an inactivating mutation in glycerol-3-phosphate O-acyltransferase, respectively?
choices: Elevated levels of glycerol-3-phosphate and decreased levels of lysophosphatidic acid
Elevated levels of DHAP and elevated levels of phosphatidic acid
Elevated levels of glycerol-3-phosphate and elevated levels of phosphatidic acid

problems.prompt: In this study, phospholipids were isolated from cerebral (cerebrum) tissue collected from rats. In order to collect these brain samples, which of the following steps would NOT be required?
choices: Penetrate three membranes of connective tissue (dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater)
Isolation of the cerebellum, which is located posterior to the pons

problems.prompt: Recall from the passage that phospholipids were analyzed from cerebral tissue, that adipocytes have a higher mass ratio of phospholipids than all other cells, and that DHAP (a glycolytic intermediate) can be reduced to a phospholipid precursor. Which of the following statements is best supported by information in the passage?
choices: The experimental samples contained at least two cell types.
Neurons have the highest concentration of phospholipids.
The activities of glycerol kinase and 1-acylglycerol-3-phosphate O-acyltransferase require ATP.
There are no first-order connections between carbohydrate and lipid metabolic pathways.

concepts.title: Terpenes and Steroids
concepts.content: Terpenes are a broad class of compounds built from isoprene units (C5H8) with the general formula (C5H8)n; they may be linear or cyclic and are classified by how many isoprene units they contain, so a monoterpene has two, a sesquiterpene three, and a diterpene four. Squalene is a triterpene of six isoprene units that the body uses to build steroids, and functionalized terpenes such as vitamin A are called terpenoids. Steroids are grouped with lipids because of their hydrophobicity, and all share the tetracyclic ring system based on cholesterol. Cholesterol is both obtained from the diet and made in the liver, is an important component of the lipid bilayer, and is carried in the blood packaged into lipoproteins, one of which is implicated in atherosclerotic plaques. Steroid hormones such as testosterone and estrogen are made from cholesterol and, being highly hydrophobic, diffuse through the membrane to reach receptors located inside the cell, unlike peptide hormones that bind receptors at the cell surface.

problems.prompt: Taxadiene is a diterpene and a precursor to taxol, a common drug used to treat breast, lung, pancreatic, and ovarian cancers. How many isoprene units would be found in taxadiene?
All of the following statements about cholesterol are true EXCEPT that it:
choices: is the precursor for testosterone, estrogen, and progesterone.
is used by the liver to produce bile.
is the precursor for the fat-soluble vitamins A and D.
helps to maintain optimal membrane fluidity.

concepts.title: Other Lipids
concepts.content: Beyond the main lipid families, several other lipids appear on the MCAT. Sphingolipids resemble phospholipids but are built on a sphingosine backbone instead of glycerol; the main human example is sphingomyelin, a component of the myelin sheath around neurons. Waxes are long-chain fatty acids esterified to long-chain alcohols, making them extremely hydrophobic and useful as waterproof barriers. The four fat-soluble vitamins, A, D, E, and K, are absorbed with dietary fat and stored in adipose tissue and the liver: A is a terpenoid needed for vision, D is derived from cholesterol and regulates calcium and phosphate, E is a group of antioxidant tocopherols, and K is a coenzyme for activating clotting proteins. Prostaglandins are eicosanoids made from 20-carbon fatty acids that act through diverse receptors to regulate functions such as smooth muscle contraction, blood vessel diameter, and gastric protection.

problems.prompt: A patient presents with musculoskeletal issues, and laboratory tests confirm low levels of vitamin D in the person's blood. A supplement is recommended, but despite daily consumption, the patient's vitamin D levels do not increase in subsequent testing. What is the most likely cause of this outcome?
choices: The patient is consuming too little dietary fiber with the supplement.
The patient is not consuming dietary fats along with the supplement.
The patient is also taking oral contraceptives.
The patient is spending more time outdoors.

problems.prompt: Sphingomyelin can be broken down by sphingomyelinases into two components: phosphocholine, a charged polar head group, and ceramide, which consists of sphingosine linked to a fatty acid and is largely hydrophobic. One of these components diffuses through the cell membrane and participates in the apoptotic signaling pathway. The component that most likely participates in the apoptotic signaling pathway is:
choices: phosphocholine, because its size relative to ceramide allows it to diffuse through the cell membrane more easily.
phosphocholine, because its polarity relative to ceramide allows it to diffuse through the cell membrane more easily.
ceramide, because its size relative to phosphocholine allows it to diffuse through the cell membrane more easily.
ceramide, because its polarity relative to phosphocholine allows it to diffuse through the cell membrane more easily.

Increased leakage of Na+ into the extracellular fluid following an action potential. III. Decrease in maximum membrane potential during depolarization.

In an experiment, ASM activity was measured after transfecting cells with cDNA constructs (made by reverse-transcribing already-spliced mRNA, so introns are absent) that had been altered by site-directed mutagenesis. Suppose that instead of the cDNA constructs, wild-type genomic DNA constructs (which still contain introns) were mutated at the same physical nucleotide site as in the cDNA constructs. How would the ASM activity of both constructs be affected?

Increase in ASM activity of both
Decrease in ASM activity of both

The construct C1460T showed ASM activity equal to 100% of wild-type (24,579 pmol/mg/h), whereas the construct C973G showed only 3% of wild-type activity (737 pmol/mg/h). Given that Niemann-Pick disease results from a build-up of sphingomyelin caused by decreased ASM activity, what is the most reasonable conclusion from these data?
choices: Only the mutation represented by construct C1460T could be responsible for symptoms of Niemann-Pick disease.
Only the mutation represented by construct C973G could be responsible for symptoms of Niemann-Pick disease.
Both mutations represented by the two constructs could be responsible for symptoms of Niemann-Pick disease.
Neither of the mutations represented by the two constructs could be responsible for symptoms of Niemann-Pick disease.

concepts.title: Fatty Acid Metabolism
concepts.content: In fatty acid oxidation, dietary triacylglycerols are hydrolyzed to free fatty acids, which are activated at the outer mitochondrial membrane by acyl-CoA synthetase at a cost of two ATP equivalents and then transported into the mitochondrion. Inside the matrix, beta-oxidation runs a repeated four-reaction cycle that cleaves the bond between the alpha and beta carbons, releasing one acetyl-CoA plus one FADH2 and one NADH each round, with the acetyl-CoA feeding the Krebs cycle. During starvation, when glycogen is exhausted and blood glucose falls, the liver instead converts acetyl-CoA into ketone bodies (acetone, acetoacetate, and beta-hydroxybutyrate) by ketogenesis; these cross the blood-brain barrier and are reconverted to acetyl-CoA for energy. The same overload of acetyl-CoA drives dangerous, acidic ketone production in untreated type I diabetes, causing diabetic ketoacidosis. Fatty acid synthesis mirrors oxidation in reverse but occurs in the cytoplasm, adding two-carbon units; its committed step is the ATP-dependent carboxylation of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA by acetyl-CoA carboxylase, and the reductions require NADPH supplied mainly by the pentose phosphate pathway.

problems.prompt: Fatty acid catabolism will cause which of the following:
choices: increased utilization of the malate-aspartate shuttle.

In humans, leucine and lysine are exclusively ketogenic. This means their alpha-keto acid carbon skeleton is degraded into acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate, an acetyl-CoA precursor. These amino acids can be:

converted to acetone, acetoacetate, or beta-hydroxybutyrate via ketogenesis, or enter gluconeogenesis to generate new glucose in the liver or kidney.

problems.prompt: Unsaturated fats produce less energy during beta-oxidation than saturated fats with an equal number of carbons. What is the primary difference leading to this lower level of production?
choices: The need to create a double bond within a saturated fat also generates FADH2.
The FADH2 generated by saturated fats stores more energy than those generated by processing unsaturated fats.
The number of NADH molecules produced by saturated fats is greater than for unsaturated fats.

problems.prompt: A Type I diabetic is admitted to the emergency department with rapid breathing, fruity breath, and confusion. Blood tests reveal very low blood insulin levels. Which of the following correctly explains the biochemical process happening within the patient?
choices: Ketones are being produced to supply the liver with energy; they are oxidized via glycolysis.
Ketones are being produced to supply the brain with energy; they are reduced via the Krebs cycle.
Ketones are being converted to acetyl-CoA and oxidized in the mitochondrial matrix to generate energy.
The patient has an abnormally high blood pH from a surge in ketoacids.

concepts.title: Phosphorus-Containing Compounds
concepts.content: Phosphoric acid is a triprotic inorganic acid (pKa values about 2.1, 7.2, and 12.4), so at physiological pH it is largely dissociated, existing mostly as hydrogen phosphate (HPO4^2-) and dihydrogen phosphate (H2PO4^-). Two orthophosphates joined by an anhydride linkage form pyrophosphate, whose P-O-P bond is a high-energy phosphate bond because its hydrolysis is very favorable (about -7 kcal/mol at standard conditions, and even more negative inside the cell). Phosphoanhydride bonds store so much energy because the linked phosphates repel each other's negative charges, and free orthophosphate has more resonance forms and better interaction with water than the linked form. ATP is the universal short-term energy storage molecule: energy from oxidizing food is stored in its phosphoanhydride bonds and released to power cellular processes, while GTP and UTP fill similar but more specialized energy roles.

problems.prompt: Ribose 5-phosphate is converted into phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP) by the enzyme ribose-phosphate diphosphokinase, and PRPP can react with nitrogenous bases to generate purines. Which of the following is a true statement?
choices: Both ribose 5-phosphate and PRPP are hexose phosphates.
Ribose 5-phosphate contains one covalent phosphoester bond, while phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate contains two.
Adenosine monophosphate and cytidine monophosphate biosynthesis require PRPP.
The pentose phosphate pathway supports nucleotide biosynthesis primarily through generating NADPH, but secondarily by producing ribose 5-phosphate.

concepts.title: Nucleotides and Nitrogenous Bases
concepts.content: A nucleotide, the building block of nucleic acids, has three parts: a five-carbon sugar (deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA), a nitrogenous aromatic base, and one to three phosphate groups esterified to the 5' carbon of the sugar. The base attaches to the 1' carbon of the sugar through a beta-N-glycosidic linkage; a base plus sugar with no phosphate is a nucleoside (for example, adenine plus ribose gives adenosine). The bases are the purines adenine (A) and guanine (G), which have a fused double-ring structure, and the pyrimidines cytosine (C), thymine (T, in DNA), and uracil (U, in RNA), which have a single six-membered ring. Because the sugar-phosphate portion is invariant it is called the backbone, and the base is the only variable part, so the specificity of anything that binds a particular DNA sequence comes from interactions with the bases.

problems.prompt: NADH (shown) plays important roles in cell metabolism and is best described as a:
choices: dideoxynucleotide with a pyrimidine base and nicotinamide group.
dinucleotide with a pyrimidine base and nicotinamide group.
dideoxynucleotide with a purine base and nicotinamide group.
dinucleotide with a purine base and nicotinamide group.

concepts.title: Polynucleotides and the Sugar-Phosphate Backbone
concepts.content: Nucleotides are joined into a chain by phosphodiester bonds that link the 3' hydroxyl of one sugar to the 5' phosphate of the next. Polymerizing nucleoside triphosphates is thermodynamically favorable because pyrophosphate is hydrolyzed and released as each nucleotide is added, driving the reaction forward. A few linked nucleotides form an oligonucleotide and many form a polynucleotide, and because only the base varies, a sequence can be abbreviated by simply listing its bases. By convention the sequence is written 5' to 3', with the end bearing a free 5' phosphate first and the end bearing a free 3' hydroxyl last.
