Of the following sources, which can damage DNA in a similar manner to that of zinc finger nucleases (that is, by causing double-stranded breaks)? I. UV radiation  II. X-ray radiation  III. Benzene

In an HIV zinc finger domain, two cysteine and two histidine residues coordinate a Zn2+ cation to stabilize the fold. The antiviral drug azodicarbonamide is electrophilic and disrupts this domain's folding. Since azodicarbonamide is electrophilic, it will most likely be reactive at the molecular level with which of the following components of the zinc finger domain?
choices: Valine side-chains within the zinc finger
Cysteine residues coordinating the zinc cation
Nitrogen lone-pairs within the peptide bonds of the peptide backbone

problems.prompt: Zinc-finger nucleases (ZFNs) damage DNA by causing double-stranded breaks. Which of the following is the most likely repair method for DNA damage caused by zinc finger nucleases?

concepts.title: The Watson-Crick Model of DNA Structure
concepts.content: In the Watson-Crick model, cellular DNA is a right-handed double helix in which two long polynucleotide strands run antiparallel, so the 5' end of one strand is paired with the 3' end of the other. The strands are held together by specific hydrogen bonds between bases: adenine always pairs with thymine (two H-bonds) and guanine always pairs with cytosine (three H-bonds), so every base pair is one purine plus one pyrimidine and every pair takes up the same width. This complementary pairing underlies Chargaff's rule ([A] = [T] and [G] = [C]) and keeps the helix a constant 20 angstroms wide, with bases stacked 3.4 angstroms apart and one full turn every 10 base pairs. Because each G-C pair has an extra hydrogen bond, GC-rich DNA is harder to pull apart, so the melting (denaturation) temperature Tm, the temperature at which half the DNA is melted, rises with GC content.

problems.prompt: When designing a protocol to perform polymerase chain reactions (PCR), temperatures for each stage of the cycle must be optimized based on the sequences involved. What would allow for the lowest melting temperatures in the cycle?
choices: Template sequences with a high level of guanine
Primers with a high level of cytosine
Primers with a high level of thymine
Template sequences with a high percentage of adenine

problems.prompt: The diameter of the DNA helix measures 20 A and is constant throughout the genome. What allows this measurement to remain the same?
choices: Pyrimidines consist of one ring, while purines consist of two rings.
The phosphodiester bonds in the backbone compress the aromatic bases.
Hydrogen bonding determines the diameter and the bonds are always the same length.
Pyrimidine dimers control the diameter of the DNA molecule.

problems.prompt: A zinc-finger nuclease (ZFN) combines one or more zinc finger domains, each of which binds a specific DNA sequence, with an endonuclease that cuts DNA. How will adding more zinc finger domains to a zinc finger nuclease complex likely impact the quantity of resulting fragments when mixed with DNA?
choices: No effect on number of fragments
Increase number of fragments only if DNA is palindromic

problems.prompt: Four strains of a (+)-single-stranded RNA virus are each reverse transcribed into dsDNA, and each DNA sample is then heated to separate the strands. Recall that a G-C base pair is held by three hydrogen bonds and an A-T base pair by two. Which initial viral sequence results in a dsDNA molecule with the most negative change in enthalpy during separation?

concepts.title: Chromosome Structure and Packing
concepts.content: An organism's complete genetic information is its genome; eukaryotes package their DNA into several linear chromosomes (humans have 46), while most prokaryotes carry a single circular chromosome. In bacteria the enzyme DNA gyrase uses the energy of ATP to twist the circular chromosome into supercoils that make it compact, whereas eukaryotic DNA is wound around octamers of histone proteins to form nucleosomes (a beads-on-a-string appearance) that stack into chromatin. Histones are mostly basic, being rich in arginine and lysine, so they are attracted to the acidic sugar-phosphate backbone, and the denser heterochromatin is transcriptionally quiet while looser euchromatin is actively transcribed. Centromeres are heterochromatic, repetitive regions where kinetochores anchor spindle fibers during cell division, and telomeres are guanine-rich repeated sequences that cap the ends of linear chromosomes to prevent deterioration and fusion, shortening with each round of division.

problems.prompt: Biological aging, or senescence, is the process by which molecular changes that disrupt metabolism accumulate in cells with time. All of the following would contribute to cellular senescence EXCEPT:
choices: mitotic debris divided unevenly among daughter cells.
persistence of mutations from errors in DNA synthesis during mitosis.
activation of the apoptotic pathway following a metabolic insult.
shortening of chromosomal telomeres with increasing divisions of the cell.

problems.prompt: The primary difference between euchromatin and heterochromatin is their accessibility for transcription: euchromatin is the accessible form ready for transcription, while heterochromatin is the less accessible form in which DNA is stored. Which of the following is the protein around which DNA is wrapped during storage?
A strain of Streptococcus is found to have a premature stop codon in the sequence for its DNA gyrase. What is the most likely effect this will have on the strain?
choices: The bacteria will not be able to remove primers.
The bacteria will not be able to compress its chromosome.
The bacteria will not be able to initiate replication.
The bacteria will not engage in DNA repair.

problems.prompt: Cells expressing an active transposon are being characterized. Which of the following would NOT be an experimental finding?
choices: The cells express an active transposase enzyme that facilitates transposon mobility.
Transposon integration into a target gene could turn gene expression on or off.
The transposon sequence is flanked by inverted repeats which allows mobilization.
Each transposon integration into the genome alters protein structure or function.

concepts.title: Characteristics of RNA
concepts.content: RNA differs chemically from DNA in three main ways: it is usually single-stranded (except in some viruses), it uses uracil in place of thymine, and its sugar is ribose rather than 2'-deoxyribose. The 2' hydroxyl makes RNA less stable, because it can nucleophilically attack the backbone phosphate and hydrolyze the chain, which is why high-quality RNA is much harder to extract and preserve than DNA. Messenger RNA (mRNA) is the only coding RNA and carries genetic information to the ribosome for translation; in eukaryotes it is first transcribed as hnRNA that must be capped, tailed, and spliced (with the help of snRNPs) to mature. The major non-coding RNAs are transfer RNA (tRNA), which brings amino acids to the ribosome and reads the genetic code, and ribosomal RNA (rRNA), which forms the bulk of the ribosome and provides its catalytic ribozyme activity.

problems.prompt: A substantial part of the information in the human genome does not lead to translation of functional proteins. The initial RNA transcript is hnRNA, which includes both introns (non-coding regions) and exons (protein-coding regions). Small nuclear ribonucleic particles (snRNPs) facilitate splicing, which involves removal of the introns and ligation of the exons. Which of the following is NOT a process by which splicing of introns and exons leads to unique mRNAs?

A researcher collects animal tissue, accidentally leaves it out at room temperature overnight, and the next day still isolates relatively high-quality DNA. A week later another researcher makes the same mistake but, when isolating RNA from the same tissue type, recovers only very low-quality RNA at an extremely low concentration. The difference in these two scenarios is most likely due to the fact that:
choices: RNA is more stable than DNA because it contains uracil and is single stranded.
DNA is more stable than RNA because DNA is double-stranded and its 2' OH group allows increased hydrogen bonding with the second strand.
RNA is less stable than DNA because it is single stranded and has a nucleophilic OH group on carbon 2 of ribose.
DNA is easier to handle and isolate than RNA.

concepts.title: Genome Structure and Genomic Variations
concepts.content: The human genome is about 3.2 billion base pairs spread across 24 different chromosomes (22 autosomes plus X and Y) and encodes roughly 21,000 genes. Gene-rich regions with high transcription rates are separated by long stretches of intergenic, noncoding DNA that may help organize chromatin or tune nearby genes. A gene includes both regulatory regions (such as promoters and stop sites) and a segment that codes for a protein or a noncoding RNA. Genomic variation takes several forms: single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs, roughly one changed base per 1,000), copy number variations (large duplicated or deleted regions), tandem repeats, and transposons. Tightly packed heterochromatin is largely untranscribed and rich in repeats, while loosely packed euchromatin is transcriptionally active and less repetitive.

problems.prompt: What type of DNA is LEAST likely to contain repeated sequences such as single nucleotide polymorphisms and tandem repeats?

concepts.title: The Role of DNA and the Genetic Code
concepts.content: Experiments by Avery (bacterial transformation) and by Hershey and Chase (phage infection) established that DNA, not protein, carries genetic information. The central dogma describes the one-way flow DNA -> RNA -> protein: transcription reads DNA into RNA, and translation builds protein from mRNA. The genetic code is read in three-nucleotide codons; with four bases there are 4^3 = 64 codons, 61 specifying amino acids and 3 serving as stop (nonsense) codons. The code is degenerate, meaning most amino acids are specified by more than one codon, yet unambiguous, because each codon specifies only a single amino acid. This lets a given mRNA be read in exactly one way.

problems.prompt: What is the nature of the relationship between an mRNA transcript and the amino acids that are determined by its codons?
choices: The relationship is ambiguous and bidirectional.
The relationship is ambiguous and degenerate.
The relationship is unambiguous and degenerate.
The relationship is unambiguous and bidirectional.

concepts.title: DNA Replication
concepts.content: Replication is semiconservative (shown by Meselson and Stahl): each daughter duplex keeps one parental strand and one newly made strand. It begins at a specific origin of replication, where helicase unwinds the double helix using ATP, topoisomerases relieve the resulting supercoiling, and single-strand binding proteins stabilize the exposed strands. Primase lays down short RNA primers because DNA polymerase can only extend an existing 3' end and cannot start a chain from scratch. Polymerization always runs 5' to 3', so the leading strand is made continuously into the fork while the lagging strand is made discontinuously as Okazaki fragments. The RNA primers are later replaced with DNA and the fragments joined by DNA ligase.

problems.prompt: The goal of an experimental procedure is to stop genome replication in tissue culture as early as possible, so researchers seek a chemical that targets the enzyme acting earliest in replication. Which enzyme would be the best target?

concepts.title: DNA Polymerases
concepts.content: Prokaryotes have five DNA polymerases, and the MCAT emphasizes I and III. DNA polymerase III performs the fast, highly accurate 5' to 3' elongation of the leading strand and has 3' to 5' exonuclease (proofreading) activity that removes a mismatched base right after it is added. DNA polymerase I starts synthesis at the RNA primer and, importantly, uses 5' to 3' exonuclease activity to remove those RNA primers while filling in DNA behind them; it also has 3' to 5' proofreading and works in excision repair. Because these enzymes can add tens of thousands of nucleotides before dissociating, they are described as processive. Losing a polymerase's 3' to 5' exonuclease activity raises the point-mutation rate because errors are no longer corrected.

problems.prompt: Growth of a bacterial culture stopped unexpectedly. Sequencing the genomes of the stalled colonies showed that RNA sequence was mixed into the DNA genome. Which enzyme has likely become disabled in these cells?

concepts.title: Prokaryotic vs. Eukaryotic Replication
concepts.content: A prokaryote has a single circular chromosome with a single origin, so its partially replicated genome takes on a shape resembling the Greek letter theta; this is called theta replication. Eukaryotic chromosomes are far larger and linear, so each has many origins that open into multiple replication bubbles in order to finish copying quickly. As the many forks widen and eventually meet, the daughter segments are ligated together. Eukaryotic replication is also more complex because the machinery must unwind DNA from histones, so the eukaryotic replisome contains many more proteins than the prokaryotic one.

concepts.title: Telomeres and Telomerase
concepts.content: Because DNA polymerase needs a primer and only builds 5' to 3', it cannot copy the very ends of a linear chromosome, so chromosomes shorten with each round of replication. Telomeres are disposable repeated sequences (in humans, repeats of TAGGG) that cap the ends and are consumed during division, shortening by roughly 50 to 200 base pairs each time. When telomeres become critically short, cells may enter senescence or undergo apoptosis; the Hayflick limit is the number of divisions a normal cell can complete before this happens. Telomerase, a ribonucleoprotein carrying reverse transcriptase activity and its own RNA template, rebuilds telomeres. It is normally active mainly in germ cells, embryonic stem cells, and some white blood cells, but cancer cells often reactivate it to become effectively immortal.

concepts.title: Genetic Mutation
concepts.content: A mutation is any change in the DNA sequence of an organism's genome. Germline mutations occur in the cells that give rise to gametes and can be passed to offspring, whereas somatic mutations occur in non-gametic cells and affect only the individual, not future generations. Mutations may arise spontaneously but are more often induced by mutagens. These include physical mutagens such as ionizing or ultraviolet radiation, chemical mutagens such as base analogs, and biological mutagens such as viruses or faulty DNA polymerases. Cells have evolved elaborate repair pathways to counter this damage.

concepts.title: Types of Mutations
concepts.content: Point mutations are single base substitutions, classed as transitions (purine for purine or pyrimidine for pyrimidine) or transversions (purine for pyrimidine or the reverse). A point mutation may be missense (changes one amino acid), nonsense (creates a premature stop codon), or silent (changes a codon but not the amino acid, exploiting the code's degeneracy). Insertions add nucleotides and deletions remove them; if the number added or removed is not a multiple of three, they cause a frameshift that scrambles every codon downstream and often introduces a premature stop. Frameshift mutations are generally very serious, while inserting or deleting whole codons changes the protein without shifting the reading frame.

concepts.title: Large-Scale Mutations and Transposons
concepts.content: Beyond single bases, larger rearrangements alter chromosomes. An inversion reverses a chromosome segment end to end, and amplification duplicates a segment (similar to copy number variation). Translocations move a segment onto a nonhomologous chromosome and can create a gene fusion, a frequent event in cancer; they may be balanced (no net loss) or unbalanced. Transposons are mobile elements that encode transposase, which cuts and pastes them into new locations, potentially disrupting a gene or altering nearby expression. Loss of heterozygosity occurs when one allele is lost by deletion or recombination, leaving the locus hemizygous, so a remaining defective allele is now fully expressed.

problems.prompt: An autosomal recessive disease presents in a child who has one homozygous dominant parent and one heterozygous parent. What type of mutation would make this expression possible?

concepts.title: DNA Repair
concepts.content: Before extensive damage triggers apoptosis, cells attempt several repair strategies. A few lesions are directly reversed, such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers fixed by photoreactivation in bacteria and plants. Homology-dependent pathways use the undamaged complementary strand: excision repair removes and replaces defective bases before replication, while mismatch repair corrects mispairs missed by proofreading, using strand methylation (in some bacteria) or gaps and free 3' ends to tell the new strand from the template. Double-strand breaks are repaired by homologous recombination, which uses a sister chromatid as an accurate template, or by nonhomologous end joining, which simply religates the ends and is error-prone. Faulty repair can produce deletions or translocations.

concepts.title: Characteristics and Types of RNA
concepts.content: RNA differs from DNA by being single-stranded, using uracil in place of thymine, and containing ribose rather than deoxyribose; its 2' hydroxyl makes RNA less chemically stable than DNA. Messenger RNA is the only coding RNA and carries a 5' untranslated region, an open reading frame running from a start codon to a stop codon, and a 3' untranslated region. Eukaryotic mRNA is usually monocistronic (one gene, one protein), whereas prokaryotic mRNA is often polycistronic, encoding several related polypeptides. Noncoding RNAs are not translated; the key examples are transfer RNA, which brings amino acids to the ribosome, and ribosomal RNA, which forms part of the ribosome and provides its catalytic (ribozyme) activity.

concepts.title: Transcription
concepts.content: Transcription synthesizes RNA from a DNA template and, like replication, is template-driven and runs 5' to 3', but RNA polymerase needs no primer and lacks proofreading, making it lower fidelity. Only one DNA strand, the template (antisense) strand, is read; the other, the coding (sense) strand, matches the transcript except that it carries T instead of U. The promoter is the sequence that positions RNA polymerase, and transcription begins at the start site (+1) and proceeds downstream. In bacteria a single RNA polymerase makes all RNA; its core enzyme needs a sigma factor to form the holoenzyme that recognizes promoters (the Pribnow box near -10 and the -35 sequence) during initiation, after which sigma leaves and the core elongates until it reaches a termination signal, sometimes aided by the protein rho.

problems.prompt: Which of the following is used to regulate prokaryotic transcription? I. Pribnow box; II. Promoters; III. TATA box

concepts.title: Eukaryotic RNA Processing
concepts.content: Prokaryotic transcription and translation occur together in the cytoplasm, and the primary transcript is already mRNA. Eukaryotes instead make a precursor called hnRNA in the nucleus that must be processed before export and translation. Splicing, carried out by the spliceosome (snRNPs built from protein and small nuclear RNA), removes noncoding introns and joins the coding exons; alternative splicing lets one gene yield several different mRNAs and proteins. A 5' methylguanine cap and a 3' poly-A tail are also added, protecting the transcript from exonucleases, with the cap additionally required for translation. Eukaryotes use several RNA polymerases: pol I makes most rRNA, pol II makes hnRNA (and thus mRNA), and pol III makes tRNA and other small RNAs.

concepts.title: Translation
concepts.content: Translation builds a polypeptide from the codon sequence of mRNA at the ribosome, which is made of rRNA and many proteins. Transfer RNAs have a cloverleaf structure with an anticodon that base-pairs with the mRNA codon and an amino acid acceptor site (always ending in CCA) that carries the matching amino acid; wobble allows some flexibility at the third codon position. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charge each tRNA with its correct amino acid in an ATP-requiring activation step. The ribosome reads mRNA 5' to 3', forming peptide bonds through initiation, elongation, and termination, and methionine (codon AUG, anticodon UAC) is always the first amino acid. Eukaryotes use 80S ribosomes (40S + 60S) and prokaryotes use 70S ribosomes (30S + 50S), and protein synthesis costs about 4 ATP-equivalents per amino acid added.

problems.prompt: In an experimental cell line, the tRNA with an anticodon sequence of UAC has a folding error that makes it nonfunctional 10% of the time. The UAC anticodon pairs with the AUG codon. What impact would this have on translation?
choices: Translation would proceed as normal because other tRNAs would take over the work of the nonfunctional copies.
The initiation of translation would be facilitated by an increased association with sigma factors.
Translation rates would be reduced because delivery of methionine to the ribosome would be curtailed.
The completion of translation would be impaired by a lost ability to recognize stop codons.

problems.prompt: Under what circumstances would a cell be likely to trigger cap-independent translation (a mechanism associated with conditions that may require apoptosis)? I. Dysregulated cell growth; II. Sustained anaerobic respiration; III. Viral infection
Fumarase is a 510-amino acid protein that functions both in the citric acid cycle and in cytosolic amino acid metabolism. In hepatocytes (liver cells, which are eukaryotic), this enzyme:
choices: would be translated in the nucleus after being transcribed in the cytoplasm.
is localized to both the mitochondria and the cytoplasm.
would require approximately 1,250 ATP-equivalents to translate.
is made by a 30S + 50S ribosome in the cytoplasm.

concepts.title: Controlling Gene Expression
concepts.content: Cells differ because they express different genes, and expression is controlled at many levels. Epigenetic control at the DNA level includes cytosine methylation, which usually silences genes by blocking transcription-factor access (and is central to X-chromosome inactivation), and chromatin remodeling that changes how tightly DNA is packaged. In bacteria, groups of related genes are regulated together as operons: the lac operon is inducible (its repressor releases the operator when lactose is present, and the CAP-cAMP complex boosts expression when glucose is low), while the trp operon is repressible by its end product tryptophan. Eukaryotic transcription is further tuned by enhancers bound by activator proteins and by transcription factors with DNA-binding domains. Expression can also be regulated after transcription, including by RNA interference that blocks translation of specific transcripts.

problems.prompt: All of the following statements regarding methylation of bases in DNA are true EXCEPT:
choices: methylation plays an important role in X chromosome inactivation.
methylation protects bacterial genomes from digestion by their restriction enzymes.
methylation increases the rate of DNA mutation.
methylation marks a section of DNA for activation by transcription factors.

problems.prompt: In brown fat cells, epinephrine activates a beta-3 adrenergic receptor (a G-protein coupled receptor) that stimulates production of type 2 5'-deiodinase (D2), the enzyme that converts thyroxine (T4) to active triiodothyronine (T3). problems.prompt: A figure shows that thyroid hormone (T3) acts inside brown fat cells by binding a thyroid hormone response element to regulate gene expression. This intracellular, gene-level mechanism of action is most analogous to that of which hormone?

concepts.title: Viral Structure and Function
concepts.content: A virus is an obligate intracellular parasite: it can reproduce only inside a host cell, and outside cells it is metabolically inactive and cannot make ATP or macromolecules on its own. Every virus is a nucleic acid genome packaged in a protein coat called a capsid, and it commandeers host machinery to build copies of itself. The genome may be DNA or RNA, single- or double-stranded, and linear or circular, but a given virus uses only one type; if a DNA virus's adenine to thymine ratio is not 1:1, its genome must be single-stranded (or RNA). Because the rigid capsid limits genome size, viral genomes are economical, relying on host ribosomes and sometimes using overlapping reading frames to encode more than one protein in the same stretch of nucleic acid. Capsids may be helical or polyhedral, and many animal viruses add an envelope of host-derived membrane, while naked viruses (all phages and plant viruses) lack one. Surface proteins bind specific host receptors, which is why infection is highly species- and tissue-specific.

problems.prompt: All functional viruses contain the following structure(s): I. protein-based capsid; II. genomic DNA or RNA; III. phospholipid envelope.

concepts.title: Bacteriophage Lytic and Lysogenic Cycles
concepts.content: A phage infects by attaching (adsorption) to the bacterial surface and injecting its genome (penetration or eclipse) while the empty capsid stays outside the cell. In the lytic cycle, host polymerases and ribosomes immediately express phage genes; an early gene such as a hydrolase can degrade the host chromosome, new genomes and capsid proteins are made and self-assemble, and a late gene, lysozyme, breaks the cell wall so the cell bursts and releases about 100 progeny. In the lysogenic cycle the phage genome instead integrates into the host chromosome as a silent prophage (the host is called a lysogen), kept dormant by a phage-encoded repressor that blocks phage promoters. Each time the host divides, the prophage is copied along with it, until it eventually excises and enters the lytic cycle. Imperfect excision can carry adjacent host genes to a new host, a form of gene transfer called transduction.

problems.prompt: The lysogenic act of an obligate, intracellular parasite excising portions of host DNA and transferring it to the next host is called:

concepts.title: Replication of Animal Viruses
concepts.content: Animal viruses follow the same general life cycle as phages but differ in several steps. They bind specific host cell-surface receptors that normally serve other cellular functions; for example, HIV's gp120 protein binds the T-cell protein CD4. After binding, animal viruses commonly enter by endocytosis or by fusing with the plasma membrane, then uncoat to release the genome. An animal virus may then follow a lytic cycle, a lysogenic cycle (its dormant integrated genome is called a provirus, as in herpes simplex), or a productive cycle. The productive cycle resembles the lytic cycle but does not kill the host cell: enveloped viruses bud out through the plasma membrane, acquiring their envelope as the membrane reseals.

problems.prompt: Which of the following is true regarding the productive cycle of viruses?
choices: The last stage of the cycle involves breaking open the host cell wall to release progeny viruses.
The virus inserts its genome into the host cell genome and hides within the host cell.
Imperfect excision can result in transduction of host cell genes to other host cells.
The virus acquires an envelope from the host cell plasma membrane.

concepts.title: Viral Genomes
concepts.content: The type of genome determines which enzymes a virus must encode or physically carry in its capsid. A (+) RNA virus's genome acts directly as mRNA, so it is infective on its own; it must encode an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (to make a (-) template and then new (+) genomes) but need not carry it. A (-) RNA virus's genome is only the template for mRNA, so host ribosomes cannot use it directly; the virus must carry an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase in its capsid to first make usable (+) strands. Retroviruses are (+) RNA viruses that integrate as proviruses; they encode reverse transcriptase (an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase) to convert their RNA into DNA, and because their genome can be translated by host ribosomes they only need to encode, not carry, it (though HIV happens to carry it). Double-stranded DNA viruses often have large genomes encoding enzymes for dNTP synthesis and DNA replication, and some drive the host cell into division, occasionally causing cancer.

problems.prompt: Which of the following nitrogenous bases would NOT be expected in the genome of a retrovirus?

Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is a lysogenic, (+)RNA retrovirus that carries a copy of reverse transcriptase in its capsid. What would happen to the virulence of its progeny that neglected to package reverse transcriptase within the capsid?
choices: The virulence will be unaffected; reverse transcriptase is not necessary for successful viral propagation.
The virulence will be reduced, because reverse transcriptase will need to be translated by the host cell machinery before the virus can propagate.
The virus will be rendered ineffective, because reverse transcriptase is necessary to copy the RNA genome into DNA for insertion into the host genome.
The virus will be rendered ineffective, because reverse transcriptase is necessary for the virus to enter the host cell.

concepts.title: Subviral Particles: Prions and Viroids
concepts.content: Subviral particles are infectious agents smaller and simpler than viruses, and they include prions and viroids. A prion is a misfolded version of a normal cellular protein (PrP) that acts as a template, forcing normally folded copies to refold into the misfolded, infectious shape; because a protein directs its own propagation, prions violate the central dogma. Prions cause transmissible spongiform encephalopathies, fatal neurodegenerative diseases; the misfolded proteins resist heat and chemicals, can spread by ingestion, can be inherited (for example fatal familial insomnia and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease), and have very long incubation periods. Viroids are short circular single-stranded RNA molecules (about 200 to 400 bases) with extensive self-complementarity, no capsid, and usually no protein-coding capacity. They mostly infect plants; the only human viroid disease is Hepatitis D, which requires coinfection with Hepatitis B to supply a capsid.

problems.prompt: Which of the following is true regarding prions?
choices: They are transmissible viruses that primarily attack neuromuscular junctions.
They manifest themselves in the digestive tract of animals after ingestion of other animals within the same species.
They are non-living, acellular structures only transmissible via ingestion and not inheritance.
They are transmissible misfolded proteins responsible for several encephalopathies.

concepts.title: Prokaryotes and Cell Theory
concepts.content: Cell theory holds that all living organisms are made of one or more cells, that the cell is the basic unit of life, and that new cells arise only from pre-existing cells. All living organisms, which excludes viruses, are classified as either prokaryotes or eukaryotes based on internal cell structure. The defining feature of prokaryotes is that they lack membrane-bound organelles such as a nucleus and mitochondria, even though both prokaryotes and eukaryotes can carry out processes like photosynthesis, the Krebs cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation. Unlike viruses, prokaryotes are true living cells that possess all the machinery required for life. Taxonomy recognizes three domains: Bacteria and Archaea, which are prokaryotic, and Eukarya, which are eukaryotic and are further divided into kingdoms.

problems.prompt: Which of the following structures is present in prokaryotes?

concepts.title: Bacterial Structure and Shape
concepts.content: A prokaryotic cell has no membrane-bound organelles, but it does contain ribosomes, which are not membrane-bound. Its genome is usually a single circular double-stranded DNA chromosome that is not enclosed in a nucleus and is not wrapped around histones. Because there is no nuclear membrane, transcription and translation happen together, with ribosomes translating an mRNA before it is fully transcribed, forming a polyribosome. Many bacteria also carry plasmids, small circular extrachromosomal DNA molecules that can replicate autonomously, often encode advantages such as antibiotic resistance, and mediate conjugation. Bacteria are also classified by shape as round cocci, rod-shaped bacilli, or spiral spirilla and spirochetes.

problems.prompt: Passage context: A PCR assay for Bacillus anthracis targets three loci on the bacterial chromosome and one locus on each of its two virulence plasmids (pXO1 and pXO2); the amplified fragments are then separated by gel electrophoresis. In the PCR detection of the bacterium, a laboratory technician obtains a positive result. How many bands should the technician detect on the gel?

Passage context: Bacillus anthracis, which causes anthrax, is a rod-shaped bacterium, but other pathogens have different shapes. A culture from a sputum sample develops into colonies of round bacterial cells. Which of the following could be the pathogen causing infection in this patient?

concepts.title: Cell Wall and Gram Staining
concepts.content: The bacterial cytoplasm is bounded by a lipid bilayer and, outside it, a rigid cell wall made of peptidoglycan (cross-linked chains of sugars and amino acids, including D-alanine) that prevents osmotic lysis. This cell wall is the target of antibiotics such as penicillin and of the enzyme lysozyme, which digests peptidoglycan and leaves an osmotically fragile protoplast that bursts in a hypotonic environment. Gram staining separates bacteria by wall structure: Gram-positive cells have a thick peptidoglycan layer and stain dark purple. Gram-negative cells have a thin peptidoglycan layer plus an additional outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide, so they stain light pink. The periplasmic space of Gram-negative bacteria can hold antibiotic-degrading enzymes, contributing to their greater antibiotic resistance.

concepts.title: Bacterial Surface Structures
concepts.content: Some bacteria have extra external structures beyond the cell wall. The capsule, or glycocalyx, is a sticky polysaccharide layer that helps bacteria resist immune cells and adhere to surfaces such as host tissues or rocks. Flagella are long whip-like filaments that provide the only means of bacterial motility; a cell may be monotrichous (one flagellum at one end), amphitrichous (flagella at both ends), or peritrichous (many flagella), and the prokaryotic flagellum is structurally different from the eukaryotic one. Pili are surface projections used for attachment, and the sex pilus connects an F+ (male) and an F- (female) cell to form a conjugation bridge. Fimbriae are smaller projections used to adhere to surfaces and can help pathogenic bacteria colonize tissues.

concepts.title: Bacterial Nutrition, Growth Media, and Temperature
concepts.content: Bacteria are classified by carbon source and energy source: autotrophs fix CO2 while heterotrophs use organic molecules, and chemotrophs get energy from chemicals while phototrophs get it from light, giving four types (chemoautotroph, chemoheterotroph, photoautotroph, photoheterotroph). An auxotroph carries a mutation that blocks synthesis of a needed molecule, so it grows only when that molecule is supplied; for example, an arg- strain forms colonies only on medium supplemented with arginine. Bacteria are cultured on media such as agar in a Petri dish, where a single cell grows into a colony, while minimal medium supplies only glucose, and a plaque is a clear zone of killed cells within a bacterial lawn. Each species also has an optimal growth temperature: mesophiles prefer moderate temperatures near 30 C, thermophiles tolerate up to about 100 C in hot springs and vents, and psychrophiles thrive near 0 C.

problems.prompt: An auxotroph is a bacterium that has lost the ability to synthesize a compound. If the following auxotrophs were plated onto a growth medium containing arginine, lactose, and ampicillin, which would survive?

Hydrothermal vents on the sea floor emit geothermally heated water rich in minerals. They support thriving biological communities, including bacteria that oxidize sulfur compounds to generate energy, which is then used to produce organic material. How would these bacteria be classified?

Passage context: Bacillus anthracis (the cause of anthrax) can be detected by culturing live bacteria from a blood sample and by an ELISA that detects anti-PA IgG antibodies made against the anthrax toxin protein. A physician collects two blood samples and sends them to the lab for culture and an ELISA. The culture comes back negative but the ELISA is positive for human anti-PA IgG. What is a possible reason for this result?
choices: The patient is infected with a virus producing similar symptoms.
The patient does not have an active infection.
The ELISA results are not conclusive because the test is nonspecific.
B. anthracis do not grow in culture.

concepts.title: Oxygen Use, Fermentation, and Respiration
concepts.content: Bacteria differ in how they handle oxygen: obligate aerobes require it, facultative anaerobes use it when present but can live without it, tolerant (aerotolerant) anaerobes grow with or without it but do not use it, and obligate anaerobes are poisoned by it because they lack enzymes to detoxify oxygen free radicals. Respiration is glucose catabolism that passes electrons to an inorganic final acceptor and yields far more ATP than fermentation. Fermentation uses no external electron acceptor; instead it regenerates NAD+ by transferring electrons to an organic molecule, releasing a reduced waste product such as lactate or ethanol. Anaerobic respiration still uses electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation but with a final electron acceptor other than O2, such as sulfate, CO2, or nitrate.

problems.prompt: Which of the following organisms would be forced to undergo fermentation in the presence of a toxin that blocks oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria?
choices: Escherichia coli, a facultative anaerobic bacterium
Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a facultative anaerobic yeast
Propionibacterium acnes, an obligate anaerobic bacterium
Mycobacterium tuberculosis, an obligate aerobic bacterium

concepts.title: Bacterial Life Cycle and Growth Phases
concepts.content: Bacteria reproduce asexually by binary fission: a cell grows, replicates its single chromosome, and splits into two identical daughter cells, so reproduction by itself does not create genetic diversity. In culture, a population passes through a lag phase (no division while cells build biosynthetic machinery), an exponential log phase (numbers rise exponentially, so the log of population size grows linearly), a stationary phase (division stops as nutrients run out and wastes accumulate, defining the carrying capacity), and eventually death. Cells transferred from log phase into fresh medium skip the lag phase because they are already equipped to divide. Under harsh conditions some Gram-positive bacteria form a single endospore, a tough peptidoglycan-shelled dormant structure holding the genome, ribosomes, and RNA that can survive temperatures above 100 C. Germination reactivates the spore; because one cell makes only one spore, sporulation is a survival strategy, not a means of reproduction.

concepts.title: Genetic Exchange Between Bacteria
concepts.content: Although bacteria reproduce asexually, they increase genetic diversity through three transfer mechanisms, none of which is reproduction: transduction, transformation, and conjugation. Transduction is transfer of host DNA between bacteria by a phage, while transformation is uptake of naked DNA from the environment. In conjugation, two cells make physical contact through a bridge and one cell copies and transfers DNA in one direction only. The key element is the F (fertility) factor: an F+ (male) cell carries it, builds a sex pilus, and transfers a copy to an F- (female) cell, converting it to F+. When the F factor integrates into the chromosome the cell becomes an Hfr cell, whose conjugation also transfers adjacent chromosomal genes, allowing researchers to map gene order by interrupting mating at timed intervals.

problems.prompt: Tetracycline-resistant (TetR) and tetracycline-sensitive (TetS) bacteria of the same species are mixed together and grown in liquid culture in the lab. 10% of the population was initially resistant to tetracycline, but after 18 hours, 90% of the population is resistant. This is best explained by:
choices: an enhanced rate of binary fission of the TetS substrain.
a prolonged lag phase and shortened log phase for both substrains.
transduction between the two substrains, where DNA is obtained from the media.
conjugation between the two substrains, where a TetR plasmid is transferred to TetS bacteria.

concepts.title: Archaea, Parasitic, and Symbiotic Bacteria
concepts.content: Archaea are prokaryotes distinct from typical (eu)bacteria; many live in extreme environments such as hot springs, thermal vents, and hypersaline water, and their cell walls lack peptidoglycan. Genetically they resemble eukaryotes in some respects, including the presence of introns and similar mRNA features, but as single cells they still reproduce by fission or budding, so reproduction alone does not increase their diversity. Their heat- and stress-tolerant enzymes make them useful in industry, such as food processing and sewage treatment. Parasitic bacteria damage a host and may be obligate (must live inside a host cell) or facultative (can live inside or outside a host), and they must modulate the damage they cause to keep a supply of resources. Symbiotic bacteria instead benefit their host, as with Rhizobia, which fix nitrogen in the root nodules of legumes and often have reduced genomes because the host supplies some of their needs.

problems.prompt: Passage context: According to a passage on Bacillus anthracis, infection is diagnosed as anthrax when it is cutaneous, pulmonary, or gastrointestinal, but as meningitis when the bacterium reaches the cerebrospinal fluid; diagnostic samples include blood, sputum, feces, and cerebrospinal fluid. According to the passage, which of the following samples is LEAST likely to result in an anthrax diagnosis?

Passage context: Bacillus anthracis infection can be confirmed by culturing the bacterium, and a serum ELISA detects the anti-PA IgG antibodies a patient produces against the anthrax toxin, an antibody response that develops over time after infection. A new blood sample arrives at a lab and grows a gram-positive bacterium later identified as B. anthracis; however, the ELISA registers a negative result. Is this patient infected with B. anthracis, and what most likely accounted for this result?
choices: No; the laboratory sample was contaminated.
No; the cultured bacteria were part of the natural flora of the body.
Yes; the tested blood sample would register a positive ELISA in approximately seven days.
Yes; the infection was recently acquired.

problems.prompt: Passage context: An ELISA measured mean anti-PA IgG antibody levels (against the Bacillus anthracis toxin protein) in the sera of five patient groups over days 1, 3, 5, and 7, as shown in Table 1. Based on the data in Table 1, which of the following is most likely true?
choices: The patients in Group 3 were exposed to less anthrax toxin protein than Group 2.
At Day 7, the sera of patients in Group 2 contained the greatest amount of human anti-PA IgG.
Patients in Group 4 were exposed to anthrax before patients in Group 3.
Patients in Groups 1 and 5 were not recently exposed to anthrax toxin protein.

concepts.title: The Nucleus and the Genome
concepts.content: The nucleus is the defining feature that separates eukaryotes from prokaryotes; it holds the genome inside the nuclear envelope, isolating it from the cytoplasm and other organelles. In eukaryotes, DNA replication, transcription, and RNA splicing occur in the nucleus, while translation happens in the cytoplasm. The genome is divided into several linear double-stranded DNA molecules called chromosomes (humans have 23 different ones, and most cells are diploid with two copies of each). Each chromosome has a centromere near its middle to help sort replicated copies during division and telomeres at its ends, repetitive sequences maintained by the enzyme telomerase. Genes sit at specific loci, and their expression depends partly on packing: tightly packed heterochromatin tends to keep genes off, whereas loosely packed euchromatin allows them to be active.

problems.prompt: A study examines both the nuclear genome and the circular, double-stranded mitochondrial genome. The genes most likely to be actively transcribed are found:
choices: in the nuclear genome, specifically those in heterochromatin regions.
in the nuclear genome, specifically those in euchromatin regions.
in the mitochondrial genome, which is circular and made of double-stranded DNA.
in both the nuclear and mitochondrial genome, both of which are made of double-stranded DNA.

concepts.title: The Nucleolus and Nuclear Envelope
concepts.content: The nucleolus is a region within the nucleus, not bounded by its own membrane, that acts as a ribosome factory containing loops of DNA, RNA polymerase I, rRNA, and ribosomal proteins. RNA pol I transcribes rRNA there, and ribosomes are partially assembled before being exported to the cytoplasm where assembly finishes; the nucleolus is largest in cells making large amounts of protein. The nucleus is enclosed by the nuclear envelope, two lipid bilayer membranes whose outer membrane is in places continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum. The envelope is punctuated by nuclear pores: molecules smaller than about 60 kilodaltons diffuse through freely, but larger proteins are excluded unless they carry a nuclear localization sequence of basic amino acids that lets specific transporters import them.

problems.prompt: An evolutionary biologist proposes that the eukaryotic nucleus originated from an engulfed prokaryotic ancestor (an endosymbiotic origin). Which of the following observations would best support this hypothesis?
choices: The inner membrane possesses fatty acids found predominately in bacteria.
The outer membrane possesses fatty acids found predominately in bacteria.
The nucleus possesses only a single lipid bilayer.

concepts.title: Mitochondria
concepts.content: Mitochondria carry out oxidative phosphorylation and are bounded by two membranes. The inner membrane, folded into cristae to increase surface area, is impermeable to polar molecules and holds the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, while the smooth outer membrane has large pores that let small molecules pass; the enclosed matrix contains pyruvate dehydrogenase and the Krebs cycle enzymes. The proton gradient built across the inner membrane drives ATP synthesis, and the ATP is then exported to the cytoplasm. Mitochondria have their own small circular genome and their own transcription and translation machinery (including a distinct genetic code), though most mitochondrial proteins are actually encoded by nuclear genes. These traits support the endosymbiotic theory that mitochondria descended from free-living bacteria engulfed by an ancestral cell, and because the egg supplies the zygote's cytoplasm, mitochondria are inherited only from the mother.

problems.prompt:
In a study, pools of five different siRNA molecules were used to knock down the proteins MBG-1 and MBG-2, and protein levels were measured over time. Which additional experiments could have been conducted to better support the interpretation of the data?
I. A positive control in which scrambled siRNA is transfected into cells to determine only the potential cell-toxicity effects of the procedure
II. Quantifying MBG-1 and MBG-2 mRNA in the cells via reverse-transcriptase quantitative PCR
III. Transfecting the siRNA molecules individually rather than in pools, to rule out synergistic effects of multiple siRNAs against the same target

In a knockdown study, siRNA pool 1 markedly reduced MBG-1 protein levels over time, whereas siRNA pool 2 did not appreciably reduce MBG-2 protein levels. siRNAs act by binding complementary mRNA and promoting its degradation. The data best support which conclusion?
choices: Both siRNA pools were effective at binding their target transcript and promoting its degradation.
siRNA pool 1 directly caused the degradation of MBG-1 protein, but siRNA pool 2 was not as effective.
siRNA pool 1 caused degradation of the MBG-1 transcript; siRNA pool 2 is either not effective or MBG-2 proteins have a long half-life.
Neither siRNA pool was effective at knocking down mRNA levels, but pool 1 was more effective at inhibiting translation.

problems.prompt: A knockdown study introduced siRNA into growing human (eukaryotic) cells, isolated and quantified mitochondrial and nuclear DNA, and measured protein levels. The experiments would require each of the following procedures EXCEPT:
MBG-1 and MBG-2 both carry mitochondrial localization signals. If future experiments confirm that both proteins promote mitochondrial biogenesis, it would most likely be true that:
choices: some tissues (such as heart, muscle, pancreas, and kidney) have high levels of MBG-1, MBG-2, and mitochondrial biogenesis.
cell stress, proliferation pathways, and pro-apoptotic pathways can promote mitochondrial biogenesis.
mitochondrial biogenesis occurs primarily in G1 of the cell cycle, with negligible levels in G2.
MBG-1 and MBG-2 are both synthesized by 80S ribosomes docked on the rough endoplasmic reticulum membrane.

concepts.title: The Endoplasmic Reticulum and Secretory Pathway
concepts.content: The endoplasmic reticulum is an extensive folded membrane network with two forms: rough ER, studded with ribosomes, synthesizes proteins bound for the secretory pathway, while smooth ER lacks ribosomes and instead makes steroid hormones (in gonads) or detoxifies compounds (in liver). Proteins destined for secretion, the plasma membrane, or the interior of the ER, Golgi, or lysosomes begin translation in the cytoplasm but carry an N-terminal signal sequence recognized by the signal recognition particle (SRP), which docks the ribosome on the rough ER so the growing chain is threaded into the ER lumen. A signal peptidase then removes the signal sequence, and the protein moves in vesicles from the ER to the Golgi and onward. Integral membrane proteins instead have internal hydrophobic transmembrane domains that are not removed and that anchor them in the membrane. The ER lumen is also where disulfide bonds form and some glycosylation begins; the default destination of the secretory path is the plasma membrane unless extra targeting signals redirect the protein.

problems.prompt: A researcher trying to express a eukaryotic protein finds that, instead of being secreted, large quantities of the protein accumulate inside the endoplasmic reticulum. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The researcher needs to select a different strain of bacteria to express the protein.
The protein lacked a signal sequence.
The protein failed to bind to a cytoplasmic carrier protein responsible for transport to the cell surface.
The protein did not fold appropriately.

problems.prompt:
Which of the following cell types would be expected to be relatively rich in rough endoplasmic reticulum?
I. Plasma cells (a type of B cell)
II. Mucus-secreting goblet cells in the small intestine
III. Adrenal cortex cells

concepts.title: The Golgi Apparatus, Lysosomes, and Peroxisomes
concepts.content: The Golgi apparatus is a stack of membranous sacs that modifies proteins arriving from the rough ER (especially their oligosaccharide chains), sorts them to their destinations, and synthesizes some secreted polysaccharides. Vesicles from the ER fuse with the Golgi's cis face nearest the ER, and proteins are progressively modified as they move through the medial stack to the trans face, where they exit in transport vesicles directed by signals within the protein. Lysosomes are membrane-bound organelles filled with acid hydrolases that digest macromolecules; these enzymes work only at the lysosome's acidic pH (around 5), a safety feature because they are inactivated by the neutral cytoplasm if the organelle ruptures. Lysosomes degrade worn-out organelles by autophagy and material taken in by phagocytosis. Peroxisomes handle lipid breakdown and detoxification, producing hydrogen peroxide that their enzyme catalase then converts to water and oxygen, keeping these reactive species away from the rest of the cell.

concepts.title: The Plasma Membrane
concepts.content: All cellular membranes are lipid bilayers built mainly from phospholipids, along with glycolipids and cholesterol; these molecules have hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails, so in water they spontaneously arrange with tails inward and heads facing the water. The hydrophobic interior blocks ions, carbohydrates, and amino acids, while nonpolar molecules like O2, CO2, and steroids cross easily and water passes through protein channels. Membranes also contain proteins: integral proteins are embedded via hydrophobic transmembrane domains, whereas peripheral proteins merely attach to them. The fluid mosaic model describes the membrane as a two-dimensional fluid in which lipids and proteins diffuse laterally but do not flip-flop, so the inner and outer faces stay distinct (for example, glycosylation is found only on the outer face). Fluidity depends on lipid composition: unsaturated fatty acids with kinked tails and cholesterol keep the membrane fluid, while straight saturated tails pack tightly and stiffen it.

concepts.title: Concentration and Colligative Properties
concepts.content: Solution concentration can be expressed as molarity (moles of solute per liter of solution), molality (moles of solute per kilogram of solvent, which does not change with temperature), or mole fraction. When ionic solutes dissolve they dissociate into ions (electrolytes), and the van't Hoff factor i counts how many particles one formula unit yields, for example i = 1 for glucose, 2 for NaCl, and 3 for CaCl2. Colligative properties depend only on the number of dissolved particles, not their identity, so the effective particle concentration is iM (or im). Adding solute lowers a solvent's vapor pressure, raises its boiling point, and lowers its freezing point, with boiling-point elevation and freezing-point depression given by delta-T = k*i*m. Because these effects scale with particle count, a solute that dissociates has a larger effect than a nondissociating one at the same concentration.

problems.prompt: Four cultures of E. coli are suspended in media containing different solutes, then slowly cooled from 22 C until all cultures freeze. Which suspension will freeze first (i.e., has the fewest dissolved particles and thus the least freezing-point depression)?

concepts.title: Diffusion, Osmosis, and Osmotic Pressure
concepts.content: Diffusion is the spontaneous, entropy-driven spreading of particles down their concentration gradient until they are evenly distributed, after which movement continues but there is no net change. Osmosis is diffusion of solvent (water) rather than solute across a semipermeable membrane that blocks the solute, drawing water toward the more concentrated side. Tonicity describes these gradients: a hypertonic solution has more solute than the cell (water leaves and the cell shrinks), a hypotonic solution has less (water enters), and an isotonic solution is balanced. The osmotic pressure needed to stop this water flow is given by the van't Hoff equation, pi = M*i*R*T, where M is molarity, i the van't Hoff factor, R the gas constant, and T the temperature in kelvin. Like the other colligative properties, osmotic pressure depends on the number of dissolved particles, not their identity.

problems.prompt: A point mutation abolishes the function of aquaporin-2, a transmembrane water channel in the kidney collecting duct, in patients with excessive urine output. What directly causes these patients' symptoms?
choices: Increased expression of aquaporin-2 in the collecting duct
Decreased active transport of water out of the collecting duct
Decreased osmotic flow of water out of the collecting duct

concepts.title: Passive Transport: Channels and Carriers
concepts.content: Passive transport is any movement of solute down its gradient without energy input. In simple diffusion the solute crosses the bilayer unaided, as hydrophobic steroid hormones do, but the membrane is impermeable to large or hydrophilic solutes. Facilitated diffusion moves such solutes down their gradient with the help of integral membrane proteins: channel proteins form selective pores (many are gated, opening in response to voltage changes or ligand binding), while carrier proteins bind a molecule and change shape to shuttle it across (uniports move one substance, symports two in the same direction, antiports two in opposite directions). Unlike the wide, nonselective pores formed by porins, these channels and carriers give the plasma membrane its selective permeability. Because facilitated diffusion relies on a limited number of transport proteins, it shows saturation kinetics, plateauing once all the proteins are occupied, whereas simple diffusion keeps rising with the driving force.

problems.prompt: A cell line expresses an ion channel. On a graph of ion flux across the membrane versus increasing driving force, curve A rises and plateaus at a high maximum, while curve B rises and plateaus at a lower maximum. Which of the following could account for the change from curve A to curve B?
choices: Simple diffusion across the membrane has decreased.
The channels fail to reach saturation.
The channels no longer require the addition of ATP to function.

concepts.title: Active Transport and the Na+/K+ ATPase
concepts.content: Active transport moves molecules against their electrochemical gradient and therefore requires energy and a protein. In primary active transport the movement is coupled directly to ATP hydrolysis, whereas in secondary active transport ATP first builds a gradient (often of sodium) whose potential energy then drives another solute's transport, as when sodium flowing in cotransports glucose against its gradient. The Na+/K+ ATPase, present in all cells, pumps 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP hydrolyzed. Potassium then leaks back out through leak channels, and this net loss of positive charge creates the resting membrane potential, an interior that is negative relative to the outside (about -70 mV). The pump thus maintains osmotic balance, sets up the resting potential, and supplies the sodium gradient that powers secondary active transport.

concepts.title: Endocytosis and Exocytosis
concepts.content: Cells also move material across the plasma membrane in bulk using membrane-bound vesicles. In exocytosis a cytoplasmic vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and releases its contents, such as hormones or digestive enzymes, into the extracellular space. Endocytosis is the reverse: the membrane invaginates to bring material in as a vesicle called an endosome. There are three types: phagocytosis (cell eating), the nonspecific uptake of large particles as done by macrophages engulfing microbes; pinocytosis (cell drinking), the nonspecific uptake of fluid and small molecules; and receptor-mediated endocytosis, a highly specific process in which receptors in clathrin-coated pits bind a particular ligand, as in the uptake of cholesterol-carrying lipoproteins from the blood.

problems.prompt: Which of the following would have the LEAST impact on the phagocytic ability of a neutrophil?

concepts.title: Cell-Surface Receptors and Signal Transduction
concepts.content: Cell-surface receptors are integral membrane proteins that relay extracellular signals into the cell; each binds a specific ligand, usually a hormone or neurotransmitter, in a lock-and-key fashion to trigger a response called signal transduction. There are three main types: ligand-gated ion channels that open when a ligand binds, catalytic receptors with an enzymatic site on the cytoplasmic side that is activated by ligand binding, and G-protein-linked receptors that act through a second messenger. In G-protein signaling, ligand binding causes the G-protein to exchange GDP for GTP and activate an enzyme such as adenylyl cyclase, which makes the second messenger cyclic AMP (cAMP) from ATP. cAMP then activates protein kinases that phosphorylate target enzymes, greatly amplifying the original signal. Stimulatory (Gs) and inhibitory (Gi) G-proteins can activate or inhibit adenylyl cyclase, and some G-proteins instead trigger a pathway that raises cytoplasmic calcium.

problems.prompt:
Beta-adrenergic receptors are G-protein-coupled receptors sensitive to epinephrine. When epinephrine binds the receptor, which of the following occur?
I. The G-protein binds GTP and GDP dissociates.
II. The G-protein is inactivated and dissociates into alpha and beta-gamma subunits.
III. The intracellular concentration of a second messenger increases.

concepts.title: The Cytoskeleton, Cilia, and Flagella
concepts.content: Animal cells use an internal cytoskeleton of three noncovalently polymerized protein types for support, movement, and intracellular transport. Microtubules, the thickest, are hollow tubes of alpha- and beta-tubulin that grow from the microtubule organizing center (MTOC); they form the mitotic spindle and serve as tracks for motor proteins that carry cargo. The MTOC contains a pair of centrioles, each a ring of nine microtubule triplets, though the centrioles themselves are not required for mitosis. Cilia and flagella share a 9 + 2 arrangement (nine microtubule pairs around two central ones) anchored by a basal body, and the motor protein dynein slides these filaments past one another to produce movement. Microfilaments are the thinnest, made of actin, and drive gross cell movements such as the cleavage furrow of division and amoeboid motion, while intermediate filaments are heterogeneous, more permanent, and resist mechanical stress.

concepts.title: Cell Adhesion and Cell Junctions
concepts.content: Cells in tissues are connected by three kinds of junctions. Tight (occluding) junctions form continuous seals around cells, as in the intestinal epithelium, preventing molecules from leaking between cells and even dividing the membrane into distinct apical and basolateral surfaces with different proteins. Desmosomes (spot desmosomes) are localized points that hold cells together without sealing them, anchored inside each cell by keratin plaques; they are found where tissues must resist mechanical stress, such as skin. Gap junctions are pore-like channels that directly connect the cytoplasms of adjacent cells, letting ions and small molecules pass but not large polypeptides or organelles. In cardiac and smooth muscle, gap junctions let an action potential's depolarization spread directly from one cell to the next.

concepts.title: The Cell Cycle
concepts.content: Cells reproduce by duplicating their contents and genome and then splitting in two, cycling through four phases. During S (synthesis) phase the genome is replicated, so by its end the nucleus holds two complete copies of the DNA. M phase contains mitosis (partitioning of the cellular components) and cytokinesis (the physical division). Between M and S lie two gap phases, G1 and G2; together with S they make up interphase, where the cell spends most of its time growing and metabolizing, and some specialized cells stay permanently in G1. The two identical copies of a replicated chromosome, joined at the centromere, are sister chromatids, which are distinct from homologous chromosomes, the nonidentical maternal and paternal versions of the same chromosome.

problems.prompt: A yeast strain has a mutation in the Sal3 promoter causing its constitutive activation, which pushes cells into M phase of the cell cycle earlier than normal. Compared with wild-type cells, these mutant cells would be:
choices: larger than wild type cells and spend more time in G2
smaller than wild type cells and spend more time in G2
larger than wild type cells and spend less time in G2
smaller than wild type cells and spend less time in G2

problems.prompt: A primary spermatocyte contains 6 picograms of DNA while in the G1 phase before undergoing meiosis. How much DNA will each sperm contain at the completion of meiosis?

concepts.title: The Phases of Mitosis
concepts.content: Mitosis proceeds through four stages. In prophase the chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes, each already consisting of two sister chromatids joined at a centromere, while the nucleolus disappears, the spindle forms, the centriole pairs move to opposite poles, and the nuclear envelope breaks into vesicles. In metaphase the chromosomes line up at the center of the cell as the metaphase plate, with each sister chromatid's kinetochore attached to spindle fibers from opposite poles. During anaphase the spindle fibers shorten and pull the sister chromatids apart, the cell elongates, and cytokinesis begins as a ring of actin forms a cleavage furrow. In telophase a nuclear membrane reforms around each set of chromosomes, the chromosomes decondense, a nucleolus reappears, and cytokinesis finishes to yield two daughter cells.

concepts.title: Cancer, Oncogenes, and Tumor Suppressors
concepts.content: Cancer results when a cell loses control of the cell cycle, and a mutation in a protein that normally regulates cycle progression can cause unregulated division; malignant solid tumors invade surrounding tissue, while more diffuse cancers like leukemia arise in the bone marrow. Oncogenes are mutated genes that can convert normal cells into cancerous ones; they arise from protooncogenes, the normal growth-regulating genes, through mutation or exposure to mutagens such as UV light or benzene, and some enter cells via viral infection (the first, src, came from a chicken retrovirus). Tumor suppressor genes are the cell's built-in defense, encoding proteins that halt division so genetic damage can be repaired or that trigger cell death if the damage is too severe. p53 is a key example: normally kept at low levels, it rises when genetic damage or oncogene activity is detected and, if repair fails, drives the cell into apoptosis.

concepts.title: Apoptosis and Senescence
concepts.content: Apoptosis is programmed cell death in which a cell shrinks and dismantles itself while minimizing damage to its neighbors, unlike the uncontrolled spilling of contents that occurs in necrosis. It can be triggered by external signals (such as toxins or cytokines) or internal ones (such as p53 rising to a critical level), and it proceeds by disassembling the cytoskeleton, breaking down the nuclear envelope, fragmenting the genome, and displaying surface signals that recruit phagocytes like macrophages to clear the debris. The process is carried out by caspases, proteases with an active-site cysteine that cleave targets at aspartate residues; they are made as inactive procaspases, and initiator caspases cluster and activate one another before setting off a cascade of effector caspases. Senescence is biological aging at the cellular and organismal level, tracked by telomere length (longer telomeres indicate a younger cell), and aging cells become more prone to apoptosis. The accumulated effects of cellular senescence ultimately cause organs to fail and the organism to die.

problems.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a feature of apoptosis?
choices: Mechanism of killing via caspase activation
Results in the uncontrolled spilling of cellular contents

concepts.title: Genes and Alleles
concepts.content: One of the basic tenets of genetics is that children inherit traits from both parents. A diploid organism has two copies of the genome in each cell, while a haploid gamete has one, and a diploid zygote forms when a haploid ovum and a haploid spermatozoon fuse. The gene, a length of DNA coding for a particular gene product, is the fundamental unit of inheritance, and every gene occupies a specific location called a locus on a chromosome. The human genome is split into 24 different chromosomes: 22 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes (X and Y), arranged as 23 pairs (46 total), with one member of each pair from each parent. The two homologous chromosomes carry the same genes, but their DNA sequences may differ; these different versions of a gene are called alleles. Because a person carries two copies of every gene, one on each homolog, an individual can normally carry at most two different alleles even though many alleles may exist across a population.

concepts.title: Genotype vs. Phenotype
concepts.content: The genotype is the DNA sequence of the alleles a person carries, while the phenotype is the physical expression of that genotype. An individual carrying two different alleles at a locus is a heterozygote, and one carrying two identical alleles is a homozygote. An allele that is expressed in the phenotype regardless of the second allele present is called dominant, while an allele that is not expressed in the heterozygous state is called recessive. Because recessive alleles are masked in heterozygotes, it is not always possible to determine an individual's genotype from the phenotype alone. By convention the dominant allele is written as a capital letter and the recessive as the lowercase (for example C and c), so CC and Cc individuals share one phenotype while cc shows the recessive trait; this masking is called classical dominance.

concepts.title: Meiosis
concepts.content: Meiosis is the type of cell division that reduces the chromosome number from diploid to haploid to produce gametes, occurring in the testes to make spermatozoa and in the ovaries to make ova. Like mitosis, meiosis is preceded by one round of DNA replication (S phase) and uses the same phase names, but meiosis has two rounds of division, meiosis I and meiosis II, rather than one. In prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair in synapsis to form tetrads (bivalents) and exchange segments by crossing over (recombination), a key source of genetic variation. During meiosis I the homologous chromosomes separate while sister chromatids stay joined, producing two haploid cells whose chromosomes are still replicated. Meiosis II then separates the sister chromatids much as mitosis does, so a single diploid parent cell ultimately yields four haploid cells.

problems.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a similarity between mitosis and meiosis?
choices: Both require the disassembly of the nuclear membrane.
Both utilize microtubules to negotiate the division of genetic material.
Both create diploid cells after one round of division.

concepts.title: Nondisjunction
concepts.content: Nondisjunction is the failure of chromosomes to separate correctly during meiosis: homologous chromosomes may fail to separate in meiosis I, or sister chromatids may fail to separate in meiosis II. The resulting gametes carry either two copies or no copies of a given chromosome, and when such a gamete fuses with a normal gamete the zygote has three copies (trisomy) or one copy (monosomy) of that chromosome. The genetic imbalance from adding or removing a whole chromosome is usually so severe that the zygote cannot develop into a normal individual. Some cases are survivable: trisomy of chromosome 21 causes Down syndrome, and nondisjunction of the sex chromosomes can produce conditions such as Turner syndrome (a single X with no Y). The harm in trisomy comes not from missing information but from gene dosage, because many genes are present in one extra copy.

concepts.title: Mendelian Genetics
concepts.content: Gregor Mendel described the statistical inheritance of traits in pea plants long before the nature of DNA was known. His first law, the Law of Segregation, states that the two alleles of an individual are separated and passed to the next generation singly, which happens during anaphase I of meiosis. His second law, the Law of Independent Assortment, states that the alleles of one gene segregate into gametes independently of the alleles of another gene. A pure-breeding (homozygous) strain consistently yields progeny of the same type when crossed within the strain. To deduce an unknown genotype, a testcross mates the individual with a homozygous recessive partner, whose all-recessive alleles allow the other parent's alleles to be displayed in the phenotype of the F1 progeny.

concepts.title: The Punnett Square
concepts.content: The Punnett square is a visual tool for predicting the results of a cross using the Laws of Segregation and Independent Assortment. To build one, list the possible gametes from each parent on the two sides of a square, fill in the zygote genotypes produced by each gamete combination, and then read off the genotype and phenotype probabilities. For a monohybrid cross of two heterozygotes (Gg x Gg) with G dominant, three-quarters of the offspring show the dominant phenotype and one-quarter show the recessive. A dihybrid cross involving two genes uses a larger square, with independent assortment and segregation built in as assumptions. Real results rarely match the predicted ratios exactly; the larger the number of progeny, the closer the outcome comes to the prediction, and small deviations are attributed to statistical variability.

concepts.title: Incomplete Dominance
concepts.content: Some alleles display neither classical dominance nor recessiveness. In incomplete dominance, the phenotype of the heterozygote is a blended mix of both alleles, and the alleles are given different uppercase letters (for example R for red and W for white flower color). An RW heterozygote is therefore pink, a blend intermediate between the red RR homozygote and the white WW homozygote. Because the heterozygote is visibly distinct from either homozygote, incomplete dominance produces three phenotypes that correspond directly to the three genotypes: RR (red), RW (pink), and WW (white).

concepts.title: Codominance
concepts.content: In codominance, two alleles are both fully expressed in the heterozygote without blending, as seen in the ABO blood group antigens on red blood cells. There are three ABO alleles: I-A and I-B are codominant and each causes its antigen to be expressed, while i is recessive to both and produces no antigen, so an I-A/I-B individual has type AB blood. By contrast, the Rh factor follows a classically dominant pattern, with Rh-positive dominant over Rh-negative. Inheritance is further complicated by pleiotropy (one gene affecting many seemingly unrelated traits), polygenism (traits such as height controlled by many genes and showing a continuous range), penetrance (the likelihood that a given genotype produces the expected phenotype), and epistasis (the expression of one gene depending on a different gene).

concepts.title: The Sex Chromosomes
concepts.content: Females have two X chromosomes while males have one X and one Y; the presence of a Y chromosome drives male development, and its absence gives the default female pathway. Because females produce only X-bearing gametes and males produce either X- or Y-bearing gametes, it is the male gamete that determines the sex of the offspring. Genes on the X chromosome are present in two copies in females but only one copy in males, so a recessive X-linked allele is always expressed in a male because there is no second allele to mask it. Traits determined by genes on the X or Y chromosome are called sex-linked and show distinctive patterns of expression and inheritance.

problems.prompt: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked recessive trait. A phenotypically normal woman who carries the DMD allele mates with a phenotypically normal man. What is the probability they will have either a son with DMD or a daughter who carries DMD?
choices: Cannot be determined with the information given

problems.prompt: Hemophilia is an X-linked recessive trait. Mr. A has hemophilia; he and his wife (Ms. B, who is neither affected by hemophilia nor a carrier) produce one unaffected son (Mr. C) and one unaffected daughter (Ms. D). The son of Ms. D marries an unaffected, non-carrier woman. What is the probability they will produce a child who is a carrier of hemophilia?

concepts.title: Linkage
concepts.content: Linkage is the failure of genes to assort independently, and it occurs when genes lie on the same chromosome. Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment held for the traits he studied only because those genes were on separate chromosomes; genes on different chromosomes always assort independently, whereas a gene translocated onto the same chromosome as another may no longer do so. When two genes sit very close together on one chromosome, the alleles on a given chromosome tend to travel together into the same gamete during meiosis, which limits the possible allele combinations in the gametes. As a result, predicting the gametes of a doubly heterozygous individual requires knowing which alleles are located together on each chromosome.

concepts.title: Linkage and Recombination
concepts.content: Meiotic recombination (crossing over) is the exception to linkage, because it can separate alleles that began on the same chromosome and create new combinations not present in the parents. The frequency of recombination between two genes is proportional to the physical distance between them along the chromosome, so genes far apart recombine often and may even appear unlinked, while genes close together rarely recombine. The recombination frequency (RF) is calculated as the number of recombinant (non-parental) offspring divided by the total number of progeny. Because RF reflects distance, it can be used to map the relative positions of genes on a chromosome, and its maximum value is 50%, the point at which genes assort as though they were on separate chromosomes.

problems.prompt: A thin, agouti mouse (BbCc) is crossed with a fat, albino mouse (bbcc) and several litters of pups are phenotyped. The results are: 19 thin, agouti pups; 32 thin, albino pups; 29 fat, agouti pups; and 20 fat, albino pups. Which of the following can be concluded?
choices: The fat and agouti alleles are linked and on the same chromosome.
The fat and albino alleles are linked and on different chromosomes.
The gene for body size and the gene for coat color are unlinked.
The gene for body size and the gene for coat color are 20 mu apart on the same chromosome.

problems.prompt: A geneticist crosses two flowering plant lines. Plant Line #1 has green flowers (G) with long veins (L) and is crossed with Plant Line #2 that has yellow flowers (g) and short veins (l). Both lines are genotypically homozygous. The resulting progeny are then back-crossed to Plant Line #2, and the resulting progeny are: green, long = 410; green, short = 45; yellow, long = 45; yellow, short = 400. What is the recombination frequency?

concepts.title: Inheritance Patterns
concepts.content: There are six inheritance patterns to recognize: autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant, mitochondrial, Y-linked, X-linked recessive, and X-linked dominant.
