Autosomal recessive traits can skip generations (affected children may have unaffected parents) and affect the sexes roughly equally, whereas autosomal dominant traits do not skip generations and also affect the sexes equally. Mitochondrial traits show maternal inheritance: an affected mother passes the trait to all of her children, while an affected father passes it to none. X-linked recessive traits affect males more often, because a male expresses any recessive allele on his single X, and unaffected carrier mothers can have affected sons. Y-linked traits pass only from fathers to all of their sons, and X-linked dominant traits (the hardest to identify) do not skip generations, with affected fathers passing the trait to all of their daughters.

problems.prompt: What pattern of inheritance would be seen in a family expressing a mitochondrial disorder?
choices: All blood-related males would have the disorder and would pass it on only to male offspring.
All blood-related females would have the disorder if their father had it.
All blood-related offspring of an affected female would have the disorder.
All blood-related offspring of an affected individual would have the disorder.

problems.prompt: The pedigree shown tracks a trait across three generations (shaded symbols are affected; squares are male, circles are female). In Generation I an affected male is mated with an affected female, and their Generation II children include both affected and unaffected individuals. Which of the following is true about the trait in the pedigree?
choices: The trait displays autosomal dominant inheritance and the individuals in Generation I are both heterozygotes.
The trait displays autosomal dominant inheritance and the individuals in Generation I are both homozygotes.
The trait displays X-linked recessive inheritance and the female in Generation I is a heterozygote.
The trait displays X-linked dominant inheritance and the female in Generation I is a homozygote.

problems.prompt: Refer to the same pedigree (shaded symbols are affected; squares are male, circles are female), for which the trait is autosomal dominant. In Generation II, two couples are each expecting another child: on the left, an unaffected male with an affected female (who already have an unaffected son), and on the right, an affected male with an unaffected female (who already have two unaffected daughters). Which of the following best describes the chance of the babies being affected by the trait?
choices: The probability of the parents on the left having an affected child is 25%.
The probability of the parents on the right having an affected child is 25%.
The probability of either couple having an affected child is 50%.
The parents on the right cannot have an affected child.

problems.prompt: A passage on genetic imprinting explains that when a gene's expression is conditioned by its parental origin, only one parental allele is expressed. Prader-Willi syndrome is an autosomal disorder caused by the combination of maternal imprinting (silencing of the maternally inherited allele) and loss (deletion or mutation) of the paternally inherited gene in the same region. Is it possible for both men and women to develop Prader-Willi syndrome?
choices: Yes, both sexes have an equal probability of disease.
Yes, both sexes can have the disease, but it is found predominantly in women because of maternal imprinting.
No, because it is only maternally imprinted.
No, because imprinting is reset with each successive generation.

problems.prompt: A passage explains that methylation of one or more CG dinucleotides near a gene is associated with transcriptional repression (gene inactivation). Aberrant DNA methylation is linked to human cancers: hypermethylation at CG islands in a promoter is associated with gene inactivation, while hypomethylation may lead to the overexpression of genes. Which of the following is the most likely pattern of methylation that would lead to cancer?
choices: Hypermethylation of tumor suppressor genes and hypomethylation of proto-oncogenes
Hypermethylation of proto-oncogenes and hypomethylation of tumor suppressor genes
Hypermethylation of both tumor suppressor genes and proto-oncogenes
Hypomethylation of both tumor suppressor genes and proto-oncogenes

problems.prompt: A passage explains that Prader-Willi syndrome is an autosomal disorder caused by maternal imprinting (the maternally inherited allele is silenced by methylation) combined with inheritance of a mutated (deleted) paternal chromosome, and that imprinting is reset each generation according to the sex of the parent. Is it possible for a man with Prader-Willi syndrome who marries an unaffected woman to have children with Prader-Willi syndrome?
choices: Yes, the children will either inherit a silenced (imprinted) chromosome or a mutated chromosome from him.
Yes, the children have a 50% chance of inheriting the father's mutated chromosome and will all inherit a silenced (imprinted) chromosome from their mother.
No, the mutated chromosome can only be inherited from the mother.
No, they could inherit the mutated chromosome from him, but could inherit a normal chromosome from their mother.

problems.prompt: A passage explains that in Angelman syndrome (an autosomal disorder) the responsible gene is deleted or mutated on the maternally inherited chromosome, while the paternal copy is silenced by imprinting via methylation (methylated DNA is transcriptionally repressed). The gene responsible for Angelman syndrome is UBE3A. In a person with this syndrome, what is the difference between the maternal and paternal chromosome?
choices: There is no difference; both homologous genes are methylated.
There is no difference; both homologous genes are unmethylated.
The maternal gene is methylated and the paternal one deleted or mutated.
The paternal gene is methylated and the maternal one deleted or mutated.

concepts.title: Population Genetics
concepts.content: Population genetics studies the inheritance of alleles across an entire population over time rather than within single individuals. In this context a population is a group of members of a species that mate and reproduce with one another, and each individual is viewed merely as a temporary carrier of the population's alleles. The sum total of all genetic information in a population is called the gene pool, and a key variable describing it is allele frequency, the number of copies of a particular allele divided by the total number of copies of that gene in the population. Because each diploid individual carries two copies of a gene, allele frequencies are computed by counting alleles across all individuals rather than by inspecting any one organism.

concepts.title: Hardy-Weinberg in Population Genetics
concepts.content: The Hardy-Weinberg law states that allele frequencies in a population's gene pool will not change over time provided that there is no mutation, no migration, no natural selection, random mating, and a population large enough to prevent random drift. Mathematically, with p the frequency of the dominant allele and q the frequency of the recessive allele, p + q = 1. Squaring both sides gives p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1, where p^2 is the frequency of homozygous dominants, 2pq is the frequency of heterozygotes, and q^2 is the frequency of homozygous recessives. Segregation, independent assortment, and recombination reshuffle alleles into new combinations but cannot change an allele's overall frequency, so after one generation a population reaches Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and both allele and genotype frequencies remain constant.

problems.prompt: In a randomly mating population, the frequency of a recessive disease-causing allele is 0.2. Assuming the population follows the Hardy-Weinberg model, what is the frequency of carriers for the disease in this population?

concepts.title: Hardy-Weinberg in the Real World
concepts.content: Hardy-Weinberg describes a highly idealized set of conditions that no real population can fully satisfy, so its assumptions are all violated to some degree in nature. Mutation is inevitable, because even without chemical mutagens or radiation, inherent DNA polymerase errors introduce new alleles over time. Migration moves alleles into or out of a population, and a true absence of natural selection would require unlimited resources with no predation or disease. Non-random mating passes on trait-associated alleles preferentially from one generation to the next, and in a very small population random drift allows chance events to shift allele frequencies significantly, since the population cannot contain as great a variety of alleles.

problems.prompt: Which of the following best describes the principle that the change in allele frequency from one generation to the next occurs because alleles in offspring are a random sample of those in the parents, as well as from the role that chance plays in determining whether a given individual will survive and reproduce?

concepts.title: Evolution by Natural Selection
concepts.content: Evolution refers to the changes in life on Earth over the geologic span of its history, and Charles Darwin proposed natural selection as the mechanism that drives it. Natural selection is an interaction between organisms and their environment that causes differential reproduction of different phenotypes, thereby altering a population's gene pool. It works because individuals differ in heritable traits, some phenotypes let their carriers survive longer and produce more offspring, and over time the alleles behind those phenotypes become more abundant while others become rarer. These changes in allele frequency are the basis of evolution in populations. The central measure is fitness, defined not by how well an organism is physically adapted or fed but by its reproductive success in passing its alleles on to future generations.

problems.prompt: Which of the following is/are examples of increased fitness? I. A female guinea pig that learns to protect her pups from consumption by the male; II. A male rat that learns to run a maze in a shorter period of time in order to increase the size of the food reward; III. A sterilized female rabbit whose lifespan is extended by access to plentiful food supplies

concepts.title: Sources of Genetic Diversity
concepts.content: Natural selection can act only on the genetic diversity already present in a population; it alters allele frequencies but does not itself create new alleles. If a population contains only one allele of a gene, there is no variability for natural selection to act on and no way for allele frequencies to change. There are two sources of genetic variation: new alleles, which result from mutations in the genome, and new combinations of existing alleles, which are generated during sexual reproduction through independent assortment, recombination, and segregation in meiosis. A mutation in a somatic cell cannot contribute, because only germ-line mutations are passed to offspring, and a population that reproduces only asexually loses meiosis's ability to generate the new allele combinations that natural selection requires.

concepts.title: Modes of Natural Selection
concepts.content: Natural selection can act on a trait's distribution in several distinct ways. In directional selection, natural selection removes individuals at one extreme, so the population average shifts over time in the other direction (for example, giraffes becoming taller as short ones die for lack of food). In divergent selection, the average individuals are removed while the two extremes remain, which can split a population and perhaps lead to a new species, whereas stabilizing selection removes both extremes and drives the population toward the average. Artificial selection occurs when humans control mating to achieve desired traits, and sexual selection occurs when mates are chosen through displays and rituals rather than at random. Kin selection acts when socially living animals sacrifice themselves for relatives with whom they share alleles.

problems.prompt: Which of the following would best describe a scenario involving directional selection?
choices: Turtles living on an island become physically separated into two groups when a tropical storm divides the habitat and eventually they are no longer able to mate.
Dogs are bred to produce little or no dander and thus are hypoallergenic for pet owners with allergies.
The ability to collect a wide variety of food is valued by a certain type of monkey, and females who exhibit this skill are able to attract more sexual partners.
Field mice that are able to escape into small spaces are less likely to be consumed by predators and thus larger mice are selected against over time.

concepts.title: The Species Concept and Speciation
concepts.content: A species is a group of organisms capable of reproducing sexually with one another to produce fit offspring, and a population is a subset of a species. Two individuals are not members of the same species if they cannot mate and produce fertile offspring, which is why horses and donkeys are separate species even though they can produce a mule, a healthy but sterile hybrid. Reproductive isolation keeps species separate and takes two forms: prezygotic barriers, which prevent a hybrid zygote from forming (ecological, temporal, behavioral, mechanical, and gametic), and postzygotic barriers, which prevent hybrids from developing or reproducing (hybrid inviability, hybrid sterility, and hybrid breakdown). Common ancestry leaves homologous structures, physical features shared because of a shared ancestor, whereas analogous structures serve the same function in different species without arising from common ancestry.

concepts.title: Taxonomy
concepts.content: Taxonomy is the science of biological classification, originated by Carolus Linnaeus, who devised the binomial naming system in which each organism receives a genus and species name written in italics with the genus capitalized (as in Homo sapiens). There are eight principal taxonomic ranks: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, and species. Life is divided among the domains Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya; Bacteria and Archaea were once combined as Kingdom Monera but are now separate domains in which the kingdom and domain are the same. Among distinguishing cellular features, only animal cells lack a cell wall, while all living organisms perform glycolysis and use ATP, and every kingdom contains at least some members that carry out oxidative phosphorylation.

problems.prompt: A major cellular feature distinguishing cells in Kingdom Animalia from cells in other kingdoms is that animal cells:
choices: utilize microtubules as part of cellular motility.

concepts.title: The Origin of Life
concepts.content: Based on radioisotope dating, Earth is thought to be about 4.5 billion years old, and all life evolved from prokaryotes, with the oldest fossils being 3.5-billion-year-old prokaryotic remains preserved in stromatolites. The early atmosphere lacked oxygen and was a reducing environment, in which simple organic monomers could form spontaneously using energy from lightning, radioactive decay, volcanic activity, or the Sun; laboratory recreations yield amino acids, carbohydrates, lipids, and ribonucleotides. These monomers could polymerize abiotically, aided by metal ions and clay acting as catalysts, forming proteinoids that assemble into droplets collectively called protobionts (microspheres, liposomes, and coacervates) with a protected interior able to carry out reactions. What protobionts lacked was an organized mechanism of heredity, which was first supplied by self-replicating RNA. The final step in the evolution of the earliest cells was the switch from RNA to the more stable DNA as the genetic material.

concepts.title: Structure of the Neuron
concepts.content: Neurons are specialized cells that transmit and process information as electrochemical impulses called action potentials, which are localized waves of membrane depolarization traveling along an axon. The basic functional unit is the neuron, which has a central cell body, the soma, that contains the nucleus and carries out most of the cell's biosynthesis. Slender projections extend from the soma: dendrites receive incoming signals, while a single axon carries action potentials away from the cell body. A neuron with one dendrite is bipolar and one with many is multipolar. Axons can branch and end in synaptic knobs, where an arriving action potential triggers release of chemical messengers across a narrow gap, the synaptic cleft, onto a target cell; a neuron is a single cell, whereas a nerve is a bundle of many axons.

concepts.title: The Resting Membrane Potential
concepts.content: The resting membrane potential is about -70 mV, with the interior of the cell negative relative to the exterior. Two membrane proteins establish it: the Na+/K+ ATPase, which uses one ATP to pump three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in (primary active transport), and potassium leak channels, which let K+ (but not other ions) flow down its gradient out of the cell. The result is high sodium outside and high potassium inside, and the ongoing loss of positive charge leaves the interior net negative. Because potassium leak channels outnumber sodium leak channels roughly 100:1, the membrane is nearly impermeable to sodium at rest. A cell in this state is described as polarized, negative on the inside and positive on the outside.

problems.prompt: Which of the following is a possible sign of hypokalemia, defined as low potassium concentration in the blood?
choices: Hyperreflexia (more rapid and more sensitive reflex responses)

concepts.title: The Action Potential
concepts.content: An action potential is a wave of depolarization that travels along an axon; it is an electrochemical impulse driven by ions moving through channels, not simply an electrical current. Voltage-gated sodium channels open when the membrane depolarizes from the resting -70 mV to a threshold of about -50 mV, allowing sodium to rush in and depolarize that section to roughly +35 mV before the channels inactivate. Local current then depolarizes the neighboring membrane to threshold, propagating the impulse down the axon without any change in amplitude once it has begun. Repolarization follows because the sodium channels inactivate quickly while slower voltage-gated potassium channels open, letting potassium exit and returning the potential toward rest, often overshooting to about -90 mV before those channels close. The action potential is therefore an all-or-nothing event.

concepts.title: Saltatory Conduction
concepts.content: The axons of many neurons are wrapped in an insulating myelin sheath, which is made not by the neuron itself but by glial cells: Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system and oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system. No ions cross the membrane where it is covered by myelin, and there are no voltage-gated sodium channels in those regions. Periodic gaps in the sheath called nodes of Ranvier concentrate the voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels. Rather than impeding the signal, myelin dramatically speeds conduction by forcing the action potential to jump from node to node, a process known as saltatory conduction.

problems.prompt: Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune disease that targets and destroys the cells that myelinate neurons. Which of the following best describes the function of a neuron that has had its myelin destroyed?
choices: The neuron ceases to propagate an action potential down the axon.
The neuron propagates an action potential more slowly than it did when myelinated, but faster than a normal unmyelinated neuron.
The neuron propagates an action potential at a rate similar to a normal unmyelinated neuron.
The neuron fails to initiate an action potential at the axon hillock.

concepts.title: Glial Cells
concepts.content: Glial cells are specialized non-neuronal cells that provide structural and metabolic support to neurons; they maintain a resting membrane potential but do not generate action potentials. Schwann cells (in the PNS) and oligodendrocytes (in the CNS) form the myelin that increases the speed of action potential conduction along axons. Astrocytes guide neuronal development and regulate synaptic communication by controlling neurotransmitter levels. Microglia remove dead cells and debris, and ependymal cells produce and circulate cerebrospinal fluid.

concepts.title: Equilibrium Potentials
concepts.content: During an action potential, sodium and potassium move passively through voltage-gated channels, driven by their electrochemical gradients. The equilibrium potential for an ion is the membrane potential at which there is no net movement of that ion, and it can be predicted by the Nernst equation from the ion's concentrations on each side of the membrane and its valence. The resting potential of -70 mV reflects both the equilibrium potentials of sodium and potassium and the relative numbers of their leak channels. Because the resting potential is close to the potassium equilibrium potential of about -90 mV, the resting membrane is almost completely permeable to potassium, and only a few sodium leak channels make it slightly more positive.

concepts.title: The Refractory Period
concepts.content: There is an upper limit to how soon a neuron can conduct another action potential after one has passed, a span during which the neuron is refractory. During the absolute refractory period, no stimulus, however strong, can trigger another action potential, because the voltage-gated sodium channels are inactivated and cannot reopen until the membrane returns to the resting potential and they reset to their closed state. During the relative refractory period, an action potential can be fired, but a larger-than-normal depolarization is required because the membrane is transiently hyperpolarized by voltage-gated potassium channels that have not yet closed. Being further from threshold, a greater stimulus is needed to open the sodium channels and start a new action potential.

concepts.title: Synaptic Transmission
concepts.content: A synapse is a junction between the axon terminus of a neuron and the dendrites, soma, or axon of a second neuron, or between a neuron and an organ. Electrical synapses join the cytoplasms of two cells through gap junctions so that an action potential spreads directly from one cell to the next, which is important in smooth and cardiac muscle. Chemical synapses, common in the nervous system, convert the electrical impulse into a chemical signal by releasing neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft to act on the target cell. Whether the postsynaptic effect is excitatory (depolarizing) or inhibitory (hyperpolarizing) is determined by the receptor and its associated ion channel, not by the neurotransmitter itself, so the same neurotransmitter can be excitatory in one place and inhibitory in another. Each presynaptic neuron releases only one type of neurotransmitter, although a postsynaptic neuron may respond to many.

concepts.title: Summation
concepts.content: Because an action potential is all-or-nothing, the key regulated step in the nervous system is whether a neuron will fire, which happens when the postsynaptic membrane reaches the threshold of about -50 mV. The depolarization produced by a single synapse is usually too small, so a neuron adds up the inputs from its many synapses, both excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSPs), in a process called summation. In temporal summation, one presynaptic neuron fires so rapidly that its potentials pile up on top of each other. In spatial summation, the potentials from many different synapses are summed at a single moment in time. If the total reaches threshold an action potential fires, and a presynaptic neuron increases the intensity of its signal by firing more frequently, since it cannot change the size of an action potential.

concepts.title: Reflexes
concepts.content: A reflex is a direct motor response to sensory input that occurs without conscious thought and usually without any involvement of the brain. In the simplest case, the muscle stretch reflex, a sensory neuron detects stretch and synapses directly with a motor neuron in the spinal cord that causes the same muscle to contract; this two-neuron, one-synapse pathway is a monosynaptic reflex arc, seen when tapping the patellar tendon makes the quadriceps contract. The sensory neuron also activates an inhibitory interneuron that relaxes the opposing (antagonist) muscle, an example of reciprocal inhibition that lets the limb move. Efferent (motor) neurons carry information away from the CNS to effectors, which are muscles and glands, while afferent (sensory) neurons carry information toward the CNS.

problems.prompt: Any reflex involving skeletal muscle is considered polysynaptic. What is the best explanation for this?
choices: The somatic nervous system utilizes two neurons between the CNS and the effector organ.
The autonomic nervous system utilizes two neurons between the CNS and the effector organ.
Inhibition of the opposing muscle requires the use of an interneuron.
Activation of the contracting muscle requires the use of an interneuron.

concepts.title: Large-Scale Functional Organization
concepts.content: The peripheral nervous system divides into a somatic division, concerned with conscious sensation and deliberate, voluntary movement of skeletal muscle, and an autonomic division, concerned with involuntary processes such as digestion, metabolism, circulation, and perspiration. Both divisions include afferent (sensory) and efferent (motor) functions. The efferent portion of the autonomic division splits further into the sympathetic system, which prepares the body for fight or flight, and the parasympathetic system, which prepares the body to rest and digest. Many sympathetic effects result from epinephrine released into the bloodstream by the adrenal medulla, and in general the two systems exert opposing effects on organs such as the heart, gut, and airways.

concepts.title: CNS Anatomical Organization
concepts.content: The central nervous system consists of the brain and spinal cord, which float in cerebrospinal fluid for shock absorption and nutrient and waste exchange; most neuronal cell bodies lie in the CNS, clustered into structures called nuclei (versus ganglia in the PNS). The spinal cord relays information to and from the brain and mediates simple reflexes and primitive processes like walking. The hindbrain contains the medulla (autonomic functions such as blood pressure and respiratory rhythm), the pons (relay, balance, and some autonomic control), and the cerebellum (coordination of complex movement and balance), while the midbrain relays visual and auditory information and houses the reticular activating system for arousal. The forebrain includes the diencephalon, made up of the thalamus (a sensory relay) and the hypothalamus (the primary link between the nervous and endocrine systems and the main controller of homeostasis through the pituitary), and the telencephalon, the paired cerebral hemispheres. The cerebral cortex is divided into frontal lobes (voluntary movement and reasoning), parietal lobes (general sensation and taste), temporal lobes (auditory and olfactory processing, memory, language, and emotion), and occipital lobes (vision), with the basal nuclei aiding motor control and the limbic system handling emotion and memory.

problems.prompt: Which of the following areas of the brain is directly responsible for maintaining homeostatic mechanisms in the body?

concepts.title: Neurotransmitters
concepts.content: Neurotransmitters are broadly divided into excitatory transmitters, which increase the likelihood that the postsynaptic neuron fires, and inhibitory transmitters, which decrease it, though a given transmitter's actual effect varies with its location in the nervous system. Dopamine mediates reward, mood, pleasure, and smooth motor movement, and serotonin affects mood, digestion, sleep, and appetite; shortages of either are linked to depression. GABA is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter of the brain, whereas glutamate is the primary excitatory neurotransmitter and is involved in learning and memory. Acetylcholine excites at the neuromuscular junction and drives parasympathetic activity, while epinephrine and norepinephrine mediate the sympathetic fight-or-flight response and act as both hormones and neurotransmitters. Melatonin, technically a neurotransmitter-like substance, regulates circadian rhythm and the initiation of sleep.

concepts.title: PNS Anatomical Organization
concepts.content: All neurons entering and leaving the CNS travel in 12 pairs of cranial nerves, which connect to the brainstem, and 31 pairs of spinal nerves, which connect to the spinal cord; the vagus nerve is an important parasympathetic cranial nerve that slows the heart and increases GI activity. In the somatic system a single motor neuron runs from the CNS to a skeletal muscle using acetylcholine, and sensory neurons have their cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglia with their first synapse in the CNS. The autonomic system uses two neurons in series: a preganglionic neuron with its cell body in the CNS synapses in a ganglion with a postganglionic neuron that reaches the effector. All autonomic preganglionic neurons and all parasympathetic postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine, whereas nearly all sympathetic postganglionic neurons release norepinephrine. The sympathetic (thoracolumbar) system has few large ganglia near the spinal cord, while the parasympathetic (craniosacral) system has ganglia near the target organs.

problems.prompt: A researcher is designing an experiment to inhibit sympathetic nervous system effects. He decides to use a cholinergic antagonist for his experiment. Is this the best design for this experiment?
choices: Yes, because the sympathetic nervous system utilizes acetylcholine at the ganglion.
Yes, because the sympathetic nervous system utilizes adrenergic receptors at the organ.
No, because a cholinergic antagonist would activate the sympathetic nervous system.
No, because a cholinergic antagonist would target all divisions of the peripheral nervous system.

concepts.title: The Adrenal Medulla
concepts.content: Each adrenal gland sits atop a kidney and has an outer cortex and an inner medulla; the cortex is an endocrine gland that secretes glucocorticoids such as cortisol, mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone, and some sex hormones, but the medulla is part of the sympathetic nervous system. The adrenal medulla is embryologically derived from sympathetic postganglionic neurons and is directly innervated by sympathetic preganglionic neurons. When the sympathetic system is activated, the medulla releases epinephrine (adrenaline) into the bloodstream, so it is technically a hormone from a ductless gland even though it behaves much like a neurotransmitter. Its effects are rapid and short-lived, and ongoing release during fight-or-flight situations prolongs and enhances sympathetic effects, especially stimulation of the heart.

concepts.title: Types of Sensory Receptors
concepts.content: Each sensory receptor is designed to detect a single type of stimulus and to transmit that information to sensory neurons, which relay it to the CNS; receptors that sense the outside world are exteroceptors and those that respond to internal conditions are interoceptors, but the more important classification is by stimulus type. Mechanoreceptors respond to mechanical disturbances, such as Pacinian corpuscles that sense pressure deep in the skin and auditory hair cells that detect sound vibration in the cochlea. Chemoreceptors respond to particular chemicals and include olfactory and gustatory receptors as well as the autonomic chemoreceptors that monitor arterial pH, PCO2, and PO2. Nociceptors are pain receptors, usually simple free nerve endings that detect tissue damage, while thermoreceptors respond to temperature and electromagnetic receptors, the rods and cones of the retina, respond to light.

concepts.title: Encoding of Sensory Stimuli
concepts.content: Sensory receptors must encode four properties of a stimulus for the CNS. Modality, the type of stimulus, is signaled by which type of receptor is firing, and location is conveyed by the receptor's receptive field, with overlapping fields and lateral inhibition sharpening localization and discrimination. Intensity is coded by the frequency of action potentials, and the detectable dynamic range can be widened by range fractionation, using multiple receptor groups with limited but overlapping ranges (as cones do across the visual spectrum). Duration may or may not be explicitly coded: tonic receptors fire as long as the stimulus continues (though they show adaptation), while phasic receptors fire only when a stimulus begins or changes. Adaptation, a decrease in firing frequency when intensity stays constant, lets the brain tune out unimportant, unchanging information.

concepts.title: Proprioceptors
concepts.content: Proprioception refers to awareness of the position of one's own body parts, and proprioceptors are a broad category of receptors that provide it. An important example is the muscle spindle, a mechanoreceptor specialized to detect muscle stretch and the receptor responsible for the deep tendon reflex. Other proprioceptors include Golgi tendon organs, which monitor tension in tendons, and joint capsule receptors, which detect pressure, tension, and movement in the joints. By monitoring the musculoskeletal system, proprioception lets us know the positions of our body parts, which is most important during activity that requires precise feedback for coordinated motion, information used heavily by the cerebellum.

concepts.title: Gustation and Olfaction
concepts.content: Taste (gustation) and smell (olfaction) are senses that rely on chemoreceptors in the mouth and nasal passages, and much of what is assumed to be taste is actually smell. Taste buds can distinguish only five flavors, sweet (glucose), salty (sodium), bitter (basic), sour (acidic), and umami (amino acids and nucleotides), with each taste bud responding most strongly to one; a taste bud is an onion-shaped cluster of epithelial cells with a central taste pore and taste hairs that detect food chemicals. Taste information is carried by cranial nerves to an area of the temporal lobe. Olfactory receptors in the roof of the nasal cavity detect airborne chemicals that dissolve in the overlying mucus and project directly to the olfactory bulbs, located in the temporal lobe near the limbic system, which may explain why certain smells evoke vivid memories and emotions.

concepts.title: Hearing and the Vestibular System
concepts.content: The outer ear, consisting of the auricle and external auditory canal, is separated by the tympanic membrane from the middle ear, which contains three ossicles (the malleus, incus, and stapes) that amplify vibrations, with the stapes contacting the oval window that leads to the fluid-filled inner ear. Sound vibrations travel from air to bone to the fluids of the cochlea (perilymph and endolymph), setting the basilar membrane in motion; the basilar membrane is lined with hair cells whose cilia bend against the tectorial membrane, opening ion channels and triggering neurotransmitter release onto auditory neurons. Together the basilar membrane, hair cells, and tectorial membrane form the organ of Corti, the primary site of sound detection. Pitch is distinguished by which region of the basilar membrane vibrates, with high-frequency sounds stimulating hair cells near the oval window and low-frequency sounds at the apex, while loudness is coded by the amplitude of vibration. Having two ears allows stereophonic localization of a sound source, and auditory stimuli are processed in the temporal lobe.

concepts.title: Equilibrium and Balance
concepts.content: The vestibular complex is made up of the three semicircular canals, the utricle, the saccule, and the ampullae, all essentially tubes filled with endolymph that, like the cochlea, contain hair cells. Rather than detecting sound, these structures detect rotational acceleration of the head as well as static equilibrium and linear acceleration, which together contribute to the sense of balance. Afferent neurons carry this balance information to the pons, cerebellum, and other areas of the brain. The three semicircular canals, oriented in the three planes of space, are especially responsible for dynamic (rotational) equilibrium.

problems.prompt: Which of the following structures is involved in dynamic (rotational) equilibrium?

concepts.title: Vision: Structure and Function
concepts.content: The eye focuses an image on the retina, which detects light and converts it into action potentials sent to the brain. Light first passes through the cornea, a highly curved clear structure that does most of the refraction, then through the aqueous humor and the pupil, an opening in the pigmented iris whose muscles set its diameter, and then the lens, whose curvature is adjusted by the ciliary muscle to fine-tune focus. After crossing the vitreous humor, light reaches the retina, which contains the photoreceptors called rods and cones. Rods and cones synapse on bipolar cells, which synapse on ganglion cells whose axons form the optic nerve traveling toward the occipital lobe. The optic disk, where ganglion cell axons converge to form the optic nerve, is the blind spot because it lacks photoreceptors, whereas the fovea centralis within the macula contains only cones and provides the greatest visual acuity.

concepts.title: The Photoreceptors: Rods and Cones
concepts.content: Rods and cones contain pigment proteins called opsins, each bound to one molecule of retinal, which is derived from vitamin A and changes its tertiary structure upon absorbing light. In the dark the resting photoreceptor keeps a sodium channel open and stays depolarized, releasing the neurotransmitter glutamate onto bipolar cells; absorbing a photon converts retinal to the all-trans form, which closes the sodium channel, hyperpolarizes the cell, and reduces glutamate release. On-center bipolar cells are inhibited by glutamate while off-center bipolar cells are stimulated by it, so light produces opposite responses in the two cell types. Rods are more sensitive to dim light and motion and are concentrated in the periphery, providing night vision, while cones require abundant light, mediate color and high-acuity vision, and cluster in the fovea. Color vision depends on three types of cones tuned to blue, green, and red light, and the brain perceives hues by integrating their relative inputs.

problems.prompt: In mammalian rod cells, the inner and outer segments function together to establish a circuit of ion flow known as dark current. Given that the outer segment is continuously depolarized in the dark, which of the following best characterizes the flow of ions in a rod cell in the dark?
choices: Sodium and calcium enter the outer segment while potassium leaves the inner segment.
Sodium and calcium enter the inner segment while potassium leaves the outer segment.
Sodium leaves the inner and outer segments while potassium restores the resting membrane potential via active transport.
Sodium enters in the inner segment and is actively pumped out of the inner segment via a Na+/K+ ATPase.

concepts.title: Vision: Information Processing
concepts.content: For humans, vision is the primary sense, and its processing is highly complex and strongly shaped by expectations and past experience. Feature-detecting neurons in the visual cortex fire in response to very specific features such as lines, edges, angles, and movement, and their outputs are combined by later neurons into more complex objects, which is the basis of feature detection theory. To handle the enormous amount of visual information quickly, the brain uses parallel processing, analyzing aspects such as form, motion, color, and depth simultaneously rather than serially. The occipital lobe integrates these separate elements together with stored information to build a holistic image, and the brain devotes roughly 30 percent of the cortex to vision, far more than the small fractions given to touch or hearing.

concepts.title: General Sensory Processing
concepts.content: The absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus intensity required to activate a sensory receptor, and thus be detected, 50 percent of the time; it varies between individuals and species and changes with age, as when the ability to hear high-pitched sounds declines. The difference threshold, also called the just noticeable difference (JND), is the smallest change between two stimuli that can be detected 50 percent of the time, and its size depends on the magnitude of the original stimulus. Weber's Law states that two stimuli must differ by a constant proportion to be perceived as different, with the exact proportion varying by sense, roughly 2 percent for weight, 8 percent for light intensity, and 0.3 percent for tone frequency.

concepts.title: Hormone Types: Transport and Mechanisms of Action
concepts.content: The nervous and endocrine systems are the body's two major control systems; the nervous system is fast-acting with short-term effects, while the endocrine system is slower but has longer-lasting effects, and the two connect through the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. A hormone is a molecule secreted into the bloodstream by a ductless endocrine gland that acts on distant target cells possessing the appropriate receptor, in contrast to exocrine glands, which secrete their products through ducts. Tissue specificity of a hormone's action is determined by whether a tissue's cells carry the receptor for that hormone. Hormones fall into two classes: hydrophilic hormones, such as peptides and amino-acid derivatives, must bind receptors on the cell surface, whereas hydrophobic hormones, such as the steroids, bind receptors in the cell's interior.

problems.prompt: Which of the following is/are hormone(s) that target the intestine? I. Secretin  II. Enterokinase  III. Calcitriol

concepts.title: Peptide Hormones
concepts.content: Peptide hormones are synthesized into the rough ER, modified in the Golgi, and stored in vesicles until they are released by exocytosis, and being hydrophilic they dissolve in the plasma. Because they cannot cross the cell membrane, a peptide hormone acts as a first messenger that binds a cell-surface receptor, which then catalytically activates a second messenger cascade inside the cell, changing the activity of existing cytoplasmic proteins. A key feature of these cascades is signal amplification, so that a few activated receptors can alter the activity of many enzymes. Because they modify existing enzymes rather than making new proteins, peptide hormone effects are exerted rapidly, within minutes to hours, and are brief. The category includes polypeptides such as insulin, which has disulfide bridges, and amino-acid derivatives such as the catecholamines (including epinephrine) and thyroid hormones, both derived from tyrosine.

problems.prompt: The primary target of thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) is the thyroid gland. TSH activates the cAMP cascade in thyroid cells, which leads to downstream physiological effects that enhance thyroid hormone synthesis and thyroid gland growth. All of the following are true about TSH EXCEPT that it:
choices: is synthesized by the anterior pituitary.
binds to a cytosolic receptor that subsequently dimerizes.

concepts.title: Steroid Hormones
concepts.content: Steroid hormones are hydrophobic molecules synthesized from cholesterol in the smooth ER, and because they diffuse freely through membranes they are not stored but are made and released only as needed. Their hydrophobicity also means they cannot dissolve in the plasma, so they travel through the bloodstream bound to plasma proteins such as albumin. A steroid diffuses through the target cell's plasma membrane and binds a receptor in the cytoplasm; the hormone-receptor complex is then transported into the nucleus, where it acts as a sequence-specific regulator of transcription. Because they must change which proteins the cell makes, steroid effects appear slowly, over days, and persist for days to weeks. Steroids regulating sexuality and development come from the testes, ovaries, and placenta, while the adrenal cortex secretes steroids controlling water balance; thyroid hormone, though an amino-acid derivative, acts by a steroid-like mechanism.

problems.prompt: Anabolic-androgenic steroids are chemically derived from cholesterol and have both anabolic effects (increased protein synthesis and red blood cell production and increased skeletal muscle size) and androgenic effects (development of masculine characteristics). Endurance athletes use them for the increased red blood cell count while strength athletes use them for the increased lean mass, and although they mimic naturally produced hormones they remain among the most easily detected doping agents. Which of the following is correct about anabolic-androgenic steroids?
choices: They are difficult to detect because they are structurally similar to naturally produced hormones.
Marathon runners and anemic patients benefit from the same effect of anabolic-androgenic steroids.
Medicinal uses only take advantage of the anabolic effects.
Androgenic side effects only occur in men.

problems.prompt: Anabolic-androgenic steroids, like other steroid hormones, are derived from cholesterol. The pharmacodynamics of steroid hormones and peptide hormones differ due to the different chemical properties of these two classes of hormones. Which of the following is true regarding these differences?
choices: Steroid hormones need to be taken intravenously, whereas peptide hormones are readily taken orally.
Steroid hormones affect posttranslational changes, whereas peptide hormones only affect transcription.
Steroids begin their action with the production of second messengers, whereas peptide hormones begin their action when bound to their receptor.
Steroids activate their target intracellularly, whereas peptide hormones activate their target extracellularly.

problems.prompt: The androgenic-anabolic ratio measures whether a steroid's androgenic or anabolic effect dominates, and a smaller ratio indicates a relatively greater anabolic (weight- and muscle-building) effect. The following androgenic-anabolic ratios are reported: testosterone 1:1, fluoxymesterone 1:2, oxymetholone 1:3, nandrolone decanoate 1:4, and oxyandrolone 1:13. Which of the following steroids would be best used for a cancer patient whose weight has significantly decreased?

Anabolic-androgenic steroids are used medicinally to take advantage of their anabolic effects (such as increased muscle mass) and their androgenic effects (development of masculine characteristics, including progression of puberty in children). The passage lists acne as an adverse side effect of these steroids. Which of the following is/are medicinal use(s) of anabolic-androgenic steroids? I. Induction of puberty  II. Preventing lean muscle mass loss  III. Acne treatment

concepts.title: Organization and Regulation of the Human Endocrine System
concepts.content: Endocrine activity is coordinated automatically through feedback regulation rather than a preplanned schedule: the amount of a hormone secreted is controlled by the very variable that hormone regulates, as when rising serum calcium triggers calcitonin release that stops once calcium falls. Layered above these direct regulators are tropic hormones, which regulate other hormones; for example, adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) from the anterior pituitary stimulates the adrenal cortex to release cortisol, and cortisol in turn inhibits ACTH. Most feedback in the endocrine system is negative (feedback inhibition). The hypothalamus controls the system by secreting releasing and inhibiting factors, such as corticotropin releasing hormone, that regulate the anterior pituitary and reach it through the hypothalamic-pituitary portal system. The anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) is a true endocrine gland controlled by these factors, while the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) is composed of hypothalamic axons that release ADH and oxytocin directly into the blood.

problems.prompt: Naturally occurring anabolic-androgenic steroids, including testosterone, are products of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis: gonadotropin-releasing hormone from the hypothalamus stimulates release of LH and FSH from the anterior pituitary, which in turn stimulates testosterone production. Many of the side effects of anabolic-androgenic steroids result from feedback on this hypothalamic-pituitary axis. Which of the following is true regarding the nature of this interaction?
choices: It is a positive feedback cycle that results in an increase in hormone release from the anterior pituitary.
It is a negative feedback cycle that results in an increase in hormone release from the anterior pituitary.
It is a negative feedback cycle that results in a decrease in hormone release from the anterior pituitary.
It is a negative feedback cycle that results in a decrease in hormone release from the posterior pituitary.

concepts.title: Major Glands and Their Hormones
concepts.content: The hormones of the endocrine system govern gamete synthesis, growth, sexual development, and the maintenance of homeostasis, and the major glands and their products are summarized in the chapter. Thyroid hormone, produced from tyrosine and iodine in the thyroid under the control of anterior pituitary TSH, binds a cytoplasmic receptor to increase overall metabolic rate and body temperature and, in children, to stimulate growth. Cortisol, a glucocorticoid secreted by the adrenal cortex in response to ACTH, helps the body deal with stress by mobilizing glycogen, fat, and protein for energy, although chronically high levels suppress the immune system. The adrenal cortex also secretes the mineralocorticoid aldosterone, which makes the kidneys retain sodium and water to raise blood pressure, plus small amounts of sex steroids that an adrenal tumor can overproduce. Other examples include posterior-pituitary ADH and oxytocin, pancreatic insulin and glucagon, parathyroid hormone and calcitonin for calcium balance, and the gonadal steroids testosterone, estrogen, and progesterone.

problems.prompt: Anabolic steroids mimic testosterone in the body, producing several side effects including shrinking of the testes in males. An oversecreting tumor in which of the following glands might produce a similar result?
Addison's disease is a rare endocrine disorder in which the adrenal cortex produces insufficient amounts of steroid hormones. Patients with Addison's disease may experience which of the following?
choices: Low blood pressure and a craving for sweet foods
Low blood pressure and a craving for salty foods
High blood pressure and a craving for sweet foods
High blood pressure and a craving for salty foods

problems.prompt: The passage states that anabolic-androgenic steroid use can suppress naturally produced testosterone in men and that these steroids increase red blood cell (erythrocyte) production. Given that high testosterone levels are needed to support sperm development, a male athlete using anabolic steroids to increase muscle mass is also most likely to experience which of the following side effects?

children.title: The Circulatory, Respiratory, Lymphatic, and Immune Systems

concepts.title: Overview of the Circulatory System
concepts.content: The circulatory system distributes nutrients, oxygen, hormones, and heat while carrying carbon dioxide and metabolic wastes toward the organs that remove them, and it also handles clotting (hemostasis). Blood leaves the heart at high pressure through arteries, which branch into arterioles whose smooth muscle throttles flow into the capillaries, the thin single-cell-layer vessels where exchange with tissues occurs. Blood then collects in venules and veins and returns to the heart at low pressure. Humans have a double circuit: the right heart drives pulmonary circulation to the lungs, and the left heart drives systemic circulation to the body, so most blood crosses only one capillary bed per loop. Portal systems, such as the hepatic and hypothalamic-hypophysial systems, are exceptions in which blood passes through two capillary beds in series. The endothelial cells lining all vessels also regulate vasodilation, clotting, inflammation, and the growth of new vessels.

concepts.title: The Heart: Chambers and Valves
concepts.content: Each side of the heart has an atrium that collects returning blood and a thick-walled ventricle that pumps it out under high pressure. Deoxygenated systemic blood enters the right atrium from the venae cavae, moves to the right ventricle, and is sent through the pulmonary artery to the lungs; oxygenated blood returns via the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, then the left ventricle, and out the aorta. One-way flow is enforced by valves: the atrioventricular valves (tricuspid on the right, bicuspid or mitral on the left) stop backflow into the atria, and the pulmonary and aortic semilunar valves stop backflow from the great arteries into the ventricles. Because ventricular pressures are so high, these valves are essential to prevent regurgitation. Veins also contain valves that, aided by squeezing from surrounding skeletal muscle, keep low-pressure venous blood moving toward the heart.

problems.prompt: In a study of athlete's heart, each cohort's left ventricular mass is plotted as Z-scores relative to a healthy reference population, and a solid vertical line is drawn at a Z-score of +2. Given that the passage describes a healthy range for chamber mass whose upper limit is the point above which mass is considered dangerous, what purpose does including the solid line at a Z-score of +2 serve?
choices: To highlight the representative population mean
To highlight the smallest healthy ventricle size
To highlight the study population mean
To highlight the typical largest healthy ventricle size

problems.prompt: Which of the following is true of the left ventricle in humans?
choices: It receives blood from the left atrium via the tricuspid valve.
It has the greatest pressure in the heart.
It has the lowest pressure in the heart.
It sends blood to the lungs via the aorta.

problems.prompt: The figure plots the distribution of left ventricular mass (as Z-scores relative to a healthy reference population) for male and female athlete cohorts at ages 12, 15, and 18. The solid vertical line marks a Z-score of +2, the upper limit of the healthy reference range, and the p values comparing the male and female groups are not significant (NS) at age 12 but less than 0.01 at ages 15 and 18. Which of the following conclusions CANNOT be drawn from the passage and the figure?
choices: Only the male group had participants whose left ventricular mass was more than five standard deviations above the reference population average.
At all ages, both the male and female groups had participants whose left ventricular mass would be considered abnormal.
At all ages, the males in the study had a left ventricular mass greater than the females in the study.
At ages 15 and 18, there were more male participants with abnormal left ventricular masses than there were males with normal masses.

problems.prompt: Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM) is an autosomal dominant condition. A woman with ACM seeks genetic counseling; her partner does not have ACM and has no family history of it. Which of the following pieces of information, if true, would be the most useful in determining the likelihood of the woman having a child with ACM?
choices: The woman's mother and father both have ACM.
One of the woman's two siblings has ACM.
The woman has one child with ACM.
The woman has one child without ACM.

concepts.title: The Cardiac Cycle and Cardiac Output
concepts.content: The cardiac cycle alternates between diastole, when the relaxed ventricles fill and the atria give a final push, and systole, when the ventricles contract and eject blood. Rising ventricular pressure slams the atrioventricular valves shut (the 'lub'), and when pressure falls at the end of ejection the semilunar valves snap closed (the 'dup'); diastole is the longer phase. About two-thirds of the ventricular blood is ejected per beat, the ejection fraction, and the volume pumped per beat is the stroke volume. Cardiac output equals stroke volume times heart rate (CO = SV x HR), so a strong heart with a large stroke volume can maintain output at a low rate, which is why trained athletes have slow pulses. By the Frank-Starling mechanism, greater venous return stretches the heart muscle so it contracts more forcefully, automatically matching output to the blood delivered.

problems.prompt: In well-trained athletes, the resting heart rate often ranges between 45-50 beats/min, yet their resting cardiac output is no different from that of untrained individuals. Which of the following physiological mechanisms can account for this observation?
choices: The enlarged heart size of trained athletes physically limits their heart rate.
The stroke volume of trained athletes at rest is decreased compared to untrained individuals.
Trained athletes have developed enlarged hearts that can pump more blood per stroke.
Since cardiac output and heart rate are inversely proportional, the reduced heart rate naturally causes an increased cardiac output.

problems.prompt: On deep inhalation, increased chest capacity lowers thoracic pressure and a normal extra (third) heart sound can be heard, a phenomenon called normal splitting. What contributes to the presence of this additional heart sound?
choices: Earlier closure of the pulmonary semilunar valve due to increased pulmonary artery pressure
Earlier closure of the pulmonary semilunar valve due to decreased pulmonary artery pressure
Later closure of the pulmonary semilunar valve due to increased pulmonary artery pressure
Later closure of the pulmonary semilunar valve due to decreased pulmonary artery pressure

problems.prompt: Left ventricular ejection fraction is %LVEF = (SV / LV EDV) x 100, where SV is stroke volume and LV EDV is left ventricular end-diastolic volume. Using study data, an 18-year-old female athlete has an LV EDV of 115 mL and a 12-year-old male athlete has an LV EDV of 112 mL. Comparing an 18-year-old female with a stroke volume of 90 mL to a 12-year-old male with a stroke volume of 60 mL, which of the following is true?
choices: The 18-year-old female has a greater LVEF.
The 12-year-old male has a greater LVEF.

concepts.title: Cardiac Muscle and Electrical Conduction
concepts.content: Cardiac muscle is a functional syncytium: gap junctions in the intercalated discs let depolarization spread directly from cell to cell, so the atria and ventricles each contract as a unit. Cardiac action potentials use fast sodium channels plus slow calcium channels, which prolong depolarization into a plateau and give cardiac cells a long refractory period and a sustained contraction. The heartbeat is myogenic, arising in the sinoatrial (SA) node, whose leaky sodium channels drive spontaneous slow depolarization to threshold, making it the pacemaker; its upstroke is carried by calcium rather than sodium. The impulse travels through the atria and the internodal tract to the AV node, where it is briefly delayed, then races down the bundle of His, the bundle branches, and the Purkinje fibers to contract the ventricles from the apex upward. The autonomic system does not start the beat but tunes it: parasympathetic vagal tone releases acetylcholine to slow the SA node, while sympathetic norepinephrine and adrenal epinephrine increase rate and force.

problems.prompt: Which of the following statements is true regarding the speed of depolarization in various areas of the heart?
choices: Action potentials with rapid depolarization are found in the SA node and ventricular muscles.
Action potentials with rapid depolarization are found in the AV node, while action potentials with slower depolarization are found in the SA node.
Action potentials with slower depolarization are found in the SA node and the AV node.
Action potentials with slower depolarization are found in the AV node and ventricular muscles.

concepts.title: Hemodynamics: Resistance and Blood Pressure
concepts.content: Blood flow is driven by the pressure difference between arteries and veins and opposed by resistance, mainly friction in small vessels, summarized by an Ohm's-law analogy: pressure gradient = flow x resistance (AP = Q x R). Resistance is set chiefly by how much the arteriolar smooth muscle (precapillary sphincters) constricts, and the sympathetic nervous system maintains a baseline constriction called adrenergic tone that it can raise to increase pressure or redistribute blood between tissues. A reading such as 120/80 gives the peak systolic pressure during ventricular contraction over the minimum diastolic pressure between beats. Pressure is highest in the aorta and large arteries and falls to nearly zero by the vena cava as vessels branch. Elastic, muscular arteries stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, sustaining diastolic pressure so blood keeps flowing between beats. Local autoregulation lets an underperfused tissue vasodilate on its own as metabolic wastes accumulate, and it dominates coronary blood flow.

concepts.title: Components of Blood and Erythrocytes
concepts.content: Blood is about 55 percent plasma, water carrying electrolytes, glucose, bicarbonate buffer, wastes such as urea and bilirubin, and proteins like albumin, immunoglobulins, and fibrinogen, most of which are made by the liver. Albumin maintains oncotic pressure and fibrinogen enables clotting; if blood is allowed to clot, the remaining fluid, serum, is plasma minus the clotting proteins. The cellular formed elements are red cells, white cells, and platelets, all arising from bone marrow stem cells, and the fraction of blood volume that is red cells is the hematocrit (roughly 40-45 percent in men, somewhat lower in women). Red blood cells are produced in the marrow under the control of erythropoietin from the kidney and are removed by phagocytes in the spleen and liver after about 120 days. Lacking a nucleus and mitochondria, the red cell relies on glycolysis for ATP and uses its flat biconcave shape to maximize surface area for carrying hemoglobin and exchanging gases.

concepts.title: Blood Typing
concepts.content: Blood type is defined by the surface antigens on red cells, chiefly the ABO group (three alleles) and the Rh factor (dominant when present). Anti-A and anti-B antibodies form early in infancy without prior exposure, so a mismatched ABO transfusion triggers clumping and destruction of donor cells. Anti-Rh antibodies form only after an Rh-negative person is sensitized by Rh-positive blood, which becomes dangerous when an Rh-negative mother carries a later Rh-positive baby and can cause hemolytic disease of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis); injecting anti-Rh antibodies at delivery prevents sensitization. Type AB+ people make no anti-blood-group antibodies and are universal recipients, while type O- people carry none of these antigens and are universal donors. Matching donor and recipient types is still best whenever possible.

concepts.title: Leukocytes, Platelets, and Hemostasis
concepts.content: White blood cells fight infection and clear debris; unlike red cells they are full eukaryotic cells, and some (macrophages and neutrophils) crawl by amoeboid motility and follow chemical gradients (chemotaxis) out of capillaries into tissues. The six types are monocytes and their macrophages plus neutrophils (phagocytes), lymphocytes (B cells that make antibodies and T cells that kill infected or foreign cells and regulate immunity), eosinophils (parasites and allergy), and basophils (release histamine in allergy). Platelets are anucleate fragments of megakaryocytes that aggregate at a site of vessel damage to form a plug, the first step of hemostasis. A fibrin mesh then reinforces the plug when thrombin converts plasma fibrinogen into fibrin, a reaction requiring calcium, accessory clotting factors, and vitamin K. Defects in these clotting proteins cause hemophilia, an X-linked recessive bleeding disorder.

concepts.title: Transport of Oxygen and Hemoglobin
concepts.content: Oxygen is too hydrophobic to dissolve well in plasma, so it is carried by hemoglobin, a four-subunit protein whose heme irons each bind one O2, for four per molecule. The subunits bind cooperatively: loading the first O2 shifts hemoglobin from a low-affinity tense state toward a high-affinity relaxed state, producing the sigmoidal oxygen dissociation curve and a saturable, limited carrying capacity. Because affinity depends on conditions, hemoglobin grabs oxygen where it is plentiful (the lungs) and releases it where it is scarce (active tissues). The Bohr effect describes how low pH, high CO2, and high temperature stabilize the tense state and lower affinity, shifting the curve to the right, exactly the conditions found in metabolically active tissue. A left-shifted curve reflects higher affinity, as in the lungs, and all curves plateau at 100 percent saturation.

problems.prompt: Which of the following would LEAST increase oxygen delivery to a patient suffering from anemia due to chronic renal disease?
choices: Providing a nasal cannula with 100% oxygen
Intravenous injection of packed red blood cells
Administration of a drug stabilizing the oxygenated form of hemoglobin

concepts.title: Transport of Carbon Dioxide
concepts.content: Carbon dioxide leaves the tissues by three routes. Most (about 70 percent) is converted by the red-cell enzyme carbonic anhydrase into carbonic acid, which dissociates into bicarbonate and a proton (CO2 + H2O <-> H2CO3 <-> HCO3- + H+); these ions are very water soluble, and this reaction also makes bicarbonate the main blood pH buffer. About 20 percent binds directly to hemoglobin at sites separate from the oxygen-binding hemes, and this binding stabilizes tense hemoglobin, contributing to the Bohr effect. The remaining fraction (around 7 percent) is simply dissolved in plasma, since CO2 is more soluble than O2. In the lungs these processes reverse so that CO2 can be exhaled.

concepts.title: Capillary Exchange
concepts.content: Capillary walls are a single layer of endothelial cells with gaps (intercellular clefts) through which nutrients, wastes, and even amoeboid white cells pass, while small gases such as O2 and CO2 simply diffuse across the cells. Glucose and amino acids travel via the hepatic portal vein to the liver for storage and release, whereas dietary fats are packaged as chylomicrons that enter lacteals and lymph before reaching the blood. Water tends to leave capillaries because of the heart's hydrostatic pressure and the high osmolarity of tissues, so plasma is kept osmotically concentrated by large proteins, mainly albumin, which cannot escape the clefts; this pull is called oncotic pressure. Along a capillary, high hydrostatic pressure forces water out at the arterial end, and rising oncotic pressure draws most of it back in at the venous end, keeping net loss small. When the liver fails to make enough albumin, oncotic pressure drops and fluid collects in the tissues as edema.

concepts.title: Functions of the Respiratory System
concepts.content: The respiratory system exchanges O2 and CO2 between air and blood so that a large, complex body can supply every cell, even though gas movement across each cell membrane is still simple diffusion. Moving air in and out is ventilation, while the actual gas exchange is respiration; airways used only for airflow make up the conduction zone and gas-exchanging structures make up the respiratory zone. Breathing also regulates blood pH, because exhaling CO2 lowers carbonic acid and raises pH: overbreathing causes respiratory alkalosis and underbreathing causes respiratory acidosis, while the kidney handles slower pH adjustments over hours to days. Additional roles include thermoregulation through evaporative heat and water loss and protection against inhaled pathogens and particles via the mucociliary escalator and alveolar macrophages.

concepts.title: Anatomy of the Respiratory System
concepts.content: Inhaled air follows the conduction pathway: nose and nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, and terminal bronchioles. The nose warms, humidifies, and filters air; the larynx is made of cartilage that holds the airway open, carries the epiglottis that seals the trachea during swallowing, and houses the vocal cords. Cartilage rings keep the trachea and bronchi from collapsing, while smaller bronchioles have smooth-muscle walls (no cartilage) that adjust airflow, and their thick walls make the conduction zone unable to exchange gas. Gas exchange happens in the respiratory zone, where the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli have thin walls only one cell thick. Each alveolus is a tiny sac wrapped in capillaries so oxygen and carbon dioxide can diffuse between air and blood.

concepts.title: Respiratory Epithelium and Surfactant
concepts.content: Most of the airway is lined by tall columnar cells too thick for gas exchange; goblet cells among them secrete mucus, and apical cilia sweep this mucus, with its trapped pathogens and particles, up toward the pharynx to be swallowed or coughed out, a system called the mucociliary escalator. The gas-exchange surfaces instead use a single layer of thin, flat simple squamous epithelium so that diffusion is rapid, and because mucus cannot coat these surfaces, alveolar macrophages patrol them to engulf debris. Alveoli tend to collapse because surface tension from their thin water lining pulls the walls together. This is prevented by surfactant, a soapy phospholipid-and-protein mixture that lowers surface tension. Surfactant is made by cuboidal Type II alveolar cells, distinct from the thin squamous Type I cells that form most of the alveolar wall; premature infants may lack it and suffer collapsing alveoli.

concepts.title: Pulmonary Ventilation
concepts.content: Ventilation continually swaps alveolar gas with atmospheric air. Inspiration is active: the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the external intercostals lift the ribs, expanding the chest and lowering alveolar pressure so air flows in. Each lung is wrapped by two pleura, and the fluid-filled pleural space between them is held at negative pressure, a vacuum that keeps the lungs stuck to the chest wall and inflated. Resting expiration is passive, driven by the elastic recoil of the stretched lungs, though a forced expiration adds abdominal muscle contraction to push the diaphragm upward. Because the negative pleural pressure is the main force opposing collapse, puncturing the pleural space, either from outside or through a hole in the lung, lets air rush in and the lung collapses.

problems.prompt: Which of the following is a true statement about the diaphragm?
choices: It contains both skeletal and smooth muscle cells.
Its effector neurotransmitters are norepinephrine and acetylcholine.
It is innervated by both the phrenic nerve and the autonomic nervous system.
It receives neural signals from the cerebral cortex and the brain stem.

concepts.title: Lung Volumes and Capacities
concepts.content: Spirometry measures the air moved during the phases of breathing. Tidal volume is the small amount exchanged in normal quiet breathing (about 0.5 L), while the inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes are the extra air that can be inhaled or exhaled beyond a normal breath. The residual volume is the air always left after the strongest possible exhalation, so the lungs are never fully emptied. Capacities combine volumes: vital capacity is the most air movable between the deepest breath and the fullest exhalation, and total lung capacity is vital capacity plus residual volume. Loss of lung elasticity, as in emphysema, leaves more air trapped and raises both residual volume and total lung capacity.

concepts.title: Gas Exchange and Henry's Law
concepts.content: The pulmonary artery brings deoxygenated blood to a vast network of thin-walled alveolar capillaries that drain into the pulmonary veins, and the lungs' enormous surface area, near that of a tennis court, makes exchange efficient. Each gas in a mixture exerts a partial pressure proportional to its abundance, and the total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures (for example, oxygen is about 20 percent of 760 torr, roughly 150 torr). By Henry's law, the amount of a gas that dissolves in a liquid rises with its partial pressure and its solubility, and gases become less soluble as temperature increases. Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse down their partial-pressure gradients across the respiratory membrane, the alveolar epithelium, interstitium, and capillary endothelium, which these small nonpolar gases cross easily. If left atrial pressure rises too high, fluid is forced from the pulmonary capillaries into the lungs as pulmonary edema, which the lymphatic system normally helps prevent.

concepts.title: Regulation of Ventilation Rate
concepts.content: Breathing is normally involuntary, set by the respiratory control center in the medulla, though it can be overridden briefly. The main chemical drivers are rising PCO2 and falling pH, with low PO2 as a secondary stimulus; peripheral chemoreceptors in the aorta and carotid arteries sense PCO2, pH, and PO2 in the blood, while central chemoreceptors in the medulla sense PCO2 and pH in the cerebrospinal fluid. Because CO2 and pH are linked through the carbonic acid buffer system, changing ventilation quickly shifts blood pH: hyperventilation blows off CO2 and raises pH, while hypoventilation retains CO2 and lowers it. This lets the body compensate; for example, an acidotic diabetic breathes faster to expel CO2 and raise pH. Mechanical inputs also act: stretch receptors inhibit further inspiration, and irritant receptors trigger coughing and bronchoconstriction.

problems.prompt: A 20-year-old patient presents with acute asthma: wheezing, shortness of breath, inability to speak a full sentence, and a respiratory rate of 40 (normal 10-12). During this early phase he breathes rapidly to stay oxygenated. Which of the following arterial blood gas results would you expect? (Normal values: pH 7.4, Pco2 40 mm Hg, Po2 100 mm Hg)
choices: pH 7.40, Pco2 20 mm Hg, Po2 250 mm Hg
pH 9.40, Pco2 30 mm Hg, Po2 100 mm Hg
pH 7.50, Pco2 20 mm Hg, Po2 75 mm Hg
pH 6.90, Pco2 60 mm Hg, Po2 30 mm Hg

concepts.title: The Lymphatic System
concepts.content: The lymphatic system is a one-way network that begins as tiny lymphatic capillaries in the tissues and merges into larger vessels and ducts. Valves and smooth muscle in the larger ducts make it act like a suction pump that recovers water, dissolved solutes, protein, and white cells that leak from the periphery and returns them to the blood. The fluid, called lymph, is filtered through lymph nodes packed with white blood cells that can launch an immune response against anything foreign it carries. The vessels converge into the thoracic duct, the largest lymphatic vessel, which empties into a large vein near the neck. Intestinal lymphatics also deliver absorbed dietary fat as chylomicrons into this system.

problems.prompt:
Which of the following are most likely to be found traveling in the lymphatic system?
I. Protein
II. Fat-soluble vitamins
III. Red blood cells

concepts.title: Innate Immunity
concepts.content: Innate immunity is the body's general, nonspecific defense against invaders. The skin is a physical barrier that blocks most pathogens, and secretions such as tears, saliva, and blood contain lysozyme, an enzyme that kills some bacteria by breaking down their cell walls. The strong acidity of the stomach destroys many ingested or swallowed pathogens. Macrophages and neutrophils indiscriminately phagocytize microorganisms, and the complement system, a group of about twenty blood proteins, binds nonspecifically to foreign cell surfaces to mark or destroy them. Unlike the specific humoral and cell-mediated responses, these defenses do not target a particular antigen.

problems.prompt: Mycoplasma are bacteria that lack a cell wall and cause respiratory disorders; their infections resist many antibiotics, including penicillin. Which of the following forms of innate immune attack might Mycoplasma also be resistant to?

concepts.title: Humoral Immunity: Antibodies and B Cells
concepts.content: Humoral immunity uses antibodies (immunoglobulins), plasma proteins built from two light and two heavy chains joined by disulfide bonds, with constant regions that define the class (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, IgE) and variable regions that give each antibody its specificity. An antibody binds a small region, an epitope, of a target molecule called the antigen; very small molecules (haptens) provoke antibodies only when attached to a larger carrier. Binding can neutralize the antigen directly, tag it for phagocytosis, or activate complement to lyse the cell. Antibodies are made by B cells, each clone (assembled by gene recombination during development) recognizing one antigen; when antigen binds a matching immature B cell, it proliferates into antibody-secreting plasma cells and dormant memory cells, a process called clonal selection. The slow primary response on first exposure gives way to a fast, strong secondary response on re-exposure thanks to memory cells, which is the basis of lasting immunity and of vaccination.

problems.prompt: Multiple myeloma is a monoclonal plasma cell cancer originating in the bone marrow, and it is a common form of bone cancer in the elderly. What would be the most likely observation in a patient with multiple myeloma?
choices: Elevated IgG production from a plasma cell targeting a single epitope
Elevated IgG production from a plasma cell targeting multiple epitopes
Increased production of red blood cells

problems.prompt: mRNA vaccines can elicit a strong, broad immune response and carry no risk of integrating into the host genome. Which of the following best explains how mRNA vaccines prompt an immunogenic response?
choices: The mRNA is reverse transcribed into an immunogenic piece of DNA by reverse transcriptase.
The mRNA neutralizes host mRNA that codes for innate immune cell suppressors.
The mRNA is translated into an immunogenic protein that stimulates immune cells.
The mRNA is transcribed into an immunogenic protein that stimulates macrophages and B-cells.

concepts.title: Cell-Mediated Immunity and T Cells
concepts.content: T cells provide cell-mediated immunity and come in two main types: T helper (CD4) cells, the central controllers that activate B cells and other immune cells using signals such as lymphokines and interleukins, and T killer (cytotoxic CD8) cells, which destroy virus-infected cells, cancer cells, and foreign graft cells. T cells mature in the thymus, each carrying a T cell receptor specific for one antigen, but unlike B cells they do not secrete antibodies.
