They recognize targets by binding peptides displayed on major histocompatibility complex (MHC) proteins: MHC I is on every nucleated cell and shows samples of the cell's internal proteins so T killers can detect infection, while MHC II is limited to antigen-presenting cells such as macrophages and B cells, which phagocytize and display fragments to T helpers. Full T cell activation requires binding both the antigen and the MHC molecule, and the helper T cell is the cell that HIV infects.

problems.prompt: A cell culture is developed with an abnormal major histocompatibility complex (MHC) profile. What is the most likely profile of this cell line?
choices: Neither MHC I nor MHC II
Both MHC I and MHC II

concepts.title: Other Tissues of the Immune System
concepts.content: Several organs support immune function beyond the circulating cells. The bone marrow makes all the blood cells from a common bone marrow stem cell. The spleen filters blood, hosts immune-cell interactions like a lymph node, and also destroys aged red blood cells. The thymus is where T cells mature, and it shrinks in adults because immune maturation is most active in childhood. The tonsils are masses of lymphatic tissue at the back of the throat that trap inhaled or swallowed pathogens, and the appendix is similar in structure and function near the start of the large intestine; neither is required for survival.

concepts.title: Autoimmunity and Tolerance
concepts.content: The immune system should attack foreign antigens while ignoring the body's own molecules, a property called tolerance. Because the enormous variety of B and T cell receptors is generated randomly, many new cells recognize self-antigens and must be removed. A developing B cell that binds normal cell-surface proteins undergoes apoptosis, and one that binds normal soluble proteins becomes unresponsive (anergic); only cells that react to nothing normal are released. T cells go through a similar selection in the thymus and lymph nodes. When self-reactive cells escape this screening, they cause autoimmune disease, in which the body attacks its own tissues, as in type I diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, Graves' disease, myasthenia gravis, and celiac disease; these are often treated with immunosuppressant drugs or steroids.

concepts.title: The Excretory System Overview
concepts.content: The excretory system removes metabolic wastes and excess substances while maintaining homeostasis of water, electrolytes, pH, and blood pressure. Several organs contribute: the kidneys filter blood and make urine, the lungs expel carbon dioxide, the skin excretes water and salts in sweat, and the liver converts nitrogenous waste into urea and detoxifies compounds. The kidneys are the central organ, finely adjusting the composition and volume of body fluids. By regulating what is retained and what is excreted, the system keeps the internal environment stable. Wastes that are large or lipid-soluble are often modified by the liver before the kidney can clear them.

concepts.title: Anatomy of the Urinary System and the Nephron
concepts.content: Blood enters each kidney through the renal artery and is processed by roughly a million nephrons, the functional units. Each nephron begins at the glomerulus, a tuft of capillaries enclosed in Bowman's capsule, where blood is filtered. The filtrate then flows through the proximal convoluted tubule, the descending and ascending limbs of the loop of Henle, the distal convoluted tubule, and finally the collecting duct, which drains into the renal pelvis and ureter. The cortex holds the glomeruli and convoluted tubules, while the loops of Henle and collecting ducts dip into the medulla. The blood supply is arranged so that afferent and efferent arterioles bracket the glomerulus, giving the kidney unusual control over filtration.

concepts.title: Filtration, Reabsorption, and Secretion
concepts.content: Urine formation involves three processes: filtration at the glomerulus, selective reabsorption of useful substances back into the blood, and secretion of additional wastes into the tubule. Blood pressure drives filtration, so the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) depends on the pressure in the glomerular capillaries. The kidney can adjust GFR by changing arteriolar diameter: when blood pressure falls, dilating the afferent arteriole increases inflow while constricting the efferent arteriole traps blood in the glomerulus, both raising glomerular pressure and restoring GFR. The proximal tubule reabsorbs most water, glucose, amino acids, and ions, often by secondary active transport powered by Na+/K+ ATPase gradients. Secretion adds substances such as drugs, H+, and K+ to the forming urine.

problems.prompt: When blood pressure is low, which is the best description of the response in the renal arterioles that helps restore the glomerular filtration rate?
choices: Constriction of afferent arterioles, dilation of efferent arterioles
Constriction of both afferent and efferent arterioles
Dilation of afferent arterioles, constriction of efferent arterioles
Dilation of both afferent and efferent arterioles

concepts.title: The Loop of Henle and Urine Concentration
concepts.content: The loop of Henle works as a countercurrent multiplier, using the opposite permeabilities and flow directions of its descending and ascending limbs to build a strong osmotic gradient in the medulla. The descending limb is permeable to water but not solutes, while the ascending limb pumps out salt but is impermeable to water. This medullary gradient lets the collecting duct reabsorb water as filtrate passes through, so the kidney can produce urine more concentrated than blood. Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) increases the collecting duct's water permeability by inserting aquaporins, further concentrating the urine when the body must conserve water. Without this arrangement, mammals could not make hyperosmotic urine.

problems.prompt: The loop of Henle acts as a countercurrent multiplier within the kidney. What is the significance of this structural arrangement as part of the nephron?
choices: Na+ is secreted into the filtrate while K+ is reabsorbed into the blood.
Urine osmolarity can exceed blood osmolarity.
The countercurrent multiplier triggers the release of renin from the liver.
Aquaporins can be inserted along the descending loop of Henle to alter its permeability to water.

concepts.title: Renal Regulation of Blood Pressure and pH
concepts.content: The kidney regulates blood pressure mainly through the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. When renal perfusion or filtration falls, juxtaglomerular (JG) cells secrete renin, which ultimately generates angiotensin II, a potent vasoconstrictor that also stimulates aldosterone and ADH release to increase sodium and water reabsorption, raising blood volume and pressure. A narrowed renal artery (as in fibromuscular dysplasia) lowers GFR and triggers renin, causing systemic hypertension, which is why angiotensin II receptor antagonists lower blood pressure by blocking that receptor. Atrial natriuretic factor (ANF), released by the heart when blood pressure rises, opposes this system by increasing renal sodium and water excretion. The kidney also helps control blood pH by excreting hydrogen ions and reabsorbing bicarbonate.

problems.prompt: Fibromuscular dysplasia is an autosomal dominant disorder that causes abnormal narrowing in the renal arteries. Which of the following explains why patients with fibromuscular dysplasia often present with systemic hypertension?
choices: The decreased diameter of the renal artery causes vessel walls to exert more pressure on the blood.
The macula densa in the distal tubule responds to increased filtrate osmolarity by stimulating renin secretion.
Fibromuscular dysplasia causes systemic hypotension, so the JG cells secrete renin to compensate.
The decreased glomerular filtration rate ultimately leads to the secretion of renin by the JG cells.

problems.prompt: Angiotensin II receptor antagonists are a class of drugs commonly prescribed to treat hypertension. All of the following are possible explanations for why they can lower systemic blood pressure EXCEPT:
choices: they are similar in structure to angiotensin receptors, so they bind angiotensin II and prevent it from activating its endogenous receptor.
they are similar in structure to angiotensin II, thereby competitively inhibiting the angiotensin II receptors.
blockage of angiotensin II receptors leads to vasodilation.
blockage of angiotensin II receptors reduces aldosterone and ADH secretion.

problems.prompt: In Addison's disease, levels of aldosterone are much lower than normal. Which of the following symptoms would be expected in patients with this disease? I. Hypotension; II. Lower urine osmolarity; III. Decreased hematocrit
Atrial natriuretic factor (ANF) is a peptide hormone that is released in response to an increase in blood pressure. Which of the following is true about ANF?
choices: It is released by the kidney; it causes a decrease in renal Na+ excretion.
It is released by the heart; it causes an increase in renal Na+ excretion.
It is released by the kidney; it causes an increase in renal Na+ excretion.
It is released by the heart; it causes a decrease in renal Na+ excretion.

concepts.title: The Digestive System Overview
concepts.content: The digestive system breaks food into absorbable molecules and eliminates the residue through the coordinated steps of ingestion, digestion, absorption, and egestion. Digestion is both mechanical (chewing, churning) and chemical (enzymatic hydrolysis). Food travels through the alimentary canal, a continuous tube from mouth to anus, aided by accessory organs that secrete enzymes and other substances. Smooth muscle contractions called peristalsis move material along the tract in one direction. The end products of digestion are absorbed mainly in the small intestine, while water is reclaimed in the large intestine.

concepts.title: The Mouth, Esophagus, and Stomach
concepts.content: Digestion begins in the mouth, where chewing and salivary amylase start breaking food into a bolus that is swallowed into the esophagus. In the esophagus a primary peristaltic wave, and if needed secondary waves, propel the bolus toward the stomach and relax the lower esophageal (cardiac) sphincter; esophageal smooth muscle contracts by a calcium-calmodulin mechanism that activates myosin light-chain kinase. The stomach stores food and secretes hydrochloric acid from parietal cells, creating a low pH that begins protein digestion and, together with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori, can contribute to peptic ulcers. Because acid is central to ulcer formation, effective therapy combines an antibiotic with a parietal-cell antagonist to suppress acid. Esophageal peristalsis is not slowed by sympathetic activation, since basic swallowing must continue even during a fight-or-flight response.

problems.prompt: Helicobacter pylori, a bacterium found in the stomach and duodenum, has been implicated in the formation of peptic ulcers (lesions due to inflammation and low pH). Which of the following would be the most effective initial treatment?
choices: Solid antacids to neutralize the stomach acid
Parietal cell agonist to kill the H. pylori
Oral antibiotic and parietal cell antagonist

problems.prompt: Patients with unexplained chest pain unresponsive to acid-reflux treatment were tested for exercise-provoked esophageal spasms (EPES), and all were given long-term calcium-channel antagonists; hospital admissions for suspected acute coronary syndrome (ACS) were then tracked. Based on the text and the Kaplan-Meier curve in Figure 1, which of the following statements is supported?
choices: Ca2+ channel blockers are more effective in preventing ACS hospitalization long-term in EPES+ patients than EPES- patients.
At and after 1200 days, the EPES+ patients had approximately twice the total number of hospitalizations from ACS compared to the EPES- group.
Smoking contributed to the higher rates of hospitalizations among EPES- patients.
In the study population, the EPES+ group was demonstrated to have lower ACS hospitalization rates after two or more years since their treadmill stress test.

problems.prompt: In esophageal smooth muscle, calcium binds calmodulin, which activates myosin light-chain kinase; phosphorylation of the myosin light chain enables cross-bridging and contraction. A researcher creates an inducible knockout that limits calmodulin expression in the digestive tract. Which of the following would be a likely effect in the digestive tract?

A figure shows esophageal smooth muscle innervation: the vagus nerve releases acetylcholine (ACh) onto a postganglionic neuron, which can release ACh and Substance P (SP) that stimulate (+) smooth muscle contraction, or NO/VIP/ATP that inhibit (-) it. According to this, which of the following would lead to smooth muscle contraction in the esophagus?
choices: Destruction of the rostral portion of the dorsal motor nucleus (DMN)
Addition of a Substance P (SP) agonist

problems.prompt: In the EPES study, all participants received calcium-channel blockers, and independent variables such as smoking and BMI had p-values greater than 0.05. Which of the following is a limitation of the study?
choices: There is no consideration for participants who dropped out of the study.
There is no way to tell if the Ca2+-channel blockers contributed to ACS hospitalizations.
There is no way to determine if there are other differences between the EPES+ and EPES- groups contributing to ACS hospitalizations.
The small number of participants increased the p-value such that the data is statistically insignificant.

problems.prompt: A woman quickly eats a roll but, after a very large final bite, feels as though she cannot move it down her entire esophagus. She is not having difficulty breathing but has sharp central chest pains every few seconds that build for several minutes and then suddenly end. What is the likely source of pain and why is she having difficulty swallowing?
choices: Primary peristaltic wave, increased pyloric sphincter tone
Primary peristaltic wave, increased cardiac sphincter tone
Secondary peristaltic wave, increased pyloric sphincter tone
Secondary peristaltic wave, increased cardiac sphincter tone

problems.prompt: Activation of the sympathetic autonomic nervous system would have what effect on esophageal peristalsis?

concepts.title: The Small and Large Intestine
concepts.content: The small intestine is the main site of chemical digestion and nutrient absorption, greatly aided by folds, villi, and microvilli that expand its surface area. Absorption is further optimized by mixing contractions that spread chyme evenly, by increased blood flow during digestion that carries away absorbed nutrients, and by Na+/K+ ATPase gradients that power secondary active transport of nutrients such as glucose. Humans cannot digest cellulose because they lack the necessary enzyme, though some animals rely on gut bacteria that can. The large intestine reabsorbs water and houses bacteria that produce vitamin K, and bariatric surgery can promote weight loss by shrinking the stomach while leaving the small intestine's absorptive brush border intact to prevent malnutrition.

problems.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a way in which the absorptive capacity of the small intestine is optimized?
choices: Villi and microvilli increase the surface area of the small intestine.
Smooth muscle contractions mix the chyme, allowing evenly distributed absorption.
Blood flow to the small intestine is decreased during digestion.
Na+/K+ ATPases maintain chemical and electrical gradients across cell membranes.

problems.prompt: Some animals can digest cellulose, while humans cannot. What is a likely explanation for this phenomenon?
choices: Other animals have bacteria living in their digestive tracts that are capable of digesting cellulose.
In humans, cellulose is physically inaccessible to the enzymes that can hydrolyze it into glucose.
Humans lack a protease necessary for cellulose digestion.
Cellulose blocks absorption of nutrients by microvilli.

problems.prompt: Many techniques in bariatric surgery minimize the size or role of the stomach in the GI tract. Why does this accomplish weight loss while not contributing to malnutrition?
choices: Patients are counseled post-operatively to consume a high-protein diet that severely restricts fruits or grains.
The intestinal flora are still able to produce vitamin K.
The techniques minimize the storage capacity of the GI tract while maintaining the brush border properties of the small intestine.
Patients experience enough post-operative discomfort to discourage them from returning to their prior eating habits.

concepts.title: The GI Accessory Organs
concepts.content: Several organs aid digestion without being part of the main tube. The liver produces bile, an emulsifier derived from cholesterol that breaks fats into small droplets, and the gallbladder stores and concentrates it. The pancreas secretes digestive enzymes and bicarbonate that neutralizes stomach acid entering the small intestine. Salivary glands add amylase and lubrication in the mouth. The liver also processes absorbed nutrients and, as the source of bile, links cholesterol metabolism to digestion, since bile, steroid hormones, and vitamin D are all derived from cholesterol.

problems.prompt: Which of the following are derived from cholesterol? I. Vitamin D; II. Steroid hormones; III. Bile

concepts.title: Digestion and Absorption of Nutrients
concepts.content: Each class of macronutrient is digested by specific enzymes and absorbed in characteristic ways. Carbohydrates are broken by amylases and brush-border enzymes into monosaccharides that are absorbed into the blood. Proteins are cleaved by pepsin in the stomach and by pancreatic proteases into amino acids and small peptides; note that proteases cannot break down carbohydrates such as cellulose. Fats are emulsified by bile, digested by lipases, and absorbed as fatty acids and monoglycerides that are repackaged and enter the lymphatic system. The tightly coordinated timing and location of these steps ensure efficient extraction of nutrients.

concepts.title: Vitamins
concepts.content: Vitamins are organic micronutrients required in small amounts for normal metabolism. They are grouped as fat-soluble (A, D, E, and K) or water-soluble (the B vitamins and vitamin C); fat-soluble vitamins can be stored in body fat while water-soluble ones are generally not stored and are excreted in urine. Vitamin D is unusual in that it is produced photochemically in the skin from a cholesterol derivative and then activated by the liver and kidney to form calcitriol, the hormone that increases intestinal calcium absorption. Gut bacteria in the large intestine synthesize vitamin K, which is needed for blood clotting. Because some vitamins depend on dietary fat or gut flora, digestion and absorption strongly influence vitamin status.

concepts.title: Overview of Muscle Tissue
concepts.content: There are three types of muscle that differ in cellular physiology, anatomy, and function. Skeletal (voluntary) muscle contracts in response to conscious intent, cardiac muscle is found only in the wall of the heart, and smooth muscle lines the walls of hollow organs such as the GI tract, blood vessels, and uterus. Skeletal and cardiac muscle are described as striated because of their banded microscopic appearance, whereas smooth muscle is not striated. We have no conscious control over cardiac or smooth muscle because they are innervated only by the autonomic nervous system.

concepts.title: Movement of Joints
concepts.content: Skeletal muscle produces voluntary movement of the body in response to stimulation by somatic motor neurons, but muscle alone cannot move the body; it requires the bony framework of the skeleton. Each skeletal muscle is attached at both of its ends to two different bones, most often by tendons, which are strong connective tissue formed primarily of collagen. By contracting, a skeletal muscle draws the points of attachment on the two bones closer together.

concepts.title: Structure of Skeletal Muscle
concepts.content: A skeletal muscle contains both muscle tissue and connective tissue that holds the fibers together in bundles called fascicles. Each muscle fiber (myofiber) is a single skeletal muscle cell; these cells are multinucleate syncytia formed by the fusion of many individual cells during development, and their membrane is called the sarcolemma. Within each fiber are many myofibrils, built from the contractile proteins actin (thin filaments) and myosin (thick filaments). The overlapping arrangement of thick and thin filaments into repeating units called sarcomeres gives skeletal muscle its striated appearance. Each sarcomere is bounded by two Z lines, with thin filaments anchored to the Z lines and thick filaments spanning the middle.

problems.prompt: Which of the following are characteristics of skeletal muscle fibers? I. Striated; II. Uninucleate; III. Action potential similar to that of a neuron

concepts.title: The Sliding Filament Model of Muscle Contraction
concepts.content: Contraction occurs when the thin and thick filaments slide across one another, drawing the Z lines of each sarcomere closer together and shortening the cell, while the filaments themselves do not change length. Sliding is powered by ATP hydrolysis by myosin, which acts as an enzyme (myosin ATPase); each myosin head binds a myosin-binding site on actin to form a cross bridge. The cycle has four steps: cross-bridge formation (myosin carrying ADP and Pi binds actin), the power stroke (the head pivots to a low-energy conformation and pulls actin toward the center, releasing ADP), binding of a new ATP that is required for the head to release actin, and ATP hydrolysis that re-cocks the head for another cycle. It is key to remember that a new ATP is needed for release of actin, not to drive the power stroke.

concepts.title: Excitation-Contraction Coupling in Skeletal Muscle
concepts.content: The four contractile steps occur spontaneously if actin, myosin, ATP, and Mg2+ are mixed in a beaker, but in the myofiber contraction happens only when cytoplasmic [Ca2+] rises. This is because the thin filament also carries the troponin-tropomyosin complex: tropomyosin is a long fibrous protein that winds around actin and blocks the myosin-binding sites at rest. Troponin is a globular protein bound to tropomyosin that can bind Ca2+, and when it does it undergoes a conformational change that moves tropomyosin out of the way, exposing the binding sites so cross bridges can form. Thus the binding of Ca2+ to troponin is the switch that permits contraction.

problems.prompt: Intracellular acidosis leads to a decrease in the calcium (Ca2+) sensitivity of the myofilament. A study found that acidosis inhibits crossbridge formation at submaximal intracellular [Ca2+], but this effect disappears as [Ca2+] increases. Based on these findings, which of the following may explain the mechanism?
choices: H+ competitively inhibits troponin; tropomyosin covers the myosin binding sites on actin.
H+ allosterically inhibits troponin; tropomyosin covers the myosin binding sites on actin.
H+ competitively inhibits troponin; tropomyosin covers the actin binding sites on myosin.
H+ prevents the release of actin from myosin.

concepts.title: The Neuromuscular Junction and Impulse Transmission
concepts.content: The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) is the synapse between a motor neuron's axon terminus and a myofiber; the postsynaptic muscle membrane is the motor end plate, and the neurotransmitter is acetylcholine (ACh). An arriving action potential opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, triggering ACh release; ACh binds ligand-gated Na+ channels on the end plate, producing an end plate potential. When summation brings the membrane to threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open and propagate an action potential across the fiber, and this AP has the same steeply spiking shape as a neuronal action potential. The AP spreads into the fiber's interior through transverse (T) tubules, depolarizing the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR), which releases stored Ca2+ to trigger contraction; ACh is then broken down by acetylcholinesterase, and Ca2+ is actively resequestered by the SR to end contraction.

problems.prompt: Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) is responsible for breaking down acetylcholine (ACh) that has been released into a synapse. What would be the effect of reduced AChE at the neuromuscular junction?
choices: ACh concentrations would be lowered, and the muscle would be inhibited from contracting.
ACh concentrations would be lowered, and the muscle would be stimulated to contract continuously.
ACh concentrations would be increased, and the muscle would be inhibited from contracting.
ACh concentrations would be increased, and the muscle would be stimulated to contract continuously.

problems.prompt: Researchers developing a signal transduction inhibitor (STI) to treat fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva find that in an animal model the drug increases muscular intracellular calcium, which results in increased muscular tone. Which of the following is the LEAST likely cause of this increase in intracellular calcium?
choices: The STI acts as a receptor antagonist on the motor endplate.
The STI decreases the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane integrity.
The STI inhibits the Ca2+-ATPase of the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

concepts.title: Mechanics of Contraction
concepts.content: The smallest measurable muscle contraction is a muscle twitch, and the nervous system can increase the force of contraction in two ways. In motor unit recruitment, activating (recruiting) more motor neurons, each of which innervates a group of myofibers called a motor unit, recruits more fibers and produces a larger contraction. In frequency summation, stimulating the fiber again before the SR can resequester Ca2+ lets a second contraction build on the first; a rapidly repeating series of stimulations produces the strongest possible sustained contraction, called tetanus. This normal use of tetanus should not be confused with the disease tetanus caused by a bacterial toxin.

concepts.title: Energy Storage in the Myofiber
concepts.content: ATP powers contraction, but glycolysis and the TCA cycle cannot regenerate it fast enough during extended activity, so creatine phosphate serves as an intermediate-term energy store whose hydrolysis regenerates ATP from ADP and Pi. Muscle is highly aerobic and rich in mitochondria, and myoglobin (a globular protein similar to one subunit of hemoglobin) provides an oxygen reserve. During prolonged contraction oxygen runs low and metabolism becomes anaerobic, producing lactic acid that lowers blood pH; the liver takes up the lactate and converts it to pyruvate. Cramps can result from temporary ATP depletion, and rigor mortis is the rigidity of muscles after death caused by complete ATP exhaustion, because without ATP the myosin heads cannot release actin.

problems.prompt: When a coroner conducts a postmortem assessment, one factor examined is the onset and progression of rigor mortis, which is characterized by rigidity of the skeletal muscles. What is the best explanation for this phenomenon?
choices: The body can no longer thermoregulate, and muscles become stiff due to the cold.
The muscles become rigid in the early phases of decomposition.
The muscles can no longer perform the power stroke due to a lack of ATP.
Myosin is unable to release actin, so the crossbridges remain intact.

concepts.title: Muscle Fiber Types
concepts.content: Skeletal muscle fibers fall broadly into slow twitch and fast twitch categories, where slow and fast refer to how long they take to reach maximum tension. Type I (red, slow oxidative) fibers have high myoglobin content and a dense capillary supply, so they resist fatigue and can maintain contraction for extended periods, as in marathon running and long-distance cycling. Type II fast twitch fibers contract quickly and subdivide by fatigue resistance: Type IIA (fast twitch oxidative) fibers have more mitochondria and moderate endurance, while Type IIB (white) fibers lack mitochondria and contract very quickly with great force but fatigue within about a minute, providing explosive power. Force and speed of contraction are highest in Type IIB fibers and lowest in Type I fibers.

problems.prompt: In terms of the number of fibers, the fiber-type composition of skeletal muscle remains mostly unchanged after birth; however, it is possible to increase the size of different fibers with training. Which of the following can be expected when comparing the fiber-type composition in the leg muscles of Olympic runners?
choices: Sprinters should have larger Type I fibers, whereas marathon runners should have larger Type IIa fibers.
Sprinters should have larger Type I fibers, whereas marathon runners should have larger Type IIb fibers.
Sprinters should have larger Type IIb fibers, whereas marathon runners should have larger Type I fibers.
Sprinters should have larger Type IIa fibers, whereas marathon runners should have larger Type I fibers.

concepts.title: Cardiac Muscle Compared to Skeletal Muscle
concepts.content: Cardiac muscle resembles skeletal muscle in that its filaments are organized into striated sarcomeres, it has T-tubules, and troponin-tropomyosin regulates contraction the same way. It differs in important ways: cardiac cells each have a single nucleus (they are not syncytial) but are joined to neighbors by gap junctions at intercalated disks, making the heart a functional syncytium in which action potentials spread cell to cell. Some of the Ca2+ for cardiac contraction enters from the extracellular fluid through voltage-gated calcium channels, though the predominant source is still the SR, whereas skeletal muscle uses only SR calcium. Cardiac contraction does not depend on motor neurons, and the cardiac action potential has a distinctive plateau produced by slow voltage-gated calcium channels, giving a long refractory period that makes tetanus impossible.

problems.prompt: A researcher is measuring the movement of calcium in a cardiac muscle cell and notes that calcium can enter the cytoplasm from either the extracellular space or the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR). Which of the following statements is true regarding this calcium movement?
choices: Most of the cytoplasmic calcium comes from the extracellular space.
Most of the cytoplasmic calcium comes from the SR.
Equal amounts of calcium enter the cytoplasm from the extracellular space and the SR.
In some cardiac muscle cells calcium comes mostly from the extracellular space, while in others the predominant source is the SR.

problems.prompt: In fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP), heterotopic bone replaces skeletal muscle and connective tissue. A pathologist examines a biopsied tissue sample under high resolution and observes numerous red, uninucleate, striated cells. Is this an appropriate tissue sample for determining whether the patient is suffering from FOP?
choices: Yes, because heterotopic bone replaces skeletal muscle.
Yes, because heterotopic bone replaces connective tissue.
No, because it is not a bone sample.
No, because FOP does not affect cardiac muscle.

concepts.title: Smooth Muscle Compared to Skeletal Muscle
concepts.content: Smooth muscle contracts by the same four-step actin-myosin sliding cycle and, like skeletal muscle, is triggered by a rise in cytoplasmic [Ca2+], but it differs in many ways. Its cells are much smaller and single-nucleated, lack T-tubules, and are connected to neighbors by gap junctions, forming a functional syncytium; because their filaments are not organized into sarcomeres, the tissue appears smooth rather than striated. Smooth muscle lacks the troponin-tropomyosin complex and instead regulates contraction through calmodulin, which binds Ca2+ and activates myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK) to phosphorylate and activate myosin. Its SR is poorly developed, so the cell relies heavily on extracellular Ca2+, and it is innervated by autonomic rather than somatic motor neurons.

concepts.title: Overview of the Skeletal System
concepts.content: As vertebrates we have an endoskeleton made of bone, in contrast to the chitinous exoskeleton of arthropods. The vertebrate skeletal system serves five roles: supporting the body, providing the framework for movement, protecting vital organs such as the brain and heart, storing calcium, and synthesizing the formed elements of blood (hematopoiesis) in the marrow of flat bones. The endoskeleton is divided into the axial skeleton, which consists of the skull, vertebral column, and rib cage, and the appendicular skeleton, which comprises all the other bones.

concepts.title: Connective Tissue
concepts.content: Bone is an example of connective tissue, and all connective tissue cells derive from a single progenitor, the fibroblast, which secretes fibrous proteins such as collagen (strong) and elastin (which lets tissue stretch and recoil). Unlike epithelial, muscle, and nervous tissue, which are mostly cellular, connective tissue is primarily extracellular material with a few scattered cells; this matrix consists of fibers plus a thick, viscous ground substance. The ground substance is made largely of proteoglycans, whose attached glycosaminoglycan (GAG) chains are highly hydrophilic and hold water, giving tissues their characteristic thickness and firmness. Connective tissue is classified as loose (such as areolar and adipose tissue) or dense (such as tendons, ligaments, cartilage, and bone), with cartilage and bone sometimes called supportive connective tissue.

concepts.title: Bone Structure
concepts.content: Bones are either flat (such as the scapula, ribs, and skull bones), which are the sites of hematopoiesis and protect organs, or long (the limb bones), whose main shaft is the diaphysis and whose flared ends are the epiphyses. Bone tissue is either compact (hard and dense) or spongy (porous, made of spikes called spicules or trabeculae surrounding marrow cavities), and spongy bone is always surrounded by a shell of compact bone. Red marrow, found in the spongy bone of flat bones, is the site of hematopoiesis and increases its activity in response to erythropoietin from the kidney, while yellow marrow in the shafts of long bones is filled with fat and is inactive. Microscopically, bone is built from collagen laid down in an ordered framework and hardened by hydroxyapatite (calcium phosphate crystals); the structural unit of compact bone is the osteon, with concentric lamellae around a central canal and osteocytes sitting in lacunae connected by canaliculi.

concepts.title: Cartilage
concepts.content: Cartilage is a strong but very flexible extracellular tissue secreted by cells called chondrocytes, and it comes in three types. Hyaline cartilage is strong and somewhat flexible and reinforces the larynx and trachea and lines joints as articular cartilage; elastic cartilage contains elastin and provides more flexibility in structures such as the outer ear and epiglottis; and fibrous cartilage is very rigid and is found where strong support is needed, such as the pubic symphysis and the intervertebral disks. Cartilage is avascular and is not innervated, receiving its nutrition and immune protection from the surrounding fluid. Because its cells have a low metabolic rate and are not directly supplied by blood, cartilage injuries heal slowly.

concepts.title: Ligaments, Tendons, and Joints
concepts.content: Ligaments and tendons are strong tissues made of dense connective tissue; ligaments connect bones to other bones, and tendons connect bones to muscles. A joint is the point where one bone meets another: immovable joints (synarthroses) are essentially fused, as in the skull; slightly movable joints (amphiarthroses) provide movability plus support, as in the vertebral joints; and freely movable joints (diarthroses), such as ball-and-socket and hinge joints, are supported by ligaments. Movable joints are lubricated by synovial fluid held within the synovial capsule, and the contacting bone surfaces are covered by smooth articular (hyaline) cartilage. Because this articular cartilage lacks blood vessels it is easily damaged by overuse or infection, and inflammation of the joint (arthritis) destroys it, causing pain and stiffness.

concepts.title: Bone Growth and Remodeling; The Cells of Bone
concepts.content: Most bone forms by endochondral ossification, in which hyaline cartilage is produced and then replaced by bone. Long bones lengthen at the epiphyseal plate, a disk of hyaline cartilage between the diaphysis and epiphysis; growth hormone stimulates ossification, and around age 18 the plate fully ossifies (becoming the epiphyseal line) so lengthening stops. In adults bone is continually remodeled: osteoblasts build bone by laying down collagen and hydroxyapatite and become osteocytes once surrounded by matrix, while osteoclasts, large phagocytic relatives of macrophages, dissolve bone. The ratio of osteoclast to osteoblast activity controls the release of calcium and phosphate into the blood and is regulated by hormones: PTH and calcitriol (derived from vitamin D) raise blood calcium by promoting resorption and absorption, while calcitonin lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts.

problems.prompt: Bisphosphonates are a class of medications that inhibit bone resorption and are frequently used to prevent or reduce the bone loss that occurs during osteoporosis. Which of the following is a potential mechanism of action for bisphosphonates?
choices: Increase calcium absorption in the small intestine
Trigger apoptosis (programmed cell death) in osteoclasts
Prevent renal losses of calcium into the urine

problems.prompt: Osteopetrosis, also known as marble bone disease, is a disorder caused by a failure of normal bone resorption, which leads to thickened, dense bones. Bone cells are found in normal numbers, and hormone levels are usually normal. Which of the following is LEAST likely to be true about osteopetrosis?
choices: Decreased marrow space may lead to anemia and thrombocytopenia (deficiency of platelets).
Osteoclast cells are involved in the disorder.
The number of osteoclast cells must be decreased.
It may result in stunted growth.

problems.prompt: In end-stage renal disease (ESRD), patients have decreased production of active vitamin D, which in turn results in decreased serum calcium levels. The low serum calcium results in hyperplasia of the parathyroid glands and leads to hyperparathyroidism. Which of the following would be expected as a result?
choices: Osteitis fibrosa cystica - cystic bone lesions due to increased bone resorption
Osteopetrosis - thickened, dense bones due to decreased bone resorption
Osteitis deformans - abnormal bone architecture caused by an increase in both osteoblastic and osteoclastic activity
Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia - bone replaced by fibroblasts, collagen, and irregular bony trabeculae

problems.prompt: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) is caused by a missense mutation in the activation domain of the ACVR1 gene, which encodes activin receptor protein IA, a bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) receptor that becomes constitutively active. Which of the following is a potential molecular mechanism by which a patient could develop FOP?
choices: A mutation that generates a stop codon early in the coding region
A mutation in the promoter region of the gene
A mutation in the coding region that changes an amino acid
An insertion mutation in an intron

problems.prompt: In fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP), progressive heterotopic ossification replaces skeletal muscle and connective tissue but spares the diaphragm, tongue, and extraocular muscles. Which of the following physical exam findings would you expect to find in a patient with FOP?
choices: The tongue deviates to one side when the patient is instructed to stick it out
Nystagmus (rapid involuntary oscillations of the eye)

problems.prompt: For fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP), attempts to surgically remove heterotopic bone stimulate more robust bone growth, and current treatment focuses on supportive therapy and managing inflammation. According to the passage, which of the following is the most effective treatment for FOP?
choices: Sonification of overgrown bone to aid in bone particle removal

concepts.title: The Skin
concepts.content: The skin is the body's outermost covering and its first line of innate, nonspecific defense, forming an excellent barrier against the entry of microorganisms. Its epithelial cells are held tightly together by desmosomes, but unlike the tight junctions that seal the lining of the gut they do not form a complete seal. The skin also acts as a secondary excretory organ, producing sweat that contains water, ions, and urea (and is therefore similar to dilute urine), although sweating is controlled mainly by temperature and sympathetic nervous system activity rather than by the amount of waste to be removed.

problems.prompt: Immunohistochemical stains are used to classify cell types in biopsies of carcinomas. A stain for which of the following proteins would likely be positive in a cancer originating from cells in the epidermis (squamous epithelial cells)?

Bullous pemphigoid and pemphigus vulgaris are both autoimmune disorders of the skin. Bullous pemphigoid is caused by IgG antibodies acting against epidermal basement membrane cellular adhesions (hemidesmosomes) and is characterized by separation of the skin layers at that site, whereas pemphigus vulgaris is caused by IgG antibodies acting against intra-epidermal desmosomes. Which of the following is true?
choices: In bullous pemphigoid the roof of the large blisters should include the dermis.
In pemphigus vulgaris the blisters should include disruption of blood vessels.
If slightly rubbed, the blisters in pemphigus vulgaris should be more flaccid and more easily ruptured than those of bullous pemphigoid.
Direct immunofluorescence showing a straight line of IgG antibodies on a skin biopsy is more likely to indicate pemphigus vulgaris than bullous pemphigoid.

concepts.title: The Male Reproductive System
concepts.content: The external male reproductive structures are the scrotum, which holds the testes, and the penis. The testes both make sperm (spermatogenesis) in the seminiferous tubules and secrete androgens such as testosterone; the tubule walls contain sustentacular (Sertoli) cells that nurture developing sperm, while the interstitial (Leydig) cells between the tubules make testosterone. Sperm pass from the seminiferous tubules into the epididymis, then the ductus (vas) deferens, which joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct that empties into the urethra. Three accessory glands nourish and carry the sperm: the seminal vesicles (about 60 percent of semen volume, rich in fructose), the prostate, and the bulbourethral glands (alkaline mucus that lubricates and neutralizes acid). The penis contains erectile tissue, the two corpora cavernosa and one corpus spongiosum, that becomes rigid when blood accumulates in it at high pressure.

concepts.title: The Male Sexual Act
concepts.content: The male sexual act has three stages, arousal, orgasm, and resolution, coordinated by an integrating center in the spinal cord that the brain can either activate or inhibit. Arousal depends on parasympathetic input and includes erection (dilation of the arteries fills the erectile tissue and obstructs venous outflow) and lubrication (mucus from the bulbourethral glands). Orgasm requires sympathetic stimulation and consists of emission, the movement of sperm and semen into the urethra by smooth muscle contraction, followed by ejaculation, the expulsion of semen by rhythmic contractions at the base of the penis. Resolution, also under sympathetic control, constricts the erectile arteries so trapped blood drains and the penis returns to a flaccid state over a few minutes.

concepts.title: Spermatogenesis
concepts.content: Gametogenesis is the only human process that uses meiosis, in which diploid germ cells divide to form haploid gametes; in males these gametes are spermatozoa. Spermatogenesis begins at puberty and continues throughout adult life in the seminiferous tubules with the aid of sustentacular cells, with immature precursors in the outer wall and nearly mature sperm released into the lumen. A spermatogonium first divides by mitosis, then becomes a primary spermatocyte that undergoes the two meiotic divisions to yield secondary spermatocytes and finally four haploid spermatids. Each spermatid matures into a spermatozoon with a head (haploid nucleus plus the enzyme-filled acrosome), a mitochondria-rich neck, and a flagellar tail; the surface protein bindin lets it attach to the egg's zona pellucida. Because only a haploid nucleus from the sperm enters the egg, all other components of the zygote, including mitochondria, are inherited maternally.

concepts.title: Hormonal Control of Spermatogenesis
concepts.content: Testosterone is essential for stimulating the division of spermatogonia. Luteinizing hormone (LH) from the anterior pituitary acts on the interstitial (Leydig) cells to make them secrete testosterone, while follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) stimulates the sustentacular (Sertoli) cells. The sustentacular cells also secrete inhibin, whose role is to inhibit FSH release. Rising blood testosterone feeds back to decrease FSH and LH production, so the axis is self-regulating; note that it is GnRH from the hypothalamus, not LH, that travels through the hypothalamic-hypophysial portal system.

problems.prompt: Nondisjunction during anaphase of meiosis may lead to a trisomy known as Klinefelter's syndrome (XXY). The resulting individual has a male phenotype but has testicular atrophy, a slender body shape, gynecomastia, and female hair distribution. This syndrome usually results in dysgenesis of the seminiferous tubules as well as abnormal Leydig cell function. Which of the following hormones would be expected to be increased, compared to a normal male, in a patient with Klinefelter's syndrome?

concepts.title: Development of the Male Reproductive System
concepts.content: An embryo's sex is set by its chromosomes (XX or XY), but early male and female embryos look identical, possessing undifferentiated gonads plus both Wolffian ducts (potential male internal genitalia) and Mullerian ducts (potential female internal genitalia). In the absence of a Y chromosome, the Mullerian ducts develop by default and female internal and external genitalia form. In an XY embryo, genes on the Y chromosome drive the gonads to become testes, which secrete testosterone and Mullerian inhibiting factor (MIF). MIF causes the Mullerian ducts to regress, preventing female internal genitalia, while testosterone promotes the Wolffian ducts and, after conversion to dihydrotestosterone in target tissues, the male external genitalia. Testosterone secretion begins around week 7 of gestation and testes are formed by week 9.

problems.prompt: If the mother of a child with an XY genotype is exposed to testosterone-blocking chemicals during the first trimester of her pregnancy, what tissues/structures will develop in the infant?
choices: Ovaries, internal and external female genitalia
Testes, internal and external female genitalia
Testes and external male genitalia only
Testes and external female genitalia only

concepts.title: Androgens and Estrogens
concepts.content: Androgens are the hormones that build and maintain male characteristics and estrogens those for female characteristics; the main androgen from the testes is testosterone (converted to dihydrotestosterone in target tissues) and the main ovarian estrogen is estradiol. After a childhood lull, testosterone rises at puberty to drive male secondary sexual characteristics such as facial and body hair, a deeper voice, and increased muscle mass, and it causes the pubertal growth spurt and fusion of the epiphyses. Estrogen plays the analogous role in females, regulating the uterine cycle and producing female secondary sexual characteristics and epiphyseal fusion. Sex steroid production is controlled by the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary: GnRH triggers release of the gonadotropins FSH and LH, which in men drive testosterone production and the sustentacular cells and in women drive estrogen and the corpus luteum. The steroids and inhibin exert feedback inhibition on GnRH, LH, and FSH.

problems.prompt: When injected, an anabolic androgenic steroid (AAS) such as testosterone cypionate becomes testosterone in the blood. When this occurs, the testosterone level naturally produced by the body:
choices: increases because negative feedback causes FSH to decrease.
increases because positive feedback causes GnRH to increase.
decreases because negative feedback causes FSH to decrease.
decreases because negative feedback causes LH to decrease.

concepts.title: The Female Reproductive System
concepts.content: Because male and female genitalia arise from a common precursor, female external structures are homologous to male ones: the labioscrotal swellings that fuse into the scrotum in males instead form the labia majora, and the structure that becomes the penis becomes the clitoris. The internal genitalia (vagina, uterus, and uterine tubes) derive from the Mullerian ducts and have no male homologs; the uterus opens into the vagina at the cervix, its inner endometrium is shed monthly and nourishes an embryo, and it is wrapped in the muscular myometrium. The uterus ends in two uterine (fallopian) tubes tipped by fimbriae that sweep the released oocyte from the ovary, the female gonad, into the tube. The female sexual act mirrors the male, with parasympathetic arousal (the clitoris and labia minora contain erectile tissue) and sympathetic orgasm, but there is no ejaculation and resolution takes longer.

problems.prompt: Which of the following are appropriate analogous pairs of a male structure and a female structure? I. Labia majora, crus of the penis; II. Labia minora, spongy urethra; III. Ovary, testis

concepts.title: Oogenesis and Ovulation
concepts.content: Oogenesis begins before birth: germ cells in the female fetus divide mitotically into oogonia that enter meiosis and arrest in prophase I as primary oocytes, peaking near 7 million at mid-gestation and falling to about 400,000 by puberty, of which only around 400 are ever ovulated. A primary oocyte can stay frozen in prophase I for decades; beginning at puberty, monthly hormonal changes complete meiosis I to produce one large secondary oocyte and a small first polar body. Meiosis II finishes only if the secondary oocyte is fertilized, yielding a large ovum and a second polar body, so only one egg (not four) results. Each oocyte sits within supporting granulosa cells to form a follicle; as it matures the granulosa cells multiply, the oocyte lays down a zona pellucida, and surrounding thecal cells appear. Only one follicle each month becomes a mature Graafian follicle that bursts at ovulation, releasing the oocyte with its corona radiata, while the leftover follicular cells become the estrogen- and progesterone-secreting corpus luteum.

problems.prompt: A new fertility clinic claims to have developed a lower cost method for in vitro fertilization. The physician would harvest primary oocytes from immature follicles before placing them in a dish containing the donor's sperm. Any resulting ova would then be implanted into the expectant mother. Is this method viable?
choices: Yes, although the risk of having fraternal twins will be significantly increased.
Yes, although the risk of having monozygotic twins will be significantly increased.
No, it is not possible to induce implantation with an in vitro fertilized embryo.
No, the oocytes would not provide viable zygotes when fertilized.

concepts.title: The Ovarian Cycle
concepts.content: The roughly 28-day menstrual cycle has an ovarian component with three phases. During the follicular phase (about 13 days) a primary follicle matures and secretes estrogen under the control of FSH from the anterior pituitary. The ovulatory phase, triggered by a surge of LH around day 14, releases a secondary oocyte and converts the follicle's remnants into the corpus luteum. In the luteal phase (about 14 days) the corpus luteum secretes both estrogen and progesterone and lives for about two weeks before degenerating if fertilization does not occur. The hormones released by the ovary during this cycle drive the parallel events of the uterine cycle.

problems.prompt: A woman suffers a hemorrhage into her pituitary gland which destroys only the portion of the anterior pituitary responsible for producing luteinizing hormone. What will be the effect of this destruction on her menstrual cycle?
choices: Her menstrual cycle will not be affected by the destruction.
She will still ovulate and release estrogen, but not progesterone.
She will still ovulate and release progesterone, but not estrogen.

concepts.title: The Uterine Cycle
concepts.content: The uterine cycle covers the same 28 days but focuses on preparing the endometrium for implantation, and it too has three phases. Menstruation begins when the corpus luteum degenerates and the resulting drop in estrogen and progesterone makes the previous endometrial lining slough off as bleeding, lasting about 5 days. In the proliferative phase, estrogen from the maturing follicle induces a new endometrium to grow, lasting about 9 days. After ovulation the secretory phase follows, in which estrogen and progesterone from the corpus luteum further build the endometrium and load it with glycogen and lipids; if pregnancy does not occur, the corpus luteum dies and the falling hormone levels trigger menstruation again.

problems.prompt: A patient attempting to get pregnant has her blood drawn and has elevated levels of progesterone. Given it has been two weeks since her last menstruation, what best describes the uterine phase she is currently in?

concepts.title: Hormonal Changes During Pregnancy
concepts.content: Endometrial shedding happens because estrogen and progesterone fall as the corpus luteum degenerates, and the corpus luteum degenerates because LH drops due to feedback inhibition from the very estrogen and progesterone it secretes. During pregnancy, constant high estrogen and progesterone suppress the LH surge so ovulation stops, but this would normally also doom the corpus luteum and the endometrium needed to nourish the embryo. The solution is the chorion, the part of the placenta derived from the zygote, which secretes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG). hCG substitutes for LH to maintain the corpus luteum, keeping estrogen and progesterone high so that menstruation does not occur; because its presence confirms an embryo, hCG is the hormone detected by pregnancy tests.

concepts.title: Fertilization and Cleavage
concepts.content: After ovulation the secondary oocyte, wrapped in its corona radiata and zona pellucida, remains fertile for about a day, while sperm deposited near the cervix are capacitated and survive two to three days. Fertilization normally occurs in the uterine tube: a sperm penetrates the corona radiata and uses the acrosome reaction to release hydrolytic enzymes, extends an actin-filled acrosomal process whose bindin binds the zona pellucida, then fuses with the oocyte, which completes meiosis II so the two nuclei can fuse into a diploid zygote. Polyspermy is blocked twice, first by a fast block (depolarization of the egg membrane) and then by a slow block (a calcium influx, or cortical reaction, that also triggers egg activation). Cleavage then begins, a series of mitotic divisions that turn the zygote into a solid ball called the morula without increasing its overall size. Continued division and blastulation form the blastocyst, a hollow trophoblast (which becomes the chorion of the placenta) enclosing an inner cell mass (which becomes the embryo).

problems.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes the development of the placenta?
choices: zygote -> blastocyst -> inner cell mass -> placenta
zygote -> morula -> inner cell mass -> placenta

problems.prompt: A researcher studying the fast block to polyspermy has narrowed down a potential mechanism to a few possibilities. Which is most likely?
choices: Potassium efflux out of the ovum

concepts.title: Implantation and the Placenta
concepts.content: About a week after fertilization the blastocyst reaches the uterus and implants, with its trophoblast secreting proteases that digest endometrial cells so the blastocyst can sink in and absorb nutrients; this is why the secretory-phase endometrium stores glycogen and lipids. Because the placenta takes roughly three months to develop, hCG is essential during the first trimester to maintain the endometrium, after which the placenta itself secretes enough estrogen and progesterone. The placenta forms from chorionic villi that project into the endometrium and are bathed in maternal blood-filled sinuses, allowing exchange of nutrients, gases, and antibodies between maternal and fetal blood without the two bloodstreams actually mixing. Besides the embryo, the inner cell mass gives rise to the amnion (whose fluid-filled cavity surrounds the embryo and is the water that breaks), the yolk sac (the first site of red blood cell synthesis), and the allantois (which forms the umbilical blood vessels).

problems.prompt: All of the following are true of the placenta EXCEPT:
choices: it takes approximately three months to develop.
it is the site of exchange of fetal/maternal nutrients.
it secretes hCG to maintain the corpus luteum.
it contains tissue derived both from the mother and developing zygote.

problems.prompt: A passage describes fetal heart rate (FHR) monitoring, which plots the FHR and amniotic pressure over time. An 'acceleration' (a brief rise in FHR) is caused by normal fetal movements; an 'early deceleration' is a gradual fall in FHR that mirrors a uterine contraction and is usually due to head compression; a 'variable deceleration' is an abrupt fall in FHR below baseline (lasting more than 15 seconds but less than 2 minutes) most often caused by umbilical cord compression secondary to oligohydramnios (reduced amniotic fluid). A bradycardic baseline (FHR < 110 bpm) or tachycardic baseline (FHR > 160 bpm, which can be caused by maternal fever) is also evaluated. Figure 2 shows the FHR trace (top) and amniotic pressure (bottom) recorded from Patient #2. Which of the following is the most probable cause of the FHR pattern seen in Figure 2?
choices: Fetal movements due to increased maternal activity
Premature rupture of amniotic membranes (PROM) resulting in oligohydramnios

concepts.title: Post-Implantation Development
concepts.content: After blastulation comes gastrulation, when the three primary germ layers become distinct; in humans they form from a two-layered embryonic disk rather than an invaginating ball. The ectoderm gives rise to the entire nervous system, the epidermis and its derivatives, and structures such as the lens and cornea; the mesoderm forms all muscle, bone, and connective tissue plus the entire cardiovascular and lymphatic systems and the urogenital organs; and the endoderm forms the epithelial linings of the GI and respiratory tracts and glands such as the liver and pancreas. Next is neurulation, in which ectoderm forms the neural plate that folds into the neural tube (the future brain and spinal cord), while neural crest cells migrate off to become melanocytes, the adrenal medulla, some neurons, and other cell types, induced by the mesodermal notochord. Neurulation is part of organogenesis, and by the eighth week all major organ systems are present and the embryo becomes a fetus. During this first-trimester window the prenatal environment strongly affects the fetus, so factors such as folic acid deficiency, maternal infections, hypoxia from smoking, or alcohol can cause serious defects.

problems.prompt: Suppose that gastrulation proceeded abnormally such that the ectoderm did not develop. Which of the following organs would fail to form?

Ventricular septal defects (VSDs) are the most common congenital heart malformations and are due to a failure of the ventricular septum to fully close during development. Which of the following primary germ layers is responsible for forming the septum of the ventricles of the heart?

concepts.title: Differentiation
concepts.content: Differentiation is the specialization of cell types during development, making a cell better at one task but less able to do others, and it is preceded by determination, the point at which a cell's fate becomes fixed even before its appearance changes. Cells of the zygote and morula are totipotent, able to form any cell of the blastocyst including both the trophoblast and the inner cell mass. Cells of the inner cell mass are pluripotent, able to become any of the three germ layers and thus any of the body's 220-plus adult cell types, but not the trophoblast; in humans the only known pluripotent cells are embryonic stem cells isolated from the inner cell mass. After gastrulation the germ-layer cells are only multipotent, able to become many but not all cell types. A specialized cell can occasionally dedifferentiate and regain potency, and uncontrolled proliferation of such a cell can produce cancer; importantly, every cell keeps the same genome, since differentiation reflects cytoplasmic and nuclear regulators rather than genetic change.

concepts.title: Pregnancy
concepts.content: The embryonic stage (gastrulation and neurulation, the first eight weeks) makes up most of the first trimester, during which all major organ systems appear; from eight weeks until birth is the fetal stage, spanning the second and third trimesters. In the second trimester the organs continue developing and the fetus grows to roughly 0.6 kg and looks distinctly human. The third trimester is a time of rapid growth and fat deposition, and most organ systems become functional, so a baby born one to two months early has a reasonable chance of survival. Pregnancy places heavy demands on the mother: her respiratory rate rises, her blood volume increases about 50 percent (with a matching rise in glomerular filtration rate), and her need for nutrients climbs while the uterus and mammary glands enlarge.

problems.prompt: A passage on fetal heart rate (FHR) monitoring notes that the fetal heart rate is normally about 110 to 150 bpm, which is significantly faster than a typical resting adult heart rate. The sinoatrial (SA) node is the pacemaker of the healthy heart. Which of the following is the most likely cause for the difference in fetal and adult heart rate?
choices: Increased parasympathetic activity at the adult AV node
Increased norepinephrine release at the adult AV node
Decreased parasympathetic activity at the fetal SA node
Decreased norepinephrine release at the fetal SA node

concepts.title: Birth and Lactation
concepts.content: Birth, or parturition, depends on contraction of the uterine wall muscle; the high progesterone of pregnancy represses contractions, but near term uterine excitability rises as the estrogen-to-progesterone ratio shifts, oxytocin is released, and the uterus and cervix are stretched. Labor is driven by a positive feedback reflex in which pressure on the cervix makes the posterior pituitary release oxytocin, which strengthens contractions that push harder on the cervix and release still more oxytocin. Labor proceeds in three stages: dilation of the cervix, birth of the baby through the birth canal, and expulsion of the placenta. During pregnancy the placenta's estrogen and progesterone develop the breasts but inhibit prolactin and milk production; after delivery these hormones fall and prolactin, surged by suckling, drives milk production. Milk is not released until oxytocin, also triggered by suckling, causes milk let-down.

problems.prompt: Lactation occurs in a mother after giving birth in order to provide nutrition and immune protection to her infant(s). A new mother is experiencing abnormally low levels of milk production. Which of the following could explain her condition? I. Hyposecretion of oxytocin; II. Damage to the anterior pituitary causing a decrease in prolactin; III. A post-partum infection that has caused minor damage in ovarian hormone secreting cells

In fetal heart rate monitoring, 'early decelerations' are gradual drops in fetal heart rate that mirror uterine contractions and are usually caused by head compression from the contraction. Which of the following would most likely exacerbate early decelerations observed during FHR monitoring?
choices: Injection of epinephrine (a sympathetic agonist) in the umbilical vein

problems.prompt: All of the following are changes that occur to either the baby or the mother after childbirth EXCEPT:
choices: levels of estrogen and progesterone fall.
the inhibition on prolactin is released.

concepts.title: Experimental Design
concepts.content: Experimental design is used when researchers need to test whether one variable causes changes in another, not just whether the variables are associated. The chapter uses Mediterranean diet and cardiovascular health to show why correlation alone cannot establish causation, because reverse causation and third variables remain possible explanations. To set up an experiment, researchers first define a population of interest and accept practical limits in who can be studied. Those choices make studies feasible but can narrow how broadly the results apply.

problems.prompt: In Study 2, researchers compared an experimental group with a control group. In Study 3, the same participants were assessed over time. Which of the following describes the comparisons made in Study 2 and Study 3, respectively?
choices: Within subjects for Study 2 and within subjects for Study 3
Between subjects for Study 2 and within subjects for Study 3
Within subjects for Study 2 and between subjects for Study 3
Between subjects for Study 2 and between subjects for Study 3

concepts.title: Operationalize the Independent and Dependent Variables
concepts.content: Researchers must operationalize variables by defining exactly what is manipulated and what is measured. The independent variable is the manipulated condition, and the dependent variable is the measured outcome, which should be quantitative so statistical testing is possible. The chapter emphasizes precise, replicable definitions, such as a specific diet protocol and numerical physiological measurements. It also notes that operational definitions can introduce limits, because practical proxies may only indirectly capture the broader outcomes researchers care about.

problems.prompt: In a study of the impact of personality type on the interpretation of a social symbol, which of the following is a possible operational definition of the independent variable?
choices: Personality type is the independent variable, so it can be defined as results on a questionnaire designed to measure five-factor model personality traits.
Personality type is the independent variable, so it can be defined as degree of sympathetic arousal and amygdala activation when seeing a symbol.
Symbol interpretation is the independent variable, so it can be defined as average ranking, from positive to negative, of a series of neutral symbols.
Symbol interpretation is the independent variable, so it can be defined as degree of sympathetic arousal and amygdala activation when seeing a symbol.

problems.prompt: In a study that grouped students by digital-media usage, which of the following pairs represents a qualitative and quantitative variable, respectively?
choices: Type of coping response and level of depression
Attending fluidity ability and reaction time

problems.prompt: In the same digital-media study, researchers measured cognitive and mental-health outcomes. Each of the following could be an operational definition of the dependent variable EXCEPT:
The research examined video-game effects using correlational and experimental follow-up studies. Which of the following is a dependent variable from the research?

concepts.title: Carefully Select Control and Experimental Groups
concepts.content: Experimental conclusions require a treatment group and a control group that are as similar as possible except for the treatment variable. Researchers try to minimize extraneous or confounding variables by matching groups on relevant characteristics and controlling shared conditions. The chapter also highlights placebo effects and explains why double-blind procedures help prevent expectancy effects from participants and staff. Even with careful design, some confounds may remain unavoidable, so limitations must be acknowledged.

problems.prompt: In a digital-media study, students were split into high-usage and low-usage groups and tested on cognition and psychopathology measures. A likely confounding variable created by the experimental design was:
In Study 2, researchers wanted to isolate video-game-like training effects on object tracking in male participants. The best control condition would be a group of:
choices: 25 boys and girls assigned a movie to watch and given similar object tracking tasks.
50 boys assigned a different set of video games.
25 boys of similar age assigned a movie to watch and given the same measure of object tracking to test the effect.
50 boys and girls assigned a different set of video games.

concepts.title: Randomly Sample from the Population and Randomly Assign Individuals to Groups
concepts.content: Random sampling means every member of the target population should have an equal chance of selection, though this ideal is often hard to achieve in social science. Random assignment means enrolled participants should be equally likely to enter treatment or control groups, often aided by randomization or block techniques. These steps reduce systematic bias and improve group comparability. The chapter also warns about attrition, because non-random dropout can introduce new confounds.

problems.prompt: Attrition, or subjects dropping out of a study before its completion, is a threat to:
choices: internal validity, because it introduces a potential confounding variable.
internal validity, because the group may no longer be representative.
external validity, because it introduces a potential confounding variable.
external validity, because the group may no longer be representative.

concepts.title: Measure the Results and Test the Hypothesis
concepts.content: Measurements should be standardized and reliable, especially when constructs such as mood, memory, or attitude are assessed with surveys or newer instruments. Scientists begin with the null hypothesis and look for evidence strong enough to reject it rather than assuming an effect exists from the start. Statistical significance is evaluated with p-values, with p < 0.05 commonly used as a cutoff, though other thresholds may be chosen in advance. The chapter also emphasizes adequate sample size and study power so real effects can be detected.

problems.prompt: A study at one Midwestern university split 62 first-year students into low and high digital-usage groups based on self-reported phone, social media, and Internet use. Researchers measured reaction time, working memory, distractor resistance, depression, and anxiety. Which of the following conclusions can be most reasonably drawn from the study in passage?
choices: Stress plays a critical role in the relationship between technology and cognitive effects because it provides the most plausible mediating variable.
There was a relationship between technology use and psychopathology because the research utilized various psychometrics.
Cultural lag regarding digital media is an ongoing problem on college campuses because the research conducted used random assignment and random sampling to test the hypotheses.
Use of social media caused detrimental effects on cognition because of the strain placed on the attentional mechanism, as demonstrated by comparison with the control group.

problems.prompt: In the same digital-media study, researchers proposed that stress response might mediate links between high digital usage and worse outcomes. If this conclusion is correct, what is likely to happen in a second study of elderly adults who are known to be more sensitive in their response to stress?
choices: They will have difficulty attending to stimuli.
They will score higher on depression.
The low digital usage group will have slower reaction times.
The high digital usage group will demonstrate increased anxiety.

concepts.title: Internal and External Validity and Ethical Considerations
concepts.content: External validity concerns whether findings generalize beyond study conditions, while internal validity concerns whether the design supports a causal conclusion inside the study itself. Threats to internal validity include confounding variables, weak controls, unreliable measurements, and attrition; threats to external validity include restrictive sampling and artificial settings. The chapter gives examples such as single-campus sampling and highly controlled laboratory diets that may not reflect real-world behavior. It also emphasizes ethics: modern studies require independent review, participant disclosure/informed consent, and debriefing after procedures.

problems.prompt: Due to scheduling and logistical limitations, researchers could only conduct a study on Tuesdays and Thursdays between 7 pm and 9 pm, so they were limited to individuals available at that time. This setup would have created issues in:
choices: external validity, due to the selection criteria.
external validity, due to the lack of a control group.
internal validity, due to impression management.
internal validity, due to a potential Hawthorne effect.

problems.prompt: A digital-media study sampled first-year students at one Midwestern university and compared high-usage and low-usage groups. The methodology described created threats to external validity due to each of the following considerations EXCEPT:

In video-game follow-up studies, Study 2 used a laboratory setup with a control group, while Study 3 observed four participants with amblyopia in home settings on a varied game regimen. Compared to the first follow-up study, the second follow-up study had:
choices: high internal validity and low external validity.
high internal validity and high external validity.
low internal validity and low external validity.
low internal validity and high external validity.

concepts.title: Correlational Studies
concepts.content: Correlational studies evaluate relationships between two quantitative variables without manipulating either variable. The chapter highlights the Pearson correlation, which ranges from -1 to +1: negative values indicate inverse movement, positive values indicate same-direction movement, and 0 indicates no linear relationship. Correlations can be tested for statistical significance to estimate whether an observed relationship is likely due to chance. Because variables are observed rather than experimentally controlled, correlations do not by themselves establish causation.

problems.prompt: A team of researchers measures a negative correlation between income and length of labor time in a group of pregnant women. It is expected that as income increases, labor time:
choices: The change in labor time cannot be determined.

problems.prompt: A team of researchers finds that sociability is highest for individuals within one standard deviation of mean IQ, and decreases for both very high and very low IQ scores. Which of the following correlations would be measured in this instance?

Video-game research reported that more game play was associated with greater sensory integration and with less time needed to learn new visual tasks. Which of the following pairs of correlations is consistent with the research described in the passage?
choices: +0.60 between video game play and sensory integration and -0.33 between video game play and time to learn new tasks
+0.35 between video game play and sensory integration and +0.21 between video game play and time to learn new tasks
+0.07 between video game play and sensory integration and -0.40 between video game play and time to learn new tasks
-0.47 between sensory integration and time to learn new tasks and +0.44 between sensory integration and response flexibility

concepts.title: Ethnographic Studies
concepts.content: Ethnographic research is a qualitative method in which researchers immerse themselves in a group or culture and observe with minimal interference. These studies are usually lengthy and detailed, and they are useful when a naturalistic, context-rich description is needed. A key tradeoff is limited generalizability, because deep observation of one culture may not transfer well to other populations. The chapter illustrates this with the idea of closely studying daily life in a specific Sicilian village.

problems.prompt: Which of the following is a limitation of the ethnographic method?
choices: Cultural validity is low, since the observer is not a member of the society of interest.
External validity is low, because the experimental conditions do not match the real world.
External validity is low, because only one culture is sampled.
Construct validity is low, since the instruments have not been checked for reliability.

concepts.title: Twin Studies
concepts.content: Twin studies are used to separate genetic and environmental contributions to traits. They are a central method for estimating heritability by comparing similarities in monozygotic and dizygotic twins, or in identical twins raised together versus apart. When identical twins share more similarity than fraternal twins, genetics is implicated more strongly. When identical twins differ more across different rearing environments, environmental effects are implicated.

concepts.title: Longitudinal Studies
concepts.content: Longitudinal studies repeatedly measure the same people over long periods to track how variables develop. The chapter uses the New York Longitudinal Study as an example, where infant temperament categories were followed to see whether early disposition predicted later outcomes. This design is resource-intensive and often vulnerable to attrition. Its major benefit is direct observation of change over time rather than a one-time snapshot.

problems.prompt: Which of the following research methodologies would best explore the development of human memory over time?

concepts.title: Case Studies
concepts.content: Case studies involve intensive analysis of a single case, often one person, to gather comprehensive detail about a phenomenon. They can generate rich hypotheses by examining many interacting factors in depth, such as diet, sleep, exercise, and social context in one unusually healthy individual. The main limitation is weak control over variables and limited ability to generalize from one case to broader populations. They also make it difficult to disentangle which variables are driving observed outcomes.

concepts.title: Phenomenological Studies
concepts.content: Phenomenological studies focus on describing lived experience, often through introspection or first-person reports. Instead of isolating variables to test causation, this approach aims to characterize how phenomena are perceived and experienced.
