problems.prompt: A passage describes a bimolecular gas-phase reaction whose rate constant is estimated from collision theory (kr = Z*p*e^(-Ea/RT)). The steric factor p reflects that a reaction's probability depends on the reactant molecules colliding with the correct orientation. Which of the following statements regarding reaction kinetics is most accurate?
choices: The activated complex can be measured in solution, although it is not a net product of the reaction.
The steric factor for more complex reactions is smaller than for simpler reactions.
The rate constant depends on the initial concentration of the reactants.
The rate law of a one-step bimolecular reaction cannot be determined using stoichiometry, but rather can only be calculated experimentally.

concepts.title: The Equilibrium Constant
concepts.content: Many reactions are reversible, and a reaction reaches equilibrium when the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same constant rate, so the overall concentrations of reactants and products no longer change even though molecules keep interconverting; this dynamic balance occurs only in closed systems. For the balanced reaction aA + bB <=> cC + dD, the equilibrium constant is Keq = [C]^c[D]^d / [A]^a[B]^b, written as products over reactants with each stoichiometric coefficient becoming an exponent. Pure solids, pure liquids, and solvents in dilute solution are left out of the expression because their concentrations do not change, while aqueous and gaseous species are included; a gaseous reaction may instead use partial pressures, giving Kp. The value of Keq is constant at a given temperature no matter the starting amounts and changes only when the temperature changes. A Keq less than 1 means reactants are favored, near 1 means comparable amounts, and greater than 1 means products are favored.

problems.prompt: Which of the following expressions accurately describes the equilibrium constant for the following Pd-catalyzed hydrogenation equilibrium? Cl2TiH2 <=> TiCl2 + H2 (Pd catalyst)
Which of the following statements is NOT necessarily true of a system at chemical equilibrium?
choices: The concentrations of reactants and products are constant.
The delta-G of the system is zero.
The amounts of reactants and products are equal.
The rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal.

problems.prompt: Synthetic creatine exists in equilibrium with creatinine in aqueous solution, creatine <=> creatinine + H2O, for which Keq = [creatinine]/[creatine] varies with temperature as shown in Figure 2. A pH-neutral creatine solution is brought to reflux in water (100 C) and found to have a creatinine concentration of 0.45 M. At this temperature, what is the expected concentration of creatine?

For the aqueous equilibrium creatine <=> creatinine + H2O, the equilibrium constant Keq = [creatinine]/[creatine] varies with temperature as shown in Figure 2. A test solution at 50 C was found to have a creatinine concentration of 1 M (with [creatine] = [creatinine]). When the temperature was raised to 85 C, what was the equilibrium concentration of creatinine?

concepts.title: The Reaction Quotient
concepts.content: The reaction quotient Q has exactly the same form as the equilibrium expression, products over reactants with coefficients as exponents, but it uses the current concentrations, which need not be the equilibrium ones (when they are, Q equals Keq). Comparing Q with Keq reveals the direction the reaction will go as it strives to reach the state where Q = Keq. If Q is less than Keq the reaction proceeds forward, making more product and less reactant to raise Q; if Q is greater than Keq the reaction proceeds in reverse to lower Q; and if Q equals Keq the system is already at equilibrium.

problems.prompt: For the decomposition of dinitrogen tetroxide to nitrogen dioxide, N2O4(g) <=> 2 NO2(g), Keq = 1.4 x 10^-1 at 25 C. If both species have a partial pressure of 0.1 atm in a reaction vessel at 25 C, which way will the reaction proceed?
choices: In both directions at equal rates
Cannot be determined without the volume of the reaction vessel

problems.prompt: Which of the following stresses always leaves the value of the reaction quotient Q unchanged?
choices: Increasing the volume of a gaseous reaction
Adding an inert gas to a gaseous reaction at constant pressure

concepts.title: Le Chatelier's Principle
concepts.content: Le Chatelier's principle states that a system at equilibrium counteracts any imposed stress in order to reestablish equilibrium. Adding a reactant or removing a product drives the forward reaction, while removing a reactant or adding a product drives the reverse reaction, exactly as predicted by comparing the disturbed system's Q to Keq. For a gaseous reaction with unequal moles of gas on each side, reducing the volume (raising the pressure) shifts the reaction toward the side with fewer moles of gas, and expanding the volume shifts it toward the side with more. Because heat can be treated as a reactant in an endothermic reaction or a product in an exothermic one, raising the temperature favors the endothermic direction and lowering it favors the exothermic direction, and unlike other stresses a temperature change alters the value of Keq. Adding an inert gas at constant volume, or adding a catalyst, does not shift the equilibrium at all.

problems.prompt: Which of the following strategies would be effective in increasing the ratio of products to reactants in the following endothermic reaction at equilibrium? FSO3H(g) <=> SO3(g) + HF(g)
choices: Increasing the initial amount of FSO3H
Running the reaction in an HF atmosphere

problems.prompt: Nitrogen is a relatively inert species, so high temperatures and pressures are required to produce appreciable ammonia by N2 + 3 H2 <=> 2 NH3. In a reactor of fixed volume containing only the equilibrium gases, with temperature fixed by external controls, which of the following relationships explains the enhanced production of ammonia at higher pressures?

Creatine exists in equilibrium with creatinine in solution, creatine <=> creatinine + H2O, and in water (present in vast excess) water is not part of the equilibrium expression. When 0.5 M creatine is instead dissolved in acetonitrile (CH3CN), a near-complete conversion to creatinine is observed. Which of the following is a plausible explanation for this observation?
choices: Acetonitrile cannot hydrogen bond with creatine.
Removal of the excess of water allows the equilibrium to shift heavily to the products.
Creatine is easily deprotonated by acetonitrile, halting equilibrium.
The formation of water is extremely thermodynamically unfavorable in acetonitrile.

concepts.title: Solutions
concepts.content: A solution is a homogeneous mixture formed when one substance dissolves in another; the component present in the smaller proportion is the solute and the one in the greater proportion is the solvent, and the dissolving process is called dissolution. When solvent molecules surround the solute the process is solvation, or hydration when the solvent is water, and a solution whose solvent is water is described as aqueous. Solutions can involve any combination of phases, though most familiar ones use a liquid solvent. The guiding rule of thumb is that like dissolves like: a solute dissolves best in a solvent whose intermolecular forces with the solute are comparable to or stronger than the forces being broken.

problems.prompt: In the active site of creatine kinase, a number of amino acids are responsible for holding and directing the phosphate and nitrogen-bearing terminus of creatine to facilitate bond formation. Which of the following amino acid residues is most likely active in this role?

concepts.title: Electrolytes
concepts.content: When ionic substances dissolve they dissociate into ions, and because a solution of free ions can conduct electricity these ions are called electrolytes. Solutes that dissociate completely, such as most ionic compounds, are strong electrolytes and are better conductors, those that remain partly ion-paired are weak electrolytes, and covalent compounds that do not ionize are nonelectrolytes. The van't Hoff (ionizability) factor i indicates how many ions one formula unit produces in solution: i = 1 for a nonionic species such as glucose, 2 for NaCl (Na+ and Cl-), and 3 for CaCl2 (Ca2+ and 2 Cl-). The factor is 1 for essentially all biomolecules, including hormones, proteins, and steroids.

concepts.title: Solubility
concepts.content: Solubility is the amount of a solute that will saturate a particular solvent, and it is specific to the identities of the solute and solvent as well as to temperature. Three phase solubility rules recur on the MCAT: the solubility of solids in liquids tends to increase with temperature, the solubility of gases in liquids tends to decrease with temperature, and the solubility of gases in liquids tends to increase with pressure. The amount of a gas dissolved is also set by the partial pressure of that gas above the liquid through Henry's law (solubility = k*P), so raising the applied pressure forces more gas into solution while the equilibrium constant stays unchanged. A saturated solution holds as much dissolved solute as it can, with dissolution and precipitation occurring at equal rates in dynamic equilibrium.

problems.prompt: Dissolved carbon monoxide can be quantified by a distinctive IR absorbance peak at about 1800 cm^-1, which grows more intense as [CO] increases. If ethanol is subjected to an applied CO pressure, which combination of pressure and temperature would yield the most intense CO peak in the IR spectrum of the solution?

concepts.title: The Solubility Product Constant
concepts.content: The extent to which a salt dissolves in water is measured by its solubility product constant, Ksp, which is simply the equilibrium constant for the dissolution of the solid salt into its dissolved ions. As in any equilibrium expression the pure solid is omitted, so Ksp equals the product of the concentrations of the dissolved ions, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient (for example Ksp = [Mg2+][OH-]^2 for Mg(OH)2). At equilibrium the solution is saturated, meaning ions go into solution at the same rate at which they precipitate out. A very soluble salt has a large Ksp, while a barely soluble one has a very small Ksp.

concepts.title: Solubility Computations
concepts.content: If the Ksp of a salt is known, its molar solubility, the number of moles that will saturate a liter of water, can be calculated. Letting x be the moles of salt that dissolve per liter, the concentration of each ion is written as x times its coefficient; for Mg(OH)2 dissolving into one Mg2+ and two OH-, [Mg2+] = x and [OH-] = 2x. Substituting these into the solubility product gives Ksp = (x)(2x)^2 = 4x^3, which is then solved for x. The same relationship can be run in reverse to obtain a Ksp from a measured solubility.

problems.prompt: The maximum solubility of sodium sulfide (Na2S) in water at 0 C is 12.4 g per 100 mL of water. What value most closely approximates the solubility product (Ksp) of Na2S at 0 C in water? (The molar mass of Na2S is about 78 g/mol.)

concepts.title: Ion Product
concepts.content: The ion product is the reaction quotient for a solubility (dissolution) reaction, denoted Qsp; it has the same form as the Ksp expression but uses concentrations that need not be those at equilibrium. Comparing Qsp with Ksp predicts what a solution will do: if Qsp is less than Ksp more salt can dissolve, if Qsp equals Ksp the solution is exactly saturated, and if Qsp is greater than Ksp the excess salt will precipitate. This lets you decide, for instance, whether mixing two soluble salts will precipitate a slightly soluble product by computing Qsp for that product and comparing it with its Ksp.

concepts.title: The Common-Ion Effect
concepts.content: When a slightly soluble salt is in equilibrium with its ions, adding a second, very soluble source of one of those same ions (a common ion) disturbs the equilibrium. Because the concentration of a product ion has increased, Le Chatelier's principle drives the dissolution equilibrium in reverse, precipitating more of the solid. The net result is that the molar solubility of the slightly soluble salt is decreased by the presence of another solute that supplies a common ion. For example, adding NaOH to a saturated solution of Mg(OH)2 raises [OH-] and forces more solid Mg(OH)2 to precipitate.

problems.prompt: Which of the following salts is most likely to fully dissolve in a 5% saline (NaCl) solution?

concepts.title: Complex Ion Formation and Solubility
concepts.content: Complex ions consist of a central metal ion surrounded by several ligands (Lewis bases), and a complexed metal ion can have very different solubility from the naked hydrated ion, so adding ligands can greatly change the solubility of a metal salt. For example silver chloride is nearly insoluble in water (very small Ksp), but adding ammonia lets it dissolve because the Ag+ is pulled into the soluble complex ion [Ag(NH3)2]+. The overall reaction AgCl(s) + 2 NH3 <=> [Ag(NH3)2]+ + Cl- has a constant that, although still less than 1, is many orders of magnitude larger than the Ksp of AgCl alone. By Le Chatelier's principle, adding excess ammonia favors dissolution even further.

problems.prompt: Tollens' reagent, used to identify aldehydes and reducing sugars, is made by adding aqueous ammonia to silver oxide (which is slightly soluble) to form the complex ion Ag(NH3)2+ (Kf = 1.7 x 10^7). Which statement best describes the reaction occurring upon the addition of ammonia?
choices: A solid dissolves, since the Q of the overall reaction is less than its K.
A solid dissolves, since the Kf for Ag(NH3)2+ increases.
A precipitate is formed, since the overall K for the reaction is greater than 1.
A precipitate is formed, since the Ksp for Ag2O decreases.

concepts.title: Thermodynamics and Equilibrium
concepts.content: A reaction proceeds spontaneously when delta-G is negative and continues, with the shifting amounts of products and reactants continually redefining delta-G, until delta-G reaches 0 and equilibrium is achieved. This links the free energy change to the reaction quotient and equilibrium constant through delta-G = delta-G-standard + RT ln Q, where delta-G-standard is the value under standard conditions. Because delta-G is 0 and Q equals Keq at equilibrium, this reduces to delta-G-standard = -RT ln Keq. Thus a negative delta-G-standard corresponds to Keq greater than 1 with products favored, a delta-G-standard of 0 gives Keq near 1, and a positive delta-G-standard gives Keq less than 1 with reactants favored. Whereas delta-G states the spontaneity of a reaction at its current composition, delta-G-standard reflects the equilibrium proportions of products and reactants.

problems.prompt: A reaction at equilibrium has a Keq of 154. All of the following are true for this reaction EXCEPT:

For the aqueous equilibrium creatine <=> creatinine + H2O (creatinine formation), the temperature dependence of Keq is shown in Figure 2, and the standard enthalpy change delta-H-standard was determined to be +4.3 kcal/mol. Which of the following must also be true?
choices: delta-G-standard at 363 K has a positive value.
delta-S-standard at 363 K has a negative value.
delta-S-standard at 363 K has a positive value.
delta-G-standard at 293 K has a negative value.

concepts.title: Bronsted-Lowry Acids and Bases
concepts.content: Under the Bronsted-Lowry definitions, an acid is a proton (H+) donor and a base is a proton (H+) acceptor, and these are the most important acid-base definitions for MCAT general chemistry. Although hydroxide ion is the familiar Bronsted-Lowry base, many other species also qualify. Because a Bronsted-Lowry base is anything capable of accepting a proton, any anion or any neutral species bearing a lone pair of electrons can act as a base. In a reversible reaction such as H2CO3 + H2O <-> H3O+ + HCO3-, the species that donate protons (H2CO3 and H3O+) are the acids, while those that accept them (H2O and HCO3-) are the bases.

problems.prompt: Which of the following statements is true about a solution of propanoic acid in equilibrium? CH3CH2COOH(aq) <-> H+(aq) + CH3CH2COO-(aq)
choices: When NaOH is added, CH3CH2COOH acts as a Lewis acid.
When HCl is added, CH3CH2COO- acts as a Bronsted-Lowry base.
When HI is added, CH3CH2COOH acts as a Bronsted-Lowry acid.
When HF is added, CH3CH2COOH acts as an Arrhenius base.

concepts.title: Lewis Acids and Bases
concepts.content: Lewis's definitions are broader than the Bronsted-Lowry ones: a Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor and a Lewis base is an electron-pair donor. Lewis acid-base reactions frequently produce a coordinate covalent bond, in which one partner supplies both of the shared electrons. For example, when AlCl3 reacts with water, water acts as the Lewis base because it donates both electrons of the new bond, while AlCl3 acts as the Lewis acid because it accepts that electron pair. This framework lets species that have no proton to donate still be classified as acids.

concepts.title: Conjugate Acids and Bases
concepts.content: When a Bronsted-Lowry acid donates its proton, the structure left behind is the conjugate base of that acid; when a Bronsted-Lowry base gains a proton, the new species is the conjugate acid of that base. An acid and its conjugate base differ by exactly one H+, as do a base and its conjugate acid. In NH3 + H2O <-> NH4+ + OH-, NH3 is the base and H2O the acid in the forward direction, so NH4+ is the conjugate acid of NH3 and OH- is the conjugate base of H2O. Reversing the reaction preserves the same conjugate relationships, with NH4+ now acting as the acid and OH- as the base.

concepts.title: The Strengths of Acids and Bases
concepts.content: Whether an acid is strong or weak depends on how completely it ionizes in water: a strong acid dissociates essentially completely, while a weak acid such as HF leaves most of its molecules undissociated. The extent of dissociation is captured by the acid-ionization constant Ka = [H3O+][A-]/[HA]; a larger Ka means a stronger acid (Ka > 1 favors products) and a smaller Ka a weaker one. The few strong acids worth memorizing are HI, HBr, HCl, HClO4, H2SO4, and HNO3, and any acid not on that list can be treated as weak on the MCAT. Bases are ranked analogously by the base-ionization constant Kb = [HB+][OH-]/[B], with a larger Kb indicating a stronger base. Common strong bases include Group 1 oxides, some Group 2 hydroxides such as Ba(OH)2, Sr(OH)2, and Ca(OH)2, and metal amides, whereas ammonia and amines are weak bases.

problems.prompt: The label "strong" versus "weak" when referring to an acid indicates which of the following?
choices: Whether the pH of the acid solution will be ~7 or significantly less than 7
How likely it is for the acid to react with a base
Whether the ratio of [acid] to [conjugate base] is < 1 or > 1
The likelihood of a color change occurring when a proton is lost

problems.prompt: Compare the two weak Bronsted-Lowry acids HBrO2 and HIO2. Which acid is stronger, and why?
choices: HBrO2 is stronger because bromine is more electronegative than iodine.
HIO2 is stronger because iodine is more electronegative than bromine.
HIO2 is stronger because iodine is a larger atom than bromine.
HBrO2 is stronger because bromine forms shorter, stronger bonds with oxygen than iodine.

concepts.title: The Relative Strengths of Conjugate Acid-Base Pairs
concepts.content: The strength of a Bronsted-Lowry acid is inversely related to the strength of its conjugate base. The conjugate base of a strong acid (for example Cl- from HCl) has no basic properties in water because the forward dissociation is essentially complete, whereas the conjugate base of a weak acid is itself a weak base. In fact, the weaker the acid, the stronger its conjugate base: because HCN (Ka about 5 x 10^-10) is a weaker acid than HF (Ka about 7 x 10^-4), cyanide is a stronger base than fluoride. The same logic applies to bases, so the conjugate acid of a strong base has no acidic properties, while the conjugate acid of a weak base is a weak acid, and the weaker the base the stronger that conjugate acid.

problems.prompt: The Ka values for HF and HCN are 6.3 x 10^-4 and 6.2 x 10^-10, respectively. Compared to the conjugate base F-, CN- is a:
choices: weak conjugate base that is weaker than F-.
strong conjugate base that is weaker than F-.
weak conjugate base that is stronger than F-.
strong conjugate base that is stronger than F-.

concepts.title: Amphoteric Substances
concepts.content: A polyprotic acid has more than one proton to donate; carbonic acid, H2CO3, is a weak polyprotic acid whose conjugate base HCO3- still bears an ionizable proton. In the first dissociation HCO3- is produced as a base, but in the second dissociation it donates a proton and acts as an acid, so it is amphoteric, able to behave as either an acid or a base. The conjugate base of any weak polyprotic acid is always amphoteric for this reason. Notably, each successive deprotonation yields a weaker acid, so HCO3- is a weaker acid than H2CO3.

problems.prompt: Ocean acidification occurs as seawater absorbs atmospheric CO2 to form carbonic acid, which dissociates in the following reactions: (Reaction 1) CO2(g) + H2O(l) -> H2CO3(aq); (Reaction 2) H2CO3(aq) <-> H+(aq) + HCO3-(aq), Ka = 2.5 x 10^-4; (Reaction 3) HCO3-(aq) <-> H+(aq) + CO3^2-(aq), Ka = 5.6 x 10^-11. Mollusk and coral shells are made of calcium carbonate: (Reaction 4) CaCO3(s) <-> Ca2+(aq) + CO3^2-(aq), Ksp = 8.7 x 10^-9. Which of the following is a consequence of increased CO2 absorption in ocean water?
choices: A decrease in the Ka of Reaction 2
A decrease in the thickness of mollusk shells
A decrease in calcium ions in seawater

problems.prompt: In seawater, calcium carbonate dissolves according to CaCO3(s) <-> Ca2+(aq) + CO3^2-(aq). The passage states that in the marine environment the solubility of calcium carbonate decreases with increasing temperature. Which of the following is true regarding the Ksp of CaCO3 in seawater?
choices: Ksp does not change with changes in temperature.
The change in Ksp is not predictable without further data.

problems.prompt: Groundwater often contains dissolved calcium and carbonate ions together with high levels of dissolved carbon dioxide while underground (CO2 + H2O <-> H2CO3 <-> H+ + HCO3-; CaCO3(s) <-> Ca2+ + CO3^2-). Which of the following will occur when this water surfaces and expels the excess carbon dioxide?
choices: Water acidity decreases and calcium carbonate may precipitate.
Water acidity decreases and calcium carbonate will remain in solution.
Water acidity increases and calcium carbonate will remain in solution.
Water acidity increases and calcium carbonate may precipitate.

problems.prompt: In seawater at 25 C, calcium carbonate dissolves as CaCO3(s) <-> Ca2+(aq) + CO3^2-(aq), Ksp = 8.7 x 10^-9. A scientist samples a liter of this seawater and observes a calcium carbonate precipitate settle to the bottom of the flask, so the solution is saturated. Roughly how many moles of calcium carbonate will be dissolved in this 1 L solution?

concepts.title: The Ion-Product Constant of Water
concepts.content: Water is amphoteric and undergoes autoionization (self-ionization), with one molecule acting as the acid and another as the base: H2O + H2O <-> H3O+ + OH-. The equilibrium expression, Kw = [H3O+][OH-], is called the ion-product constant of water and equals 1 x 10^-14 at 25 C. Because only a tiny fraction of molecules ionize and the two ions form in equal numbers, pure water has [H3O+] = [OH-] = 1 x 10^-7 M. Adding an acid or a base disturbs this equilibrium so that one ion's concentration rises and the other's falls, but their product always remains equal to Kw at a given temperature; like other equilibrium constants, Kw increases as temperature increases.

problems.prompt: Pure water will react with itself to form hydronium and hydroxide ions in a process called autoionization, represented by the following reaction: 2 H2O <-> H3O+ + OH-. In this reaction, which of the following can be considered a Bronsted-Lowry base?

concepts.title: pH
concepts.content: The pH scale expresses hydrogen-ion concentration on a logarithmic scale, pH = -log[H+], which implies [H+] = 10^-pH. At 25 C pure water has [H+] = 10^-7 M and pH 7, the neutral point; a higher [H+] gives a pH below 7 (acidic) and a lower [H+] gives a pH above 7 (basic). Most solutions fall between pH 0 and 14, though concentrated strong acids or bases can push past these limits. Basicity can equivalently be described with pOH = -log[OH-], and because [H+][OH-] = 10^-14 at 25 C, pH + pOH = 14. When [H+] = y x 10^-n for a value y between 1 and 10, the pH lies between n-1 and n.

concepts.title: Relationships Between Conjugates
concepts.content: Just as pH is a negative logarithm, pKa = -log Ka and pKb = -log Kb, so the lower the pKa the stronger the acid and the lower the pKb the stronger the base. For any acid-base conjugate pair, the product of the acid- and base-ionization constants equals the ion-product constant of water: Ka x Kb = Kw = 1 x 10^-14 at 25 C. This quantitatively links an acid's strength to that of its conjugate base, so a larger Ka forces a smaller Kb. Taking negative logarithms gives the companion relationship pKa + pKb = 14 at 25 C, a relationship that applies only between an acid and its own conjugate base.

problems.prompt: Given a pKa of 10.3 for bicarbonate (HCO3-), which of the following is FALSE?
choices: The conjugate base of bicarbonate will increase the pH of water.
The pKb of carbonic acid is 3.7.
At equilibrium, more bicarbonate is present in solution than carbonate upon dissociation.
Bicarbonate can function as an acid or a base.

concepts.title: pH Calculations
concepts.content: Because a strong acid dissociates completely, its hydrogen-ion concentration equals the acid's molarity, so the pH follows directly (a 0.01 M HCl solution has pH 2). A weak acid instead reaches equilibrium with its ions, and since it barely dissociates, its undissociated concentration far exceeds [H+], requiring the Ka equilibrium expression to find [H+]. When Ka is small (typically Ka < 10^-4 on the MCAT), the amount that dissociates, x, is negligible compared with the initial acid concentration, which simplifies the algebra. For instance, 0.2 M HCN (Ka = 4.9 x 10^-10) gives [H+] of approximately 1 x 10^-5 M and a pH near 5.

problems.prompt: The pH of a 0.5 M solution of uric acid (a weak monoprotic acid) is measured to be 2.95. Using pH = -log[H+] and Ka = [H+]^2 / [acid], which best represents the Ka value of uric acid?

concepts.title: Neutralization Reactions
concepts.content: Combining an acid and a base produces a neutralization reaction that typically yields a salt plus water, as in HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O. Mixing equimolar amounts of a strong acid and a strong base gives a pH-neutral solution, but if a weak acid or weak base is involved the product solution will not be neutral. Regardless of strength, an acid mixed with an equimolar amount of base neutralizes completely, and every neutralization releases the same characteristic heat from the reaction H+ + OH- -> H2O. The amounts needed for complete neutralization follow a x [A] x V_A = b x [B] x V_B, where a and b count the acidic protons per acid and the protons each base can accept.

concepts.title: Hydrolysis of Salts
concepts.content: A salt is an ionic compound that dissociates in water, and whether the solution becomes acidic, basic, or neutral depends on how its ions undergo hydrolysis. A cation either fails to react (Group 1 and larger Group 2 cations) or behaves as an acid stronger than water (ammonium and small, highly charged metal ions such as Al3+ or Fe3+), while an anion either fails to react (the conjugate base of a strong acid) or behaves as a base stronger than water (the conjugate base of a weak acid). Thus NaCl gives a neutral solution, NH4Cl an acidic one because NH4+ is the conjugate acid of the weak base ammonia, and sodium acetate a basic one because acetate is the conjugate base of a weak acid. To classify a salt it is often enough to identify whether its cation or anion is the reactive, non-spectator ion.

problems.prompt: Ba(NO2)2 is a basic salt due to the interaction of the nitrite ion with water according to the following reaction: NO2- + H2O <-> HNO2 + OH-. Why does the equilibrium shown favor the left side of the reaction?
choices: H2O is a weaker base than OH-.
NO2- is a weaker base than OH-.
H2O is a stronger acid than HNO2.
NO2- is a stronger base than OH-.

problems.prompt: If 50 mL of each of the following solutions are combined as indicated, which of the following will create an acidic final solution?

concepts.title: Buffer Solutions
concepts.content: A buffer resists changes in pH when a small amount of acid or base is added, a capacity that comes from having a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid) present in roughly equal concentrations. Added strong acid is consumed by the conjugate base while added strong base is consumed by the weak acid, so the pH barely shifts. The pH is given by the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, pH = pKa + log([conjugate base]/[weak acid]), which reduces to pH = pKa when the two concentrations are equal (the half-equivalence point). To design a buffer for a target pH, one chooses a weak acid whose pKa is as close as possible to that pH and then adjusts the acid-to-base ratio.

problems.prompt: Addition of what volume of 0.5 M NaOH to 100 mL of 1.0 M malonic acid (pKa1 = 2.8, pKa2 = 5.7) will generate a solution best able to resist pH change at 5.7?

concepts.title: Indicators
concepts.content: An indicator is a weak acid, HA, that displays one color in its protonated form and a different color as its conjugate base A-, following HA + H2O <-> H3O+ + A-. In an acidic solution the equilibrium lies to the left and the first color dominates, while in a basic solution it shifts right to show the second color. The transition occurs over a fairly narrow range of about two pH units centered on the indicator's pKa (roughly pKa - 1 to pKa + 1), so a useful indicator is one whose pKa suits the pH being probed; phenolphthalein, for example, has a pKa near 9. Some polyprotic indicators can change color more than once and therefore exhibit more than two distinct colors.

problems.prompt: A scientist wishes to select an indicator to demonstrate a color change upon neutralization of a solution of acetic acid with a strong base. Which of the following would be the best choice?

concepts.title: Acid-Base Titrations
concepts.content: In an acid-base titration a strong titrant of known concentration is added in small increments to a solution of the unknown acid or base while the pH is recorded, and plotting pH against titrant volume yields a titration curve. Early in the titration the analyte and the conjugate it is being converted into form a buffer, so the pH rises only gradually through this buffering region before climbing steeply near the equivalence point, where the moles of titrant added equal the moles of analyte originally present. The pH at the equivalence point reveals the analyte's strength: it lies above 7 for a weak acid titrated with a strong base, below 7 for a weak base titrated with a strong acid, and at 7 for a strong-strong titration. At the half-equivalence point the acid and its conjugate base are present in equal amounts, so pH = pKa, which is how a titration determines an unknown weak acid's pKa. A polyprotic acid shows one equivalence point for each ionizable proton.

problems.prompt: Carbonic acid is diprotic, dissociating in two steps: H2CO3 <-> H+ + HCO3- (Ka = 2.5 x 10^-4) and HCO3- <-> H+ + CO3^2- (Ka = 5.6 x 10^-11). Titration of a 1.0 M solution of H2CO3 with 2.5 M NaOH will result in a titration curve with two plateaus close to which pH values?

concepts.title: Oxidation-Reduction Reactions
concepts.content: An oxidation-reduction (redox) reaction is any reaction in which the oxidation numbers of atoms change as electrons are redistributed among them. Losing electrons is oxidation and raises an atom's oxidation number, while gaining electrons is reduction and lowers it (LEO the lion says GER; OIL RIG). The species that is oxidized donates electrons and is called the reducing agent, whereas the species that is reduced accepts electrons and is called the oxidizing agent. A redox reaction can be separated into two half-reactions, one for the oxidation and one for the reduction, each balanced for the electrons involved. For example, in Fe + 2 HCl -> FeCl2 + H2, iron goes from 0 to +2 (oxidized) while hydrogen goes from +1 to 0 (reduced).

problems.prompt: Gold can be spontaneously electrodeposited on an iron surface when clean iron is immersed in a solution of Au3+ ions, as described by the equation 3 Fe0 + 2 Au3+ -> 2 Au0 + 3 Fe2+. The reducing agent in this reaction is which of the following?

concepts.title: Galvanic Cells
concepts.content: A galvanic (voltaic) cell uses a spontaneous redox reaction to push electrons through an external wire and do electrical work. Oxidation always occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode, and electrons flow through the wire from anode to cathode ('an ox, red cat'). The two half-cells are linked by a salt bridge; to complete the circuit, anions migrate toward the anode and cations migrate toward the cathode. Ions that only balance charge and take no part in the redox chemistry, such as sulfate in a Zn/Cu cell, are spectator ions. A cell is written in shorthand as anode | anodic solution || cathodic solution | cathode, with concentrations assumed to be 1 M unless stated otherwise.

problems.prompt: A galvanic cell is constructed with two iron electrodes, one placed in a 1.0 M aqueous solution of FeCl3 and the other in 1.0 M FeCl2. Given the reduction potentials Fe3+ + e- -> Fe2+ (E = 0.77 V), Fe2+ + 2e- -> Fe0 (E = -0.44 V), and Fe3+ + 3e- -> Fe0 (E = -0.04 V), which value best approximates the initial voltage of this cell?

concepts.title: Standard Reduction Potentials
concepts.content: Every half-reaction has a reduction potential measured against the standard hydrogen electrode (2 H+ + 2e- -> H2), which is defined as 0.00 V; standard conditions are 25 C, 1 atm, and 1 M solutions. Tables list potentials for reductions, so the potential of an oxidation is obtained by reversing the sign of the corresponding reduction potential. The overall cell voltage is the sum of the cathode's reduction potential and the anode's (reversed) oxidation potential; for the Zn/Cu cell this gives E_cell = 0.76 + 0.34 = +1.10 V. Cell voltage and free energy are linked by delta-G = -nFE, where n is the moles of electrons transferred and F is the faraday (about 96,500 C per mole). A positive cell voltage makes delta-G negative, so the reaction is spontaneous; a negative voltage means it is nonspontaneous.

problems.prompt: Heavy main-group elements can access more oxidation states than lighter members of their group. Using the following reduction potentials for Pb and Sn - Pb2+ + 2e- -> Pb(s) (E = -0.13 V), Pb4+ + 2e- -> Pb2+ (E = +1.69 V), Sn4+ + 2e- -> Sn2+ (E = +0.15 V), and Sn2+ + 2e- -> Sn(s) (E = -0.14 V) - which of the following mono-elemental reactions is the most electrochemically favorable?

A galvanic cell with one Zn and one Fe electrode in 1 M solutions of their ions measures 0.33 V, consistent with the half-reactions Fe2+ + 2e- -> Fe0 (E = -0.44 V) and Zn0 -> Zn2+ + 2e- (E = +0.77 V) referenced to the standard hydrogen electrode. If enough H2SO4 is added to each chamber to make the solution 1 M in H+, how will the cell's standard free energy change? Express the answer as delta-G(2) - delta-G(1), where subscript 1 is the original cell and subscript 2 is the cell after the acid is added. (delta-G = -nFE, F = 96,500 C/mol e-, 1 J = 1 C*V)

In a water-electrolysis cell, an external voltage splits water: H2O(l) -> H2(g) + 1/2 O2(g). Using the following standard reduction potentials - 2 H+(aq) + 2e- -> H2(g) (E = 0.00 V), O2(g) + 4 H+(aq) + 4e- -> 2 H2O(l) (E = 1.23 V), 2 H2O(l) + 2e- -> H2(g) + 2 OH-(aq) (E = -0.83 V), and O2(g) + 2 H2O(l) + 4e- -> 4 OH-(aq) (E = 0.40 V) - what is the standard cell potential for the electrolysis of water?

concepts.title: Oxidizing and Reducing Agents
concepts.content: Reduction potentials also rank how strongly species tend to gain or give up electrons. The more positive a reduction potential, the stronger that reactant is as an oxidizing agent (it readily takes electrons) and the weaker its product is as a reducing agent. The more negative the reduction potential, the weaker the reactant is as an oxidizing agent and the stronger its product is as a reducing agent. For example, because Al3+ + 3e- -> Al has a very negative potential (-1.67 V) compared with Pb2+ + 2e- -> Pb (-0.13 V), aluminum metal is a stronger reducing agent than lead. A species that is already a cation is unlikely to act as a reducing agent when a neutral metal is present that gives up electrons more readily.

problems.prompt: Transition metals in very high (large, positive) oxidation states tend to be very good oxidizing agents. Based on this criterion, which of the following species is likely the best oxidizing agent?

A galvanic cell is built from platinum and iron electrodes in 1 M solutions of their respective salts, with half-reactions Pt2+(aq) + 2e- -> Pt(s) (E = +1.2 V) and Fe3+(aq) + 3e- -> Fe(s) (E = -0.036 V). Which of the following statements about this cell is correct?
choices: E = 1.164 V, and Pt2+ is the reducing agent.
E = 1.164 V, and Fe3+ is the reducing agent.
E = 1.236 V, and Pt2+ is the oxidizing agent.
E = 1.236 V, and Fe3+ is the oxidizing agent.

concepts.title: Nonstandard Conditions
concepts.content: When the reactant concentrations are not all 1 M, the tabulated standard potentials no longer apply directly, and the cell voltage must be found from the Nernst equation, E = E(standard) - (RT/nF) ln Q. This equation shows how changes in temperature and in the concentrations of reactants and products shift the voltage away from its standard value. As the cell runs, concentrations change until the reaction reaches equilibrium, at which point Q equals Keq and E drops to 0, so the cell is dead. The Nernst equation therefore connects the measurable voltage to the reaction quotient under any set of conditions.

problems.prompt: For the electrolysis of water (H2O(l) -> H2(g) + 1/2 O2(g), delta-H = +286 kJ, standard cell potential = -1.23 V), the cell voltage follows the Nernst equation E = E(standard) - (RT/nF) ln Q. In the electrolysis of pure water, E = 0 when T = 400 K. This observation is consistent with which of the following?
choices: The reaction is no longer at equilibrium.
The Keq at 400 K is greater than the Keq at 298 K.
More free energy is required from the circuit at 400 K compared to 298 K.
The standard cell potential is greater at 400 K compared to 298 K.

concepts.title: Concentration Cells
concepts.content: A concentration cell is a galvanic cell whose two electrodes are identical but whose half-cells hold the same ion at different concentrations. Because the electrodes and ions are the same, the standard cell potential E(standard) is zero, yet a real voltage still develops from the concentration difference. Electrons flow toward the half-cell with the higher ion concentration: the electrode in the dilute solution acts as the anode (its metal oxidizes, adding ions), while the electrode in the concentrated solution acts as the cathode (ions are reduced onto it). The current continues until the two concentrations become equal, at which point the reaction stops.

problems.prompt: An electrochemical cell is built with copper electrodes dipped into two separate copper sulfate solutions, one at 0.5 M and one at 1.5 M. Which of the following describes the resulting process?
choices: The cell potential is zero because the standard reduction potential of Cu2+ does not vary with concentration.
Electrons will flow toward the copper electrode in the less concentrated solution.
Sulfate will migrate toward the copper electrode in the less concentrated solution.
Bubbles of hydrogen and oxygen gas will be observed forming on the electrodes.

concepts.title: Redox Titrations
concepts.content: A redox titration finds an unknown by reacting a redox-active species with a strong oxidant or reductant of known concentration, much as an acid-base titration uses a standard acid or base. A redox indicator marks the endpoint through a color change caused by a change in oxidation state rather than the gain or loss of a proton; Ce4+ (bright yellow, becoming colorless as it is reduced to Ce3+) is a common example. While an oxidizable species remains, added Ce4+ is consumed and the solution stays colorless, then turns yellow once everything has been oxidized, marking the equivalence point. On the titration curve, the half-equivalence point is where oxidized and unoxidized reactant are equal, so Q = 1 and ln Q = 0, making the measured potential equal to E(standard) for the redox couple.

concepts.title: Electrolytic Cells
concepts.content: An electrolytic cell uses an external voltage source, such as a battery, to force a nonspontaneous redox reaction to occur, a process called electrolysis. A standard example is the electrolysis of molten NaCl into sodium metal and chlorine gas: the overall standard voltage is negative (about -4.07 V), so the battery must strip electrons from chloride ions (oxidizing them to Cl2) and force sodium ions to accept electrons (reducing them to Na). As in any cell, oxidation still occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode. Electrolytic cells are also used for electroplating, in which a thin metal layer is deposited onto an object used as the cathode, as in silver-plated cutlery or tin- and chromium-plated steel.

problems.prompt: Pennies are fabricated by the electrodeposition of copper onto zinc. Given that this is a non-spontaneous reaction, which of the following is true with respect to the zinc?
choices: It is connected to the positive terminal of the battery, where copper is oxidized.
It is connected to the positive terminal of the battery, where copper is reduced.
It is connected to the negative terminal of the battery, where copper is oxidized.
It is connected to the negative terminal of the battery, where copper is reduced.

problems.prompt: In a water-electrolysis cell, adding a soluble electrolyte to the water increases the rate of hydrogen production. Adding 10 g of which substance, NaCl or AgCl, will cause the greater increase in the rate of hydrogen production from 1 L of pure water?
choices: NaCl, because Na+ ions are much smaller and more highly solvated than Ag+.
NaCl, because Na+ will migrate toward the cathode to alleviate buildup of negative charge.
AgCl, because the standard reduction potential of Na+ is less than that of H+.
AgCl, because Cl- will migrate toward the anode to alleviate buildup of positive charge.

problems.prompt: When adding an electrolyte to water to speed the production of hydrogen gas by electrolysis, it is important to choose one that contains:
choices: a cation with a higher reduction potential than hydroxide.
a cation with a higher reduction potential than hydronium.
an anion with a higher reduction potential than hydronium.
an anion with a higher reduction potential than hydroxide.

concepts.title: Galvanic vs. Electrolytic Cells
concepts.content: In both galvanic and electrolytic cells the anode is the site of oxidation, the cathode is the site of reduction, and electrons travel through the external circuit from anode to cathode. The key difference is energetics: a galvanic cell draws on a spontaneous reaction (positive E, delta-G < 0) to produce electrical power, whereas an electrolytic cell consumes electrical power to drive a nonspontaneous reaction (negative E, delta-G > 0). The electrode polarities are therefore reversed between the two. In a galvanic cell the anode is negative and the cathode positive, while in an electrolytic cell the anode is positive and the cathode negative, because electrons are being forced to go where they otherwise would not.

problems.prompt: In an electrochemical cell, a voltage is externally applied to drive the oxidation of Pt0 and its re-deposition onto the surface of an FeO electrode. Which reaction occurs at the negatively charged (-) electrode?

Which of the following is/are true about the electrolysis of water?
I. Oxygen gas is formed at the cathode.
II. Electrons flow from anode to cathode.
III. The anode is positively charged.

concepts.title: Common Rechargeable Batteries
concepts.content: A rechargeable battery runs as a galvanic cell while discharging and as an electrolytic cell while charging. The lead-acid battery, the oldest rechargeable type and familiar as the car battery, uses a Pb anode and a PbO2 cathode in sulfuric acid; during discharge both electrodes are converted to PbSO4 as Pb is oxidized and PbO2 is reduced. Nickel-cadmium (NiCad) batteries use a Cd anode and a nickel oxide-hydroxide (NiO(OH)) cathode in an alkaline KOH electrolyte. In each case, applying an external voltage reverses the discharge reactions (electrolytic operation), regenerating the original electrode materials and restoring the cell's potential.

problems.prompt: In a lead-acid battery, a Pb0 electrode and a PbO2 electrode are oxidized and reduced, respectively, to PbSO4 during discharge. Side reactions of sulfur species are known to occur in such cells. In the concentrated H2SO4 environment under discharge conditions, which of the following sulfur side reactions is most likely to occur at the anode?

concepts.title: Faraday's Law of Electrolysis
concepts.content: Faraday's law of electrolysis states that the amount of chemical change at an electrode is proportional to the quantity of electric charge passed through the cell. To find how much product forms, first compute the charge with Q = It (current times time, in coulombs), then convert that charge to moles of electrons by dividing by the faraday (about 96,500 C per mole). Finally, use the stoichiometry of the half-reaction to turn moles of electrons into moles, and then grams, of product. For instance, passing 9650 C (0.1 mol of electrons) through molten NaCl deposits 0.1 mol (2.3 g) of Na at the cathode and releases 0.05 mol (3.55 g) of Cl2 at the anode.

problems.prompt: A small toy car is driven by a hydrogen fuel cell for 2 minutes at 2 amps of current. Hydrogen is consumed by the fuel cell in the half-reaction H2 -> 2 H+ + 2e-. What mass of hydrogen gas is consumed? (Faraday's constant = 96,500 C/mol e-)

concepts.title: Structural Formulas, Unsaturation, and Hybridization
concepts.content: An organic molecule is saturated when it has no rings and no pi bonds, and a saturated compound of n carbons carries exactly 2n+2 hydrogens. The degree of unsaturation, (2n+2 - H)/2, counts the rings and pi bonds present, with divalent atoms such as O and S ignored, each halogen treated as a hydrogen, and each trivalent atom such as N replaced by one carbon and one hydrogen. An atom's hybridization follows from how many sigma bonds plus lone pairs surround it: two regions give sp (180 degrees), three give sp2 (120 degrees), and four give sp3 (109.5 degrees). A lone pair that is delocalized into an adjacent pi system is not counted toward the hybridization. Reading these features off a drawn structure, together with the number and type of each distinct atom or proton, sets up predictions about geometry and reactivity.

problems.prompt: In the stereochemically defined chlorosulpholipid shown in Figure 1, the 1H NMR spectrum exhibits one doublet upfield and one doublet downfield. What is the ratio of their respective integrations (upfield to downfield)?

concepts.title: Reaction Intermediates: Carbocation and Carbanion Stability
concepts.content: Carbocations are electron-deficient, sp2 carbons with an empty p orbital, while carbanions carry a full negative charge on carbon; for both, the kind of carbon bearing the charge sets the reactivity. Carbocation stability rises from methyl to primary to secondary to tertiary and is boosted enormously when the empty p orbital can overlap an adjacent pi system so that the positive charge is delocalized by resonance. Carbanion stability runs the opposite way with respect to alkyl substitution, because electron-donating alkyl groups destabilize the extra electrons. In general, the more stable an intermediate is, the lower its energy and the less reactive it is. Because a planar carbocation can be attacked from either face, generating one at a stereocenter destroys that center's configuration and gives racemic product.

problems.prompt: Aluminum chloride (AlCl3) efficiently extracts Cl- from organic and inorganic species, forming [AlCl4]- and a de-chlorinated cation. If 3,5,6,7-tetrachloro-1,4-cyclooctadiene (shown, with its four chlorines labeled Cl_a, Cl_b, Cl_c, and Cl_d) is treated with an equimolar amount of AlCl3, which of the Cl atoms will be extracted?

Esters can react with nucleophiles by acyl-oxygen cleavage or alkyl-oxygen cleavage. The scheme shows both pathways for the thermal reaction of a phthalate ester, Compound I, with ammonia: acyl-O cleavage gives Compound II plus Compound III, and alkyl-O cleavage gives Compound IV plus Compound V. Reaction of optically active Compound I with ammonia is reported to afford racemic products. Which statement is most consistent with this observation?
choices: Reaction of Compound I with ammonia affords Compounds IV and V.
Reaction of Compound I with ammonia proceeds via acyl-oxygen cleavage.
Compound II is formed with inversion of configuration at the original chiral center in Compound I.
Compound IV is formed with inversion of configuration at the original chiral center in Compound I.

concepts.title: Inductive and Resonance Effects
concepts.content: Substituents shift electron density near a charge in two ways. The inductive effect travels through sigma bonds: atoms more electronegative than carbon withdraw density and stabilize electron-rich centers while destabilizing electron-poor ones, whereas alkyl groups donate density; the effect grows with the substituent's electronegativity and falls off rapidly with distance. Resonance, or delocalization, operates in conjugated systems where three or more aligned p orbitals let electrons spread over several atoms. The real molecule is a weighted hybrid of all valid resonance forms, and the most important contributors satisfy octets, minimize charge separation, and place negative charge on the more electronegative atoms. Because delocalization lowers energy, resonance-stabilized species are more stable and less reactive; a clear consequence is the restricted rotation that appears when a nitrogen lone pair conjugates with an adjacent carbonyl, as in an amide.

problems.prompt: Consider the proton NMR spectra (in CDCl3) of Compounds I, II, and III shown. Which of these compounds is/are expected to produce an NMR spectrum consisting exclusively of one singlet, one triplet, and one quartet?

concepts.title: Acidity of Organic Compounds
concepts.content: The strength of a Bronsted acid is set by how well its conjugate base accommodates the resulting negative charge: the more stable that anion, the more the acid dissociates. Charge on a more electronegative atom is more stable, so alcohols beat hydrocarbons, and resonance delocalization stabilizes the anion further, making carboxylic acids far more acidic than alcohols. Electron-withdrawing groups raise acidity inductively, an effect that strengthens with the group's electronegativity and its closeness to the acidic site, while electron-donating groups lower it. A proton flanked by two carbonyls is especially acidic because its enolate spreads charge over both groups, and among otherwise comparable systems an ester enolate is more acidic than an amide enolate because nitrogen donates electron density into the carbanion more than oxygen does. The rough order of organic acidity runs sulfonic and carboxylic acids, then phenols, then the alpha C-H of carbonyls, then alcohols, with substituents tuning each rung.

problems.prompt: Rank compounds I-IV (shown) in order of increasing acidity.
Which one of the four phenolic OH groups (labeled I, II, III, and IV) indicated in the compound shown is expected to be the most acidic?
The chlorosulpholipid shown in Figure 1, whose structure includes a strongly acidic sulfonic/sulfate (-SO3H) group, can act as a:

concepts.title: Nucleophiles and Electrophiles
concepts.content: Nucleophiles are electron-rich Lewis bases carrying a lone pair or pi bond, often with a full or partial negative charge, that seek out electron-poor electrophiles (Lewis acids); a new bond forms when the electrophile accepts the electron pair. Nucleophilicity, a kinetic measure of how readily the donor attacks, increases as negative charge increases, so an anion is a better nucleophile than its neutral conjugate acid. Down a group it increases with polarizability, so the larger, softer atom wins (for example, HS- over HO-). Across a period it increases as electronegativity falls, because a less electronegative atom holds its electrons more loosely and shares them more readily (for example, an amine nitrogen over water oxygen). Nucleophilicity and basicity often trend together but are distinct, since one is kinetic and the other thermodynamic.

problems.prompt: Rank the following species in order of increasing nucleophilicity: NH3, HS-, H2O, CH3O-.

concepts.title: Leaving Groups
concepts.content: A good leaving group departs as a stable species, so the same stability reasoning used for conjugate bases applies to it. Weak bases make the best leaving groups: the halides are excellent because their negative charge is spread over a large, polarizable atom, and resonance-stabilized groups such as tosylate, mesylate, and acetate leave readily as well. Strong bases such as hydroxide, alkoxides, and amide are poor leaving groups because they cannot stabilize the charge and instead remain bound. A poor leaving group can be upgraded by protonation; for instance, an alcohol's -OH becomes -OH2+ under acidic conditions and can then depart as neutral water, which is why many substitutions are acid-catalyzed.

concepts.title: Ring Strain
concepts.content: Ring strain appears when the bond angles a ring forces on its atoms deviate from the ideal angle set by their hybridization, raising the molecule's energy and its reactivity. Small rings suffer most: a three-membered ring is locked near 60 degrees and a four-membered ring near 88 degrees, both far from the 109.5 degrees preferred by sp3 carbons, so their C-C bonds are weakened and unusually reactive. A five-membered ring sits near 108 degrees and a chair cyclohexane reaches essentially strain-free 109.5-degree angles, so these rings behave much like open-chain alkanes. Because strain destabilizes a ring, a strained cyclic carbonyl such as a three-membered-ring lactone is far more susceptible to nucleophilic attack than a larger, relaxed lactone whose angles are close to ideal.

problems.prompt: Compared with gamma-butyrolactone (a five-membered-ring lactone), alpha-acetolactone (a three-membered-ring lactone) shows increased susceptibility to nucleophilic attack. This is due to which of the following factors? I. There is more ring strain in gamma-butyrolactone than in alpha-acetolactone. II. The bond angles deviate more from ideality in alpha-acetolactone than in gamma-butyrolactone. III. There is greater freedom of rotation about the C-C bond at the carbonyl carbon in gamma-butyrolactone than in alpha-acetolactone.

concepts.title: Constitutional and Conformational Isomerism
concepts.content: Constitutional isomers share a molecular formula but connect their atoms differently, like the straight and branched isomers of pentane. Conformational isomers are the same molecule sampled at different rotations about sigma bonds; viewed edge-on in a Newman projection, a staggered arrangement is lower in energy than an eclipsed one because bonds and their attached groups avoid repulsion. For butane the anti conformation, with the two largest groups 180 degrees apart, is most stable, gauche is a higher local minimum, and the syn eclipsed form is the maximum, although an intramolecular hydrogen bond can occasionally make gauche preferred. Cyclohexane avoids angle strain by puckering into a chair with distinct axial and equatorial sites that trade places on a ring flip. Large substituents prefer the roomier equatorial position to escape 1,3-diaxial interactions, so the most stable chair places the bulkiest group equatorial.

problems.prompt: For 4-tert-butylcyclohexanecarbaldehyde, the cis isomer is less susceptible to nucleophilic addition than the trans isomer because: I. the axial tert-butyl group sterically hinders the aldehyde from nucleophilic attack. II. the intermediate formed from addition to its equatorial aldehyde has increased steric interactions. III. the intermediate formed from addition to its axial aldehyde has increased steric interactions.
How many substituents occupy equatorial positions in the most stable chair conformation of (1R,2S,4R)-4-tert-butyl-1-ethyl-2-methylcyclohexane?

concepts.title: Chirality and Stereoisomer Counting
concepts.content: Stereoisomers share both molecular formula and connectivity but differ in the fixed spatial arrangement of their atoms, and they cannot be interconverted by rotating sigma bonds. A carbon bonded to four different groups is a chiral center (stereocenter), and a molecule that cannot be superimposed on its mirror image is chiral, whereas one with an internal mirror plane is achiral. The maximum number of stereoisomers for a molecule with n stereocenters is 2^n, but internal symmetry (meso forms) or duplicate drawings can push the actual count below that ceiling. A double bond whose geometry is already fixed, such as a locked E or Z alkene, is not counted as a stereocenter in this 2^n tally. Identifying and counting stereocenters is therefore the first step in nearly every stereochemistry problem.

problems.prompt: Malhamensilipin A (Figure 2) is known to contain one E alkene, but the rest of the stereochemistry in the molecule is unknown. What is the maximum number of stereoisomers possible for the molecule?

concepts.title: Absolute Configuration (Cahn-Ingold-Prelog and Fischer)
concepts.content: Each stereocenter is labeled R or S by the Cahn-Ingold-Prelog rules. Priorities are assigned to the four substituents by the atomic number of the first atom out, breaking ties by moving outward to the first point of difference, with a multiple bond counted as bonds to duplicated atoms and heavier isotopes outranking lighter ones. With the lowest-priority group pointed away from the viewer, tracing highest to lowest priority clockwise gives R and counterclockwise gives S; if the lowest-priority group instead points toward you, reverse the reading. A Fischer projection encodes this in two dimensions, with horizontal lines understood to project toward the viewer and vertical lines away, which is convenient for sugars. The same rules let you count how many genuine stereocenters a complex natural product contains and fix the configuration at each, including at a hemiacetal carbon.

problems.prompt: For the molecule shown (a single stereocenter bearing -COOH, -CH2OH, -CH2SH, and a tert-butyl group), which of the following is true?
choices: The highest priority group is -C(CH3)3, and the chiral center has an R configuration.
The highest priority group is -CH2SH, and the chiral center has an S configuration.
The highest priority group is -COOH, and the chiral center has an S configuration.
The highest priority group is -CH2SH, and the chiral center has an R configuration.

problems.prompt: The structure of (-)-jiadifenolide, C15H18O7, is shown with its carbons numbered. How many chiral centers are found in (-)-jiadifenolide, and what is the absolute configuration at the hemiacetal carbon atom?
choices: 6 chiral centers, and the hemiacetal carbon has the R configuration
7 chiral centers, and the hemiacetal carbon has the R configuration
6 chiral centers, and the hemiacetal carbon has the S configuration
7 chiral centers, and the hemiacetal carbon has the S configuration

problems.prompt: In the chlorosulpholipid shown in Figure 1, numbering begins at the double-bond end of the chain, and C-13 and C-14 are the two leftmost chiral carbons. What are the absolute configurations at C-13 and C-14, respectively?

concepts.title: Enantiomers and Optical Activity
concepts.content: Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images; they necessarily have opposite configurations at every stereocenter and share most physical properties such as melting point and solubility. They differ in how they rotate plane-polarized light: one enantiomer is dextrorotatory (+) and the other levorotatory (-) by equal magnitude, so a racemic 50:50 mixture shows zero net rotation. The magnitude and sign of a specific rotation must be measured experimentally and bear no fixed relationship to whether a center is R or S. Because two different chiral compounds have unrelated rotations, you cannot predict a product's rotation from a reactant's, and a reaction that leaves a stereocenter untouched keeps the product optically active without letting you forecast its exact value. Separating a racemate (resolution) usually relies on temporarily converting the enantiomers into separable diastereomers with a chiral resolving agent.

problems.prompt: In the reaction shown, (S)-2-methyl-1-butanol ([a] = -5.76 degrees) is treated with HCl and heat, converting the -OH into -Cl to give 1-chloro-2-methylbutane. What is the expected specific rotation of the product?

concepts.title: Diastereomers, Meso Compounds, and Epimers
concepts.content: Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images; they arise when at least one, but not all, stereocenters are inverted, and unlike enantiomers they differ in ordinary physical properties such as melting point, solubility, and specific rotation. A meso compound contains stereocenters yet is achiral because an internal mirror plane makes one half the reflection of the other, so it is optically inactive despite those chiral centers. Epimers are diastereomers that differ at exactly one stereocenter, and anomers are epimers created by the ring closure of a sugar. Because diastereomers have different physical properties they can be separated by ordinary achiral techniques, whereas enantiomers co-elute and require a chiral environment to be resolved. A symmetric reaction, such as syn addition to a symmetric alkene, can funnel to a single meso product rather than to a mixture of stereoisomers.

problems.prompt: Which of the following stereochemical descriptions most accurately describes the products of the reaction shown, in which an alkyl chloride bearing additional unchanged stereocenters is treated with NaI to give the two products drawn?
choices: The product is a mixture of diastereomers.
The product is a mixture of enantiomers.
The product is a racemic mixture.

problems.prompt: D-Galactose (a C-4 epimer of D-glucose) can be selectively oxidized at both of its terminal carbons (the C-1 aldehyde and the C-6 primary alcohol) to give galactaric acid, a symmetric diacid. In aqueous solution galactaric acid is in equilibrium with its cyclic form, galactarolactone. The linear structure of galactaric acid:
choices: is a structural isomer of glucose.

problems.prompt: 2,4-dibromo-3-methylpentane has three chiral centers, for which a maximum of 2^3 = 8 stereoisomers can be drawn (structures I-VIII shown). concepts.title: Geometric Isomers (cis/trans and E/Z)
concepts.content: Geometric isomers are diastereomers that differ in how substituents sit around a ring or a double bond, neither of which rotates freely. For a double bond the E/Z system assigns a priority at each carbon by atomic number: if the two higher-priority groups lie on the same side the alkene is Z, and if on opposite sides it is E; the terms cis and trans are used loosely when each carbon bears one hydrogen. The geometry stays fixed unless the pi bond is broken, so interconversion costs energy. Bulky groups forced onto the same side of a double bond create steric strain, making a crowded Z (cis) alkene higher in energy than its E (trans) counterpart. That stored strain is exactly what drives thermal Z-to-E isomerization, and the most sterically strained alkene benefits most from it.

concepts.title: Nomenclature Basics and Functional Groups
concepts.content: An IUPAC name is built by choosing the longest continuous carbon chain as the parent, numbering it so substituents receive the lowest locants, and citing substituents alphabetically with di-, tri-, and similar multiplying prefixes; a principal group such as the -ol of an alcohol is given as a numbered suffix, while halogens appear as fluoro, chloro, bromo, and iodo prefixes and rings take cyclo-. Equally important is recognizing the common functional groups, among them alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, alkyl halides, alcohols, phenols, ethers, epoxides, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, amides, amines, hemiacetals, lactones, and sulfonates, since each group fixes a molecule's characteristic chemistry. Groups built around O-H, N-H, or an ionized center are polar and hydrogen-bonding, so converting them to nonpolar derivatives, for example by methylating a hydroxyl or a sulfonate, sharply lowers a molecule's overall polarity. Abbreviated line structures, in which carbons are vertices and C-H bonds are left implied, are the standard shorthand for all of this. Fluency in reading names, functional groups, and line structures underlies every other organic chemistry topic.

children.title: Organic Chemistry Reactions: Nucleophilic Substitution and Addition

concepts.title: Nucleophilic Substitution (SN2 and SN1)
concepts.content: Nucleophilic substitution swaps a leaving group on an electrophilic substrate, usually an alkyl halide, for a nucleophile, breaking one sigma bond as another forms. The SN2 mechanism is a single concerted step in which the nucleophile attacks the carbon from the backside as the leaving group departs, so it passes through a pentavalent transition state and inverts the configuration at a chiral carbon; its rate is second order (first order in both partners), it runs fastest for unhindered methyl and primary substrates, and it is favored by strong, small nucleophiles in polar aprotic solvents. The SN1 mechanism instead loses the leaving group first to form a planar carbocation in the slow, rate-determining step, after which the nucleophile adds to either face and largely racemizes a chiral center. SN1 is first order in substrate only, is favored by substrates that give stabilized (tertiary) carbocations, by protic solvents, and by weak nucleophiles, and it can involve carbocation rearrangements.

concepts.title: Aldehydes and Ketones: Formation and Oxidation
concepts.content: Aldehydes and ketones are frequently made by oxidizing alcohols: a primary alcohol is oxidized to an aldehyde and a secondary alcohol to a ketone, while a tertiary alcohol cannot form a carbonyl because its carbinol carbon has no hydrogen for the oxidant to remove. Common aqueous oxidants such as chromic acid, chromate and dichromate salts, permanganate, and chromium trioxide tend to carry a primary alcohol past the aldehyde all the way to a carboxylic acid, whereas the anhydrous reagent PCC stops cleanly at the aldehyde. The reactivity of the resulting carbonyl comes from its strongly polarized C=O bond, since the electronegative oxygen pulls the pi electrons toward itself. That polarization leaves the carbonyl carbon electrophilic and open to nucleophilic attack, and it also makes the protons on the neighboring alpha-carbon acidic.

concepts.title: Acidity and Enolization
concepts.content: Protons on the carbon alpha to a carbonyl are unusually acidic because a strong base such as hydroxide or an alkoxide can remove one to give a resonance-stabilized carbanion, the enolate ion, whose negative charge is delocalized onto the electronegative carbonyl oxygen. The enolate is nucleophilic mainly at that alpha-carbon rather than at the oxygen. A proton flanked by two carbonyl groups is especially acidic and even exchanges with solvent deuterium. Which enolate forms can be controlled: a bulky base at low temperature removes the most accessible proton to give the kinetic enolate, while warmer, milder conditions favor the more substituted, more stable thermodynamic enolate.

concepts.title: Keto-Enol Tautomerism
concepts.content: A carbonyl compound and its enol are tautomers, readily interconvertible constitutional isomers that differ only in the position of one proton and the double bond; moving a proton from the alpha-carbon to the carbonyl oxygen converts the keto form to the enol. For simple aldehydes and ketones the equilibrium lies far toward the keto form, and only water, or a trace of acid or base, is needed to interconvert them. Because the alpha-carbon is planar in the enol, reprotonation can occur on either face, so a stereocenter at that carbon is racemized. The same tautomerization underlies the base-promoted interconversion of an aldose and a ketose, such as glucose and fructose.

problems.prompt: Glucose and fructose share metabolic pathways and can each be interconverted. Under which conditions could glucose be converted to fructose?

The reaction is quenched at 50% completion. Which statement is most consistent with the passage?
choices: If the reaction proceeds via Mechanism I, recovered Compound III will be optically inactive.

If the reaction proceeds via Mechanism II, the chiral center in recovered Compound III will have undergone inversion of configuration.

concepts.title: Nucleophilic Addition to Aldehydes and Ketones
concepts.content: Because the carbonyl double bond of an aldehyde or ketone is strongly polarized, the carbonyl carbon is electrophilic and readily attacked by nucleophiles. In a nucleophilic addition the nucleophile bonds to that carbon while the pi bond breaks and the oxygen takes the electrons to become an alkoxide, which is then protonated to an alcohol, so one pi bond is replaced by two sigma bonds. This same electrophilicity makes carbonyls easy to reduce, and hydride reagents such as NaBH4 and the stronger LiAlH4 deliver hydride to give alcohols. Converting an aldehyde to an alcohol removes the C=O stretch near 1700 cm^-1 and produces a broad O-H stretch near 3400 cm^-1.

concepts.title: Organometallic Reagents
concepts.content: Grignard reagents (RMgX) and organolithiums (RLi) place a partial negative charge on carbon, making them both strong nucleophiles and strong bases that transfer their R group to an electrophilic carbonyl carbon. Adding to an aldehyde gives a secondary alcohol and adding to a ketone gives a tertiary alcohol once acidic workup protonates the intermediate alkoxide. With an ester, the first equivalent produces a ketone that reacts again, so excess reagent yields a tertiary alcohol. Because acidic O-H, N-H, or COOH protons destroy these reagents, they must be used in aprotic solvents such as diethyl ether and kept away from such groups.

concepts.title: Acetals and Hemiacetals
concepts.content: When an alcohol adds to an aldehyde or ketone under acid catalysis, adding one -OR group gives a hemiacetal (a carbon bearing both -OH and -OR), and adding a second -OR group with loss of water gives an acetal (a carbon bearing two -OR groups). A diol such as ethylene glycol closes in a single step to give a cyclic acetal. The carbonyl compound, hemiacetal, and acetal all sit in equilibrium, and acetals hydrolyze back to the carbonyl in aqueous acid. Because acetals are stable to base and nucleophiles but easily removed with acid, a cyclic acetal is commonly used to protect a ketone or aldehyde while other reactions are run.

concepts.title: Cyanohydrin Formation
concepts.content: Cyanide is a good nucleophile that adds to the electrophilic carbon of an aldehyde or ketone, and protonation of the resulting alkoxide gives a cyanohydrin, a single carbon bearing both a hydroxyl group and a nitrile. The mechanism parallels hemiacetal formation, but here the equilibrium lies so far toward product that the addition is effectively irreversible. Because it installs a new nitrile carbon, the reaction lengthens the carbon skeleton by one. The nitrile can later be hydrolyzed to a carboxylic acid.

concepts.title: Imine and Enamine Formation
concepts.content: Amines are nucleophilic at nitrogen and add to aldehydes and ketones under mildly acidic conditions in a sequence that starts by protonating the carbonyl oxygen to make the carbon more electrophilic. A primary amine adds and then loses water to give an imine (a C=N compound, or Schiff base), while a secondary amine, lacking a second N-H to lose, instead loses an alpha-proton to give an enamine. Both reactions are reversible, and the products hydrolyze back to the carbonyl in aqueous acid. Like an enol, an enamine is nucleophilic at its alpha-carbon.

choices: attack by the amine nitrogen on the carbonyl carbon.

concepts.title: Aldol Condensation
concepts.content: In the aldol reaction a base removes an alpha-proton to form an enolate, whose alpha-carbon then attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second molecule, giving a beta-hydroxy aldehyde or ketone after protonation. It thus combines the two hallmark reactivities of carbonyls: the acidity of the alpha-proton and the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon. When the two partners differ it is a crossed aldol, and a messy mixture is avoided by choosing one partner with no alpha-protons so it can serve only as the electrophile. Heating the beta-hydroxy product drives dehydration to a conjugated alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl.

problems.prompt: Which reaction shown could be used to prepare the target beta-hydroxy ketone? (Choose the reaction.)

concepts.title: Kinetic vs. Thermodynamic Control
concepts.content: When a reaction can give more than one product, the conditions decide which one dominates: the kinetic product is the one that forms fastest over the lowest barrier, while the thermodynamic product is the most stable one. For an unsymmetrical ketone with two sets of alpha-protons, a bulky base at low temperature removes the more accessible proton to give the less-substituted kinetic enolate, whereas warmer conditions with a smaller base allow equilibration to the more-substituted, more stable thermodynamic enolate. A reaction held under conditions that let it equilibrate will drift toward the thermodynamic product, and an unchanging product ratio maintained over long times at a given temperature marks that equilibrium composition. A lower yield of the more stable product at low temperature therefore signals kinetic control.

problems.prompt: Compound J reacts with Compound K at 20 C to give products L (20%) and M (80%). At 60 C, L and M form in 80% and 20% yields, respectively. When the 20 C mixture is warmed to 60 C and left overnight, its composition slowly shifts to 80% L / 20% M and then stays constant. Which statement is most consistent with this information?
choices: An equilibrium mixture of L and M is obtained at 60 C.

concepts.title: Carboxylic Acids: Reduction and Decarboxylation
concepts.content: Carboxylic acids can be reduced to primary alcohols, but only by a strong hydride reagent: lithium aluminum hydride works because its highly polarized Al-H bond is strongly reducing, while the milder NaBH4 does not touch a carboxylic acid. A carboxylic acid that carries a carbonyl group at the beta position (a beta-keto acid) is unstable and readily loses carbon dioxide on heating. This decarboxylation passes through a six-membered cyclic transition state, expelling CO2 and first giving an enol that tautomerizes to the carbonyl product; an ordinary acid without the beta-carbonyl does not decarboxylate this easily. This is why a substrate is often oxidized to a beta-keto acid before it can lose CO2, both in acetoacetic-ester chemistry and in metabolism.

concepts.title: Carboxylic Acid Derivatives and Reactivity
concepts.content: The carboxylic acid derivatives, acid halides, anhydrides, esters, and amides, are all acyl groups bonded to an electronegative leaving group and, like aldehydes and ketones, are electrophilic at the carbonyl carbon. Because they bear a leaving group, nucleophilic addition is followed by elimination: a nucleophile adds to give a tetrahedral intermediate that then expels the leaving group, reforming the carbonyl in an addition-elimination (acyl substitution). Reactivity falls in the order acid chloride > anhydride > ester > amide, tracking the decreasing stability of the leaving group, so each interconversion is favored toward the less reactive derivative. Amides cannot be made directly from a carboxylic acid and an amine, because the fast acid-base reaction that forms an ammonium carboxylate salt outruns the desired addition-elimination.

concepts.title: Esterification and Ester Hydrolysis
concepts.content: In a Fischer esterification a carboxylic acid and an alcohol combine under acid catalysis to give an ester plus water, and because the reaction is a reversible equilibrium it is pushed toward the ester by using excess reactant or removing water, and run in reverse it is simply acid-catalyzed hydrolysis. In the mechanism the acid protonates the carbonyl to make its carbon more electrophilic, the alcohol adds to form a tetrahedral intermediate, and loss of water then delivers the ester. Transesterification follows the same pattern with an incoming alcohol replacing the alkoxy group of an existing ester. Base-promoted hydrolysis, or saponification, instead cleaves an ester to a carboxylate and an alcohol.
