concepts.title: Amino Acid Structure and Nomenclature
concepts.content: All twenty standard amino acids share a common backbone: a central alpha-carbon bonded to an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen, and a variable side chain (R-group). The side chain is the only part that differs between amino acids and sets each one's size, polarity, charge, and chemistry. Because the alpha-carbon carries four different groups, every amino acid is chiral except glycine, whose R-group is a second hydrogen. Side chains are grouped as nonpolar, polar, acidic, or basic, and the aromatic side chains (Phe, Tyr, Trp) absorb ultraviolet light near 280 nm.

problems.prompt: Ultraviolet absorbance at 280 nm is commonly used to estimate protein concentration, but it can be skewed by aromatic side chains in contaminating peptides. If present in equimolar amounts, which of the following nonapeptides is LEAST likely to affect the accuracy of a 280 nm measurement?

concepts.title: L- and D-Amino Acids and Absolute Configuration
concepts.content: Amino acids and sugars are labeled D or L by comparing the configuration of their key chiral center to glyceraldehyde, a scheme independent of the R/S (absolute configuration) and (+)/(-) (optical rotation) systems. In a Fischer projection, horizontal bonds point toward the viewer and vertical bonds away, and an L-amino acid is drawn with its alpha-amino group on the left. Nearly all amino acids in animals are L (and are S by CIP rules, with cysteine the exception), whereas naturally occurring carbohydrates are D. The three labels describe different things: D/L tracks the biosynthetic precursor, R/S the actual three-dimensional arrangement, and (+)/(-) the measured optical rotation.

concepts.title: Synthesis of Amino Acids: Strecker and Gabriel Syntheses
concepts.content: Two classic laboratory routes build racemic alpha-amino acids. In the Strecker synthesis an aldehyde reacts with ammonia (from an ammonium salt) to form an imine, which is protonated and attacked by cyanide to give an alpha-aminonitrile; acidic hydrolysis then converts the nitrile to a carboxylic acid. In the Gabriel-malonic ester synthesis, phthalimide is deprotonated to a nucleophilic anion that displaces bromide from an alpha-bromomalonic ester (an SN2 step), the alpha-carbon is alkylated with the desired side chain, and acid hydrolysis followed by decarboxylation releases the amino acid. Because a new stereocenter is created without any chiral influence, both methods give racemic products.

concepts.title: Amino Acid Acid-Base Chemistry and the Isoelectric Point
concepts.content: Each amino acid is amphoteric, carrying an acidic carboxyl group (pKa about 2) and a basic ammonium group (pKa about 9-10), plus any ionizable side chain. Whether a group is protonated depends on the solution pH relative to its pKa: below the pKa it is mostly protonated, above it mostly deprotonated, as described by the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation. Near neutral pH the molecule exists as a dipolar zwitterion with balanced positive and negative charges. The isoelectric point (pI) is the pH at which the net charge is zero; for an amino acid with only two ionizable groups it is simply the average of the two pKa values.

concepts.title: Separation and Analysis of Amino Acids and Proteins
concepts.content: Amino acids and proteins are separated by exploiting differences in charge, size, and polarity. In gel electrophoresis a molecule migrates in an electric field according to its net charge at the gel's pH: toward the positive electrode when the pH is above its pI (net negative), toward the negative electrode when below its pI, and not at all at its pI. Chromatographic methods add further options: ion-exchange separates by charge, size-exclusion by size, affinity (for example lectin) by specific binding, and reverse-phase HPLC by hydrophobicity, with nonpolar species eluting last. Choosing a suitable combination of techniques lets one resolve species that differ in any one of these properties.

concepts.title: The Peptide Bond and Protein Synthesis
concepts.content: A peptide bond is an amide linkage formed by a condensation (nucleophilic acyl substitution) between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the alpha-amino group of the next, with loss of water. The repeating N-C-C backbone runs from a free amino (N-) terminus, written first by convention, to a free carboxyl (C-) terminus, and each unit in the chain is called a residue. Peptide bond formation is thermodynamically unfavorable, so cells couple it to energy input; in the laboratory, reagents such as DCC (dicyclohexylcarbodiimide), used with protecting groups, activate the carboxyl group and drive coupling in a controlled order.

concepts.title: Hydrolysis of the Peptide Bond
concepts.content: Because the nitrogen lone pair delocalizes into the carbonyl, the peptide bond has partial double-bond character, which makes it planar, rigid, and resistant to rotation. Hydrolysis to a free amine and carboxylic acid is thermodynamically favorable but kinetically very slow, so peptide bonds persist until a catalyst is present. Strong acid with heat cleaves peptides nonspecifically into their constituent amino acids, whereas proteolytic enzymes cleave at specific residues: trypsin cuts on the carboxyl side of Lys and Arg, and chymotrypsin cuts after aromatic residues (Phe, Tyr, Trp). Overlapping fragments from different cleavages can be aligned to deduce a peptide's sequence.

problems.prompt: Partial hydrolysis of hexapeptide A gave four tripeptides (W, X, Y, Z). When the mixture was subjected to gel electrophoresis at pH 7, only one tripeptide migrated toward the negative terminal. Which of the following sequences is hexapeptide A?

An unknown heptapeptide (Compound I) was cleaved by trypsin into the peptides Ala-Leu, Trp-Arg, and Gly-Tyr-Lys, and by chymotrypsin into Gly-Tyr, Lys-Trp, and Arg-Ala-Leu. What is the amino acid sequence of Compound I?

concepts.title: Structure and Configuration of Monosaccharides
concepts.content: Monosaccharides are simple sugars with the formula (CH2O)n, a carbon chain bearing an aldehyde (aldose) or ketone (ketose) plus hydroxyl groups on the remaining carbons. They are named by carbonyl type and chain length (for example, an aldohexose is a six-carbon aldose), with carbons numbered from the most oxidized end. Each sugar is assigned D or L based on the configuration of the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl compared with glyceraldehyde; the sugars in our bodies are D. A monosaccharide with n chiral centers has up to 2^n stereoisomers, which may be related as enantiomers, diastereomers, or epimers (differing at just one chiral carbon).

concepts.title: Cyclic Structures of Monosaccharides
concepts.content: In solution, five- and six-carbon sugars cyclize when one hydroxyl intramolecularly attacks the carbonyl carbon to form a hemiacetal; the six-membered ring is a pyranose and the five-membered ring a furanose, and the cyclic forms strongly predominate. Ring closure creates a new stereocenter at the former carbonyl carbon, the anomeric carbon, giving two anomers designated alpha (anomeric OH down) or beta (anomeric OH up). The two anomers interconvert through the open-chain form in a process called mutarotation. Haworth projections depict these rings, with groups that lie on the left in a Fischer projection drawn pointing up.

problems.prompt: The figure shows D-mannose and N-acetyl-D-glucosamine, two monosaccharides commonly found in N-linked glycans. Which of the following accurately describes them?
choices: D-Mannose is shown in the alpha configuration and N-acetyl-D-glucosamine in the beta configuration.
N-acetyl-D-glucosamine can form beta-1,4 glycosidic linkages with D-mannose.
The N-acetyl group in N-acetyl-D-glucosamine can form a Schiff base.
Mannose is a structural isomer of glucose.

concepts.title: Disaccharides and Polysaccharides
concepts.content: A disaccharide forms when the anomeric carbon of one sugar joins a hydroxyl of another through a glycosidic bond, an acetal linkage created by dehydration. The linkage is specified by the carbons connected and its anomeric configuration; for example, lactose is galactose-beta-1,4-glucose and sucrose is glucose-alpha-1,2-fructose. Once a sugar's anomeric carbon is locked into a glycosidic (acetal) bond it can no longer mutarotate. Polysaccharides extend this pattern: glycogen and starch store glucose in alpha-1,4 chains with alpha-1,6 branches, while cellulose and chitin use beta-1,4 linkages that give strong, linear fibers most mammalian enzymes cannot digest.

problems.prompt: Chitin, the main structural component of arthropod exoskeletons, is a long-chain polymer of N-acetyl glucosamine (a repeating segment is shown). Which of the following best describes the glycosidic linkage in chitin?

beta-Galactosidase hydrolyzes the beta-glycosidic bond of lactose (galactose-beta-1,4-glucose) and also catalyzes transgalactosylation, which converts lactose into allolactose. Which structure most likely represents allolactose? (Choose the structure.)

concepts.title: Hydrolysis of Glycosidic Linkages
concepts.content: Glycosidic bonds are cleaved by adding water across the acetal, the exact reverse of their formation, releasing the component monosaccharides; each acetal (glycosidic) carbon in a molecule marks one cleavage site. Enzymatic hydrolysis by glycosidases is stereospecific, proceeding with net inversion or retention through single- or double-displacement mechanisms and giving a single hemiacetal anomer. Nonenzymatic acid-catalyzed hydrolysis instead goes through oxocarbenium intermediates (by endocyclic or exocyclic C-O cleavage) and typically produces mixtures of anomeric hemiacetals. Hydrolysis of glycosides is favorable thermodynamically but slow without a catalyst.

problems.prompt: Digoxin (structure shown), a foxglove natural product used to treat atrial fibrillation, contains several glycosidic (acetal) linkages. How many fragments are expected to result from acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of digoxin?

Schemes I and II (shown) depict single- and double-displacement mechanisms of enzyme-catalyzed glycoside hydrolysis, labeling five species I-V. What is the function of species I, II, III, IV, and V, respectively?
choices: I acid, II nucleophile, III base, IV nucleophile, V leaving group
I acid, II base, III nucleophile, IV base, V leaving group
I leaving group, II nucleophile, III base, IV nucleophile, V acid
I leaving group, II base, III nucleophile, IV base, V acid

problems.prompt: A cyclic acetal (Compound III) undergoes acid-catalyzed reaction with CD3OH (H+, losing isopropanol), which can proceed by endocyclic (Mechanism III) or exocyclic (Mechanism IV) cleavage of an acetal C-O bond. Based on the passage, which of the four compounds I-IV (shown) is/are expected to form as reaction products?

Primeverose and vicianose are naturally occurring disaccharides, each made of D-glucose and one other monosaccharide (their structures, with the Fischer projections of D-arabinose and D-xylose, are shown). Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of each affords D-glucose plus one other monosaccharide. What are the other monosaccharides from primeverose and vicianose, respectively?

Cleavage of the glycosidic linkage in Compound X by yeast alpha-glucosidase releases Aglycone Y, which then reacts with a nucleophilic residue in the enzyme to inhibit it irreversibly. Which compound most likely corresponds to the aglycone? (Choose the structure.)

concepts.title: Reducing Sugars, Benedict's Test, and Glycation
concepts.content: A reducing sugar has a free hemiacetal at its anomeric carbon that is in equilibrium with the open-chain carbonyl, so it can be oxidized while reducing another species. Benedict's test uses Cu2+ to oxidize such a sugar's aldehyde or ketone to a carboxylate, producing a red Cu2O precipitate; all monosaccharides and any sugar with a free anomeric carbon test positive, whereas acetals (whose anomeric carbon is fully linked) do not. Reducing agents such as NaBH4 reduce the free aldehyde form of a reducing sugar to a primary alcohol. When a reducing sugar's carbonyl condenses with an amine it forms a Schiff base (imine) that can rearrange, the basis of nonenzymatic glycation such as the Maillard reaction and hemoglobin-A1c formation.

problems.prompt: Predict the product(s) of the reaction shown, in which benzaldehyde is treated with 2 Cu2+ under basic aqueous conditions (Benedict's conditions). (Choose the structure.)
Which of the following would result from treating lactose (beta-D-galactopyranosyl-(1->4)-D-glucose) with NaBH4?
choices: Reduction of C-1 of the glucose residue to yield an acyclic primary alcohol
Reduction of C-1 of the glucose residue to yield a cyclic ether
Cleavage of the glycosidic linkage to yield galactose and glucose
No reaction, as all functional groups in lactose are stable to the conditions

problems.prompt: Hemoglobin A combines with glucose at the N-terminal Val residue (R = Val-Hb) through the sequence shown: Step 1 forms Intermediate I, Step 2 (acid-catalyzed) forms Intermediate II, and Step 3 forms Product III. Which structure most likely corresponds to Intermediate II? (Choose the structure.)
In the Maillard reaction, asparagine reacts with a reducing sugar and is ultimately converted to acrylamide (CH2=CH-C(=O)NH2). How many 1H NMR resonances will acrylamide display?

In the Maillard pathway, the Schiff base formed between asparagine and a reducing sugar is isomerized (Step 3) through an acid-catalyzed enolization and tautomerization of the proton alpha to the imine. Which of the following reagents would perform this isomerization?
Which of the following statements regarding Schiff base (imine) formation between an amine and a carbonyl compound is true?
choices: Under strongly acidic conditions, the rate of the reaction increases.
Removing water from the reaction system decreases the yield of the Schiff base product.
The loss of water is the thermodynamic driving force in the reaction.
The reaction outcome is under kinetic control, favoring formation of the Schiff base product.

problems.prompt: Glycated hemoglobin (hemoglobin-A1c) forms when glucose reacts with an amino group in hemoglobin through the first three steps of the Maillard pathway. Which of the following statements about hemoglobin-A1c is FALSE?
choices: Glucose and mannose can react to form identical hemoglobin-A1c adducts.
A sustained period of hyperglycemia will result in elevated hemoglobin-A1c levels.
High-performance liquid chromatography can effectively separate hemoglobin-A1c from non-glycated hemoglobin.
The isomerization that ultimately forms hemoglobin-A1c is reversible in an aqueous acidic environment.

concepts.title: Lipids: Fatty Acids and Micelles
concepts.content: Lipids are oily, hydrophobic molecules whose water-insolubility comes from their long nonpolar hydrocarbon regions. A fatty acid is a long unbranched hydrocarbon chain (typically 14-18 carbons, and even-numbered in humans because it is built two carbons at a time) ending in a carboxylic acid; it is saturated if it has no carbon-carbon double bonds and unsaturated if it has one or more, which are almost always cis. Because a fatty acid has a single hydrophobic tail and a polar head, it is amphipathic and spontaneously forms spherical micelles in water, driven by the hydrophobic effect. Soaps are the sodium salts of fatty acids.

problems.prompt: Which of the following best characterizes the difference between fatty acids and phospholipids?
choices: Fatty acids have two tails and form micelles; phospholipids have one tail and form membranes.
Fatty acids have two tails and form membranes; phospholipids have two tails and form micelles.
Fatty acids have one tail and form micelles; phospholipids have two tails and form membranes.
Fatty acids have one tail and form membranes; phospholipids have two tails and form micelles.

concepts.title: Triacylglycerols and Phospholipid Membranes
concepts.content: Fatty acids are stored as triacylglycerols (triglycerides, or fat): three fatty acids esterified to the three hydroxyls of glycerol, a relatively inert storage form found in adipose cells. Phospholipids, derived from diacylglycerol phosphate, replace one fatty acid with a phosphate-linked polar head group; with two hydrophobic tails and one hydrophilic head, they assemble into lipid bilayers rather than micelles. The bilayer, driven by hydrophobic interactions and stabilized by van der Waals contacts between the tails, forms the barrier of cell membranes between the intracellular and extracellular environments. Cholesterol, another membrane lipid, serves as the building block for the steroid hormones.

concepts.title: Units and Dimensions
concepts.content: Physics quantities are expressed in SI (metric) units built on three base units for mechanics: the meter for length, the kilogram for mass, and the second for time, which is why the system is called mks. Every physical quantity can be written in terms of these base units and carries a dimension that is independent of the particular unit chosen, so a length is a length whether measured in meters, miles, or furlongs. Speed, for instance, always has dimensions of length divided by time (L/T). Power-of-ten prefixes such as nano- (10^-9), milli- (10^-3), kilo- (10^3), and mega- (10^6) scale the base units, and tracking dimensions lets you check equations and convert between units reliably.

concepts.title: Kinematics
concepts.content: Kinematics describes how objects move without addressing what causes the motion, using the quantities displacement, velocity, and acceleration. Displacement is the vector change in position, distinct from the scalar total distance traveled; for a closed path the displacement is zero even though distance is not. Velocity is the rate of change of displacement and is a vector, while its magnitude, the speed, is a scalar that is never negative. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, so an object accelerates whenever its speed or its direction changes, meaning something moving at constant speed around a curve is still accelerating.

problems.prompt: Which of the following kinematic descriptions is physically impossible?
choices: An object in motion for a time interval has zero average velocity but positive nonzero average speed.
An object maintains constant speed for a time interval but has nonzero acceleration.
An object in motion for a time interval has zero displacement but nonzero total distance.
An object in motion for a time interval has an average velocity with a greater magnitude than its average speed.

problems.prompt: Assuming one-dimensional motion, which velocity-versus-time graph represents an object making a round trip (returning to its starting point)? (Choose the graph.)

concepts.title: Uniformly Accelerated Motion
concepts.content: When an object's acceleration is constant, five quantities (displacement, initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration, and time) are linked by a set of relations Princeton Review calls the Big Five, each of which omits exactly one of the five variables. You choose the right equation by identifying the variable that is neither given nor asked for. During constant acceleration the average velocity is simply the mean of the initial and final velocities. On a velocity-versus-time graph, the slope at any point equals the acceleration and the area between the curve and the time axis equals the displacement, with area below the axis counted as negative.

concepts.title: Free Fall and Projectile Motion
concepts.content: Free fall is motion under gravity alone, with the downward gravitational acceleration g taken as about 10 m/s^2 for the MCAT; it applies to any object whose only acceleration is gravitational, including a ball thrown upward. Projectile motion, launched at an angle, is handled by analyzing the horizontal and vertical directions separately: the horizontal velocity stays constant because there is no horizontal acceleration, while the vertical motion is uniformly accelerated by gravity. At the top of the parabolic path the vertical velocity is zero but the horizontal velocity persists. By the symmetry of the parabola, the time to rise equals the time to fall, so the total flight time is twice the time to reach the peak.

problems.prompt: A ball is thrown horizontally with initial velocity vx from a height Y above the ground. Assuming negligible air resistance and gravitational acceleration g, how much time does it take to reach the ground? (Choose the expression.)
An object is projected from the ground at 30 degrees above the horizontal and returns to the ground 8 seconds later. What is its maximum height? (Use g = 10 m/s^2.)
choices: There is not enough information to solve.

concepts.title: Mass, Force, and Newton's Laws
concepts.content: Mass measures an object's inertia, its resistance to changes in motion, whereas a force is a push or pull that can change an object's velocity. Newton's first law says an object keeps a constant velocity unless a net external force acts on it, so zero net force means zero acceleration but not necessarily zero speed. The second law states that the net force equals mass times acceleration (F = ma), so acceleration grows with net force and shrinks with mass, and it points in the direction of the net force. The third law says that whenever one object exerts a force on a second, the second exerts an equal and opposite force back on the first, an action-reaction pair acting on different objects.

problems.prompt: Two lead balls of unequal mass are thrown in the vertical direction on the Moon, one directly upward and the other downward with the same speed from the same height. Which statement(s) is/are true? I. The two balls reach the ground with the same speed. II. The two balls reach the ground at the same time. III. The two balls are attracted to the Moon with a force of equal magnitude.

concepts.title: Newton's Law of Gravitation
concepts.content: Weight is the gravitational force exerted on an object, computed as w = mg, and is distinct from mass, which is an intrinsic, location-independent measure of inertia; a baseball taken to the Moon keeps its mass but weighs less. Newton's law of gravitation states that every pair of masses attracts each other with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers, F = GMm/r^2. Because it is an inverse-square law, the force falls off rapidly as separation grows. Combining w = mg with this law gives g = GM/r^2, which shows why the surface gravity differs from planet to planet and decreases with altitude.

concepts.title: Contact Forces: The Normal Force, Friction, and Tension
concepts.content: When two objects touch, they exert contact forces on each other. The normal force acts perpendicular to the surface and prevents objects from passing through it, while friction acts parallel to the surface and opposes sliding. Static friction, which can rise up to a maximum of the static coefficient times the normal force, keeps surfaces from starting to slide, whereas kinetic friction equals the kinetic coefficient times the normal force once sliding occurs, and the kinetic coefficient is usually smaller than the static one. On an inclined plane of angle theta the weight splits into mg sin(theta) along the surface and mg cos(theta) into it, so the normal force is mg cos(theta). Tension is the pulling force transmitted along a rope, string, or cable, and an ideal pulley redirects it without changing its magnitude.

problems.prompt: A passage on friction notes that the frictional force depends on both the normal force and the coefficient of friction, and that applying a lubricant lowers the coefficient of friction. A nurse inserts a catheter into a patient. To minimize discomfort and shearing damage during the procedure, what should the nurse do?
choices: Squeeze harder and avoid lubricant to increase the coefficient of friction between the catheter and tissue.
Squeeze harder and use lubricant to decrease the coefficient of friction between the catheter and tissue.
Squeeze softer and avoid lubricant to increase the force of friction between the catheter and tissue.
Squeeze softer and use lubricant to decrease the force of friction between the catheter and tissue.

problems.prompt: A passage notes that coefficients of friction are not truly constant and are usually reduced at very high sliding speeds. When a copper pin slides against a copper surface, the force required to keep the pin sliding at constant speed is most likely:
choices: greater at high speeds than at low speeds.
greater at low speeds than at high speeds.

problems.prompt: A friction passage gives Table 1 of measured mean coefficients of friction (static, kinetic): PTFE on PTFE (0.04, 0.04); silicone tubing on skin, unlubricated (0.95, 0.6); silicone tubing on skin, lubricated (0.7, 0.4); zinc on cast iron (0.85, 0.21); cast iron on cast iron (1.1, 0.15). Based only on these tabulated coefficients of friction, which of the following can be validly concluded?
choices: Lubrication has a more significant effect on the coefficient of static friction than on the coefficient of kinetic friction.
If the coefficient of static friction between two materials is greater than that between two other materials, the coefficient of kinetic friction will always follow the same pattern.
The coefficient of kinetic friction is always less than or equal to the coefficient of static friction.
None of the above can validly be concluded from the given data.

problems.prompt: The static coefficient of friction between cast iron and zinc is about 0.85. What is the steepest angle at which a flat zinc surface can be tilted before a cast iron pot resting on it starts to slide?

Rubber on rubber can have a very high coefficient of friction, and for rubber the coefficient of friction actually decreases as the normal force increases. If a rubber object rests on a rubber surface and its mass is increased by adding weights inside it, what is true of the magnitude of the force required to initiate horizontal movement (Fs) and the weight of the object (w)?
choices: The ratio of Fs to w increases.
The ratio of Fs to w remains constant.
The ratio of Fs to w decreases.
The difference between Fs and w remains constant.

problems.prompt: Which best explains why polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE, or Teflon), which has an extremely low coefficient of friction, is often used to coat non-stick cookware?
choices: The toxicity of fumes given off by PTFE-coated pots is less than that of standard cooking oils.
Its extremely low coefficient of friction reduces the occurrence of food sticking to the pans.
Its extremely low coefficient of friction reduces the heat lost to friction when food slides on PTFE-coated surfaces.
PTFE was also used in the Manhattan Project to coat pipes holding radioactive uranium compounds.

concepts.title: Uniform Circular Motion
concepts.content: An object executes uniform circular motion when it travels a circular path at constant speed. Even though the speed is constant, the direction of the velocity is always changing, so the object is accelerating; this centripetal acceleration always points toward the center of the circle and is perpendicular to the velocity, with magnitude a = v^2/r. Because any acceleration requires a net force, a net inward centripetal force of magnitude mv^2/r must act on the object. This centripetal force is not a new kind of force but is supplied by real forces such as tension, gravity, friction, or the normal force. For a rigid rotator the speed grows with radius (v = r*omega), so points farther from the axis have larger centripetal acceleration.

problems.prompt: Which best explains why one can drive a car faster without skidding around a banked curved road than around a level curved road?
choices: The greater vertical component of normal force on the banked curve increases the maximum frictional force, which increases the maximum centripetal force.
The additional horizontal component of normal force on the banked curve combines with friction to increase the maximum centripetal force.
The additional horizontal component of gravity on the banked curve combines with friction to increase the maximum centripetal force.
The reduction of the gravitational force on the banked curve means less centripetal force is required than on a level road.

problems.prompt: In a centrifuge at maximum rotational speed (gravity negligible), the particulate matter at the bottom of a test tube is twice as far from the rotational axis as the fluid at the top. Because the whole tube rotates at the same angular speed, what is the relationship between the accelerations of the liquid (a_liquid) and the particles (a_particles)? (Choose the expression.)
choices: The relationship is impossible to determine without knowing the densities.

concepts.title: Center of Mass, Torque, and Equilibrium
concepts.content: The center of mass is the mass-weighted average position of an object, the point that moves as though all of the object's mass and the net external force were concentrated there; for a set of point masses along a line it is the sum of each mass times its position divided by the total mass. Torque is the rotational effect of a force, equal to r*F*sin(theta), or equivalently the force times its lever arm, the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force's line of action, and a force acting through the pivot produces no torque. An object is in equilibrium when both the net force and the net torque on it are zero, so it has neither linear nor rotational acceleration; when the velocity is also zero it is in static equilibrium.

problems.prompt: A block M rests on an incline of angle theta and is connected by a light cord running over a frictionless pulley at the top of the incline to a mass m hanging vertically. The system is in static equilibrium. What is the force of static friction between block M and the incline if M = 16 kg, m = 10 kg, theta = 30 degrees, and mu_s = 0.4? (Use g = 10 m/s^2.)

The biceps tendon attaches about 3 cm from the elbow joint; a heavy dumbbell is lifted at the midpoint of the hand about 30 cm from the elbow. With the elbow bent at 90 degrees and the forearm's weight neglected, what is the relation of the force exerted by the biceps to the dumbbell's weight? (Choose the expression.)

Amanda (650 N) and Billy (300 N) want to balance on a 3 m long, 10 kg plank placed over a fulcrum, each sitting at an opposite end. How far from Amanda's seat should the fulcrum be placed to make the game as fair as possible?

concepts.title: Work
concepts.content: Work is done when a force acts on an object as it moves, and for a constant force it equals the component of the force along the displacement times the distance moved (W = Fd cos theta). Work is a scalar, measured in joules, and can be positive, negative, or zero: positive when the force has a component along the motion, negative when it opposes the motion, and zero when the force is perpendicular to the displacement. Work is the process by which energy is transferred to or from an object. When the force varies with position, the work equals the area under a force-versus-position graph.

problems.prompt: Boxes of the same mass are lifted to a height of 3 m either up a frictionless ramp (force F_A) or straight up with a pulley (force F_B). Which method requires more work?
choices: Equal work is required for both methods.
Greater work is required to lift m with the pulley.
No work is required for either method.
Greater work is required to push m up the ramp.

problems.prompt: At the top of a hill is a well whose water level is 15 m below the top. Using a rope of negligible mass, a person lowers an empty two-liter pail down the well and then draws the pail back up full of water (density 1 kg/L). How much total work does the person do in first lowering the empty pail and then lifting the full pail out of the well? (Use g = 10 m/s^2.)
choices: It is impossible to tell without knowing the mass of the empty pail.

concepts.title: Power
concepts.content: Power measures how fast work is done, defined as the work done divided by the time taken, and is measured in watts (1 W = 1 J/s). Because speed is displacement over time, the power delivered by a constant force can also be written as P = Fv, the product of the force and the object's speed. Doing the same amount of work in less time requires more power. This relationship lets you connect a person's or engine's rate of energy use to the forces and speeds involved.

problems.prompt: A physically fit person has a mechanical efficiency of 25%, meaning 25% of the chemical energy converted in the body is output as useful work and the rest is wasted as heat. She has a mass of 50 kg and climbs stairs at a constant speed, moving upward at 25 cm/s. At what rate is she consuming energy? (Use g = 10 m/s^2.)

Jack (weight 2000 N) runs up a hill inclined at about 30 degrees along a 450 m path to the top, taking 30 minutes in total. What was Jack's net power output during his entire journey up the hill? (Use g = 10 m/s^2.)

concepts.title: Kinetic Energy
concepts.content: Kinetic energy is the energy an object has because of its motion, given by KE = (1/2)mv^2, so it increases with mass and with the square of the speed and is never negative. The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy (W_net = change in KE). Because of the speed-squared dependence, doubling an object's speed quadruples its kinetic energy.

problems.prompt: Which expression represents the kinetic energy of an object after it slides a distance d down a plane inclined at angle phi to the horizontal, with a constant frictional force F, starting from rest? (Choose the expression.)
A 1000 kg car traveling at 20 m/s applies its brakes and comes to a stop over a distance of 20 m. Assuming a constant kinetic frictional force, what is its magnitude?

Jack (weight 2000 N, mass about 200 kg) is jogging down a hill inclined at 30 degrees when he falls while moving at 10 m/s and slides 10 m down the slope before coming to a stop. How much work was done by kinetic friction in stopping him? (Use g = 10 m/s^2.)

concepts.title: Potential Energy
concepts.content: Potential energy is stored energy an object has by virtue of its position or configuration. Gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface is PE = mgh, so it changes with height, and only changes in potential energy are physically meaningful because the zero level is chosen arbitrarily. Gravity is a conservative force, meaning the work it does depends only on the change in height and not on the path taken, so gravitational potential energy converts freely to and from kinetic energy.

problems.prompt: At the top of a hill is a well whose water level is 15 m below the top. A person drops a penny from the top and hears a splash. Ignoring air resistance and the travel time of sound, how much time passes between releasing the penny and the splash? (Use g = 10 m/s^2.)

Jack throws a non-uniform block of mass m from the peak of the hill as hard as he can. Neglecting air resistance, which statement(s) is/are true? I. The block's center of mass follows a parabolic trajectory until it strikes the ground. II. Assuming it rotates, it rotates about its geometric center. III. The total displacement from the time it is thrown to when it lands depends on the block's mass.

concepts.title: Total Mechanical Energy
concepts.content: An object's total mechanical energy is the sum of its kinetic and potential energy, E = KE + PE. When only conservative forces such as gravity do work, total mechanical energy is conserved, so any decrease in potential energy appears as an equal increase in kinetic energy and vice versa. When a nonconservative force such as friction acts, mechanical energy is not conserved, and the work done by that force equals the change in total mechanical energy.

problems.prompt: A basketball player jumps straight up for a slam dunk. Neglecting air resistance, which statement(s) correctly describe the motion on the way up? I. Total mechanical energy is conserved. II. The player's weight increases as he rises. III. The work being done by gravity is negative.

Two friends start at the top of the same platform and slide down two frictionless slides to the same pool, one nearly vertical and one longer with a gentler slope. Which best describes their trips from start to finish?
choices: Both reach the pool in the same time and at the same final speed.
The friend on the vertical slide reaches the pool in the same time but at a greater final speed.
The friend on the vertical slide reaches the pool in less time but at the same final speed.
The friend on the vertical slide reaches the pool in less time and at a greater final speed.

problems.prompt: An object is launched from the top of a 40 m high building with a speed of 10 m/s at 30 degrees above the horizontal. Neglecting air resistance, with what speed does it hit the ground? (Use g = 10 m/s^2.)

Brother Alexey jumps from a height of 20 m onto a seesaw and launches Brother Boris 10 m into the air; both weigh 1000 N. Which could contribute to why Boris is not launched to a height of 20 m? I. Alexey lands on the seesaw vertically, but Boris launches off at a 45-degree angle. II. Alexey starts with 20 kJ of PE while Boris starts with 0 kJ. III. Not all kinetic energy is transferred from Alexey to Boris through the seesaw.
In which of the following real-world cases is total mechanical energy most nearly conserved?
choices: A sled sliding down an icy bobsled track
A pitched baseball being hit by a bat
A car with the driver slamming on its brakes to avoid a collision

concepts.title: Simple Machines and Mechanical Advantage
concepts.content: Simple machines such as inclined planes, pulleys, levers, screws, and wheel-and-axle systems let a task be done with a smaller applied force. In the ideal frictionless case the total work done with the machine equals the work needed without it, so the reduced effort force is paid for by moving through a correspondingly greater distance. Mechanical advantage quantifies this trade-off as the ratio of the resistance (output) force to the effort (input) force, the factor by which the machine multiplies the input force. For a frictionless ramp of incline angle theta, the needed force drops to mg sin(theta), giving a mechanical advantage of 1/sin(theta).

problems.prompt: An object of mass m is pushed up a frictionless incline of angle theta and height H by either of two forces: force F1 applied parallel to the incline (directed up the slope) or force F2 applied horizontally. What is true about the minimum work required by each force and their mechanical advantages?
Ignoring friction, how does the mechanical advantage of a hill (treated as an inclined plane at 30 degrees) compare to that of a double pulley system in which two rope segments support the load?
choices: The mechanical advantage of the hill is half that of the double pulley system.
The mechanical advantage of the hill is double that of the double pulley system.
It is impossible to answer without knowing how far up the hill a person walked or how high a mass was lifted.

concepts.title: Systems, Thermal Physics, and Thermodynamics
concepts.content: A thermodynamic system is the object or objects under study together with the ways they interact, while everything outside it is the environment; a system is open if it exchanges both matter and energy, closed if it exchanges only energy, and isolated if it exchanges neither. Thermal (internal) energy is the total random molecular motion within a system, temperature is the macroscopic measure of that energy per particle, and heat is thermal energy transferred between a system and its environment because of a temperature difference. Temperature is an intensive property that does not depend on the amount of material, whereas thermal energy is extensive. Related effects include thermal expansion, in which most materials expand when heated, and the latent heat absorbed or released during phase changes.

problems.prompt: Jointed (non-welded) steel railroad track with a coefficient of linear expansion of 1.0e-5 per degree C is laid in 25 m sections at 4 degrees C, leaving a 10 mm expansion joint between sections. What must the track temperature be when the expansion joint just closes?

On a pleasant, relaxing day a person notices no perspiration, yet the body still loses roughly 0.6 kg of moisture from the skin over the course of a day. About how much heat does the person release through this evaporation? (The latent heat of vaporization of sweat is L = 2.43e6 J/kg.)

A person sitting at room temperature (25 degrees C) with half of their body covered by clothing has a basal metabolism generating 85 W of heat. Approximately what percentage of that 85 W is lost through radiation? (Radiation coefficient about 5.6 W/(m^2 K), total body area about 2 m^2 with half exposed, skin about 34 degrees C.)

concepts.title: The Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
concepts.content: The zeroth law states that if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, then they are in thermal equilibrium with one another. Thermal equilibrium means heat is free to pass between the bodies but no net heat flows, which happens precisely when they are at the same temperature, so the law establishes temperature as a consistent, measurable state variable. Bodies reach thermal equilibrium through heat transfer, which occurs by conduction (molecular collisions), convection (bulk motion of a fluid), and radiation (electromagnetic waves).

problems.prompt: On a hot, sunny, windless day you lie on a towel on the sandy beach and feel much warmer after a few minutes. What best explains this?
choices: The hot sand transferred heat into you by conduction and the Sun's rays transferred heat into you by radiation.
The hot sand transferred heat into you by conduction and the hot air transferred heat into you by convection.
The hot sand transferred heat into you by convection and the Sun's rays transferred heat into you by radiation.
All of your accumulated heat came from conduction by the surrounding air.

problems.prompt: A passage on thermoregulation notes that the body loses heat through radiation, convection, conduction, and evaporation. What best explains why people tend to cover most of their bodies with clothing in the winter?
choices: To increase the heat created by the body
To increase heat loss through conduction
To reduce heat loss through conduction
To reduce heat loss through radiation and convection

problems.prompt: Why are people who accidentally fall into cold water instructed to remain as still as possible while awaiting assistance?
choices: Remaining still reduces the heat generated in the body through metabolism.
Remaining still reduces the rate of heat loss via conduction.
Remaining still reduces the rate of heat loss via convection.
Remaining still reduces the rate of heat loss via radiation.

concepts.title: The First Law of Thermodynamics
concepts.content: The first law is a statement of energy conservation: the internal energy of a system changes only through the heat added to it and the work it exchanges with the surroundings, written delta-E = Q - W in the physics sign convention (Q positive when heat flows in, W positive when the system does work on its surroundings). Energy may be transformed from one form to another, but the total energy of the universe is constant. For an ideal gas the internal energy depends only on temperature, and the work done by an expanding gas is W = P(delta-V), so in a constant-volume (isochoric) process no work is done and delta-E = Q.

problems.prompt: A mole of ideal gas undergoes an isochoric (constant-volume) process. Which of the following quantities remains constant?
choices: the change in internal energy, delta-E

problems.prompt: An astronaut connects a full, well-insulated oxygen tank (at maximum pressure) to an identical, evacuated tank and opens the valve. What are the work W done by the oxygen in filling the second tank and the change in internal energy delta-E after it occupies both tanks?

A perfectly insulated, frictionless piston of gas starts at 2 kPa and 0.1 m^3 and runs a reversible cycle along path 1-2-3-4 back to its starting point, as shown on the P-V diagram. What is the net work done by the gas over the cycle?

concepts.title: The Second Law of Thermodynamics
concepts.content: Entropy is a measure of a system's disorder, and the second law states that the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases during any real process; a local decrease in entropy is possible only if the surroundings' entropy increases by at least as much. Because friction and other losses make real macroscopic processes irreversible, entropy tends to increase, which sets a direction for spontaneous change. As a result, heat flows spontaneously from a hotter body to a colder one but not the reverse without an input of work, and no cyclic engine can convert absorbed heat entirely into work.

problems.prompt: To cool your coffee, you drop an ice cube into a thermos (which prevents heat transfer in or out), seal it, and wait for the cube to melt. Which best describes the situation during the waiting period?
choices: The total energy of the system (coffee + ice) decreased and the entropy remained constant.
The total energy of the system and the entropy both remained constant.
The total energy of the system decreased and the entropy increased.
The total energy of the system remained constant and the entropy increased.

problems.prompt: According to the thermoregulation passage, if the ambient temperature rises above skin temperature, what best describes what happens to a person?
choices: Since heat cannot transfer from lower to higher temperature, body temperature rises, culminating in heat stroke.
The core temperature initially rises, so the body radiates more heat to the environment, cooling the core back within range.
Perspiration increases, as evaporation becomes the only heat-loss mechanism available to keep the core within range.
The body reduces the heat it generates through metabolism to keep the core within range.

concepts.title: Hydrostatics: Fluids at Rest
concepts.content: Fluids are substances that can flow, including both liquids and gases; a liquid keeps a fixed volume while a gas expands to fill its container. The density of a fluid is its mass per unit volume, with liquid water taken as 1000 kg/m^3, and specific gravity is the unitless ratio of a substance's density to that of water. Pressure is the perpendicular force per unit area a fluid exerts and is a scalar measured in pascals (N/m^2). In a static fluid the gauge pressure increases with depth as P = rho g D, and Pascal's principle states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout it, which is the basis of the hydraulic lift.

problems.prompt: A pipe sealed at the top and open at the bottom is partially filled with a liquid of specific gravity 2.0 and stands vertically immersed in a reservoir of the same liquid; the space above the liquid column inside the sealed pipe is vacuum (negligible vapor pressure). When atmospheric pressure is 100,000 Pa, what is the height h of the liquid column in the pipe above the surface of the reservoir? (Use g = 10 m/s^2.)

concepts.title: Buoyancy and Archimedes' Principle
concepts.content: Archimedes' principle states that a submerged or floating object experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces, F_buoy = rho_fluid V_submerged g. An object floats at partial submersion when its density is less than the fluid's and sinks when it is greater; for a floating object, the fraction of its volume submerged equals the ratio of its density to the fluid's density. Because buoyancy pushes up, a submerged object's apparent (measured) weight equals its true weight minus the buoyant force, even though its actual weight is unchanged. Gases exert buoyant forces too, which is why balloons filled with a low-density gas rise.

problems.prompt: A person in physical therapy stands on a scale while submerged up to their waist in water. What physical quantity will the scale read?
choices: The normal force of the scale on the person
The normal force of the scale on the person minus the buoyant force acting on the person

problems.prompt: In hydrostatic weighing, a person is weighed on dry land (w_air) and again while fully submerged in water after a deep exhalation (w_water); neglect any residual air buoyancy. Which expression gives the person's body density, where rho_water is the density of water? (Choose the expression.)

At a depth d below the surface of pure water, a balloon experiences a buoyant force Fb. If the balloon is submerged to a depth of 4d, what is the magnitude of the buoyant force it experiences? (Assume no atmospheric pressure, constant water density, and that the balloon's volume is inversely proportional to the pressure exerted on it.)

A tank contains a layer of fluid with specific gravity 0.6 floating on a layer of water. An object of uniform density is dropped in and reaches equilibrium with one-quarter of its volume submerged in the upper fluid and three-quarters submerged in the water. What is the specific gravity of the object?

concepts.title: Hydrodynamics: Fluids in Motion
concepts.content: Flow rate f is the volume of fluid passing a point per unit time and equals the pipe's cross-sectional area times the flow speed (f = Av), which is distinct from the flow speed itself. For an incompressible fluid the continuity equation A1 v1 = A2 v2 holds, so the fluid speeds up where a pipe narrows and slows where it widens. Bernoulli's equation expresses energy conservation along a streamline, so at constant height a faster-moving region of fluid has a lower pressure. For real, viscous fluids in laminar flow, Poiseuille's law relates the pressure drop to viscosity, tube length, flow rate, and the fourth power of the radius, so small changes in radius have a large effect on flow resistance.

problems.prompt: Your little brother pinches the tube of a hose to spray you with water more effectively. What effect does this have on the water as it moves past the constriction?
choices: Its flow speed increases and its pressure increases.
Its flow speed increases and its pressure decreases.
Its flow speed decreases and its pressure increases.
Its flow speed decreases and its pressure decreases.

problems.prompt: The aorta has a cross-sectional area of 5 cm^2, and the pulmonary capillary bed has a total cross-sectional area of 4000 cm^2. If the speed of blood flow through the aorta is 33 cm/s and the total flow rate through the aorta equals that through the lungs, approximately what is the flow speed in the pulmonary capillary bed?

Poiseuille's Law gives the pressure drop per unit length for a fluid of viscosity eta flowing at flow rate f through a pipe of radius R: (delta-P)/L = 8*eta*f/(pi*R^4). Which of the following would increase the pressure drop per length as blood moves through an artery? I. Using pentoxifylline to decrease the blood viscosity. II. Inserting a stent to widen the artery. III. Increasing the blood flow rate with a saline solution.

A spirometer records a patient's lung volume per body mass (mL/kg) on the vertical axis versus time on the horizontal axis. After adjusting for a patient of known mass, what does the slope of the spirometer trace indicate?
choices: Total volume of air inhaled or exhaled
Flow speed of air through the spirometer
Volume flow rate of air through the spirometer
Acceleration of air through the spirometer

problems.prompt: A patient undergoing forced exhalation after a maximum inhalation shows an average flow rate of 800 mL/s for five seconds on a Fleisch pneumotachograph. What is the value of this patient's forced vital capacity (FVC, the total volume forcibly exhaled)?

A population-averaged spirometer trace shows lung volume per body mass varying between about 37 mL/kg and 30 mL/kg during normal (tidal) breathing. What is the tidal volume (TV) of a typical patient with a body mass of 50 kg?

In a Venturi-tube spirometer, Bernoulli's equation for continuous flow at constant height gives P1 + (1/2)*rho*v1^2 = P2 + (1/2)*rho*v2^2. A patient blows into a tube of area 20 cm^2 at a flow speed of 40 cm/s, and the tube then narrows to 4 cm^2. Taking the air density as 1.2 kg/m^3, the pressure difference between the wide and narrow regions of the tube is most nearly:

On a spirometer trace, a typical patient's maximum inhaled lung volume is 80 mL/kg, the volume after normal exhalation is 30 mL/kg, and the residual volume after maximal exhalation is 15 mL/kg. If in the first second of a forced exhalation the patient can exhale from the maximum down to the normal post-exhalation level, the typical FEV1/FVC ratio is roughly:

In a Fleisch pneumotachograph, flow rate equals the pressure differential divided by the flow resistance, and Poiseuille's resistance for laminar flow in a tube is R = 8*eta*L/(pi*r^4), where eta is the gas viscosity, L the tube length, and r the tube radius. Which expression gives the pressure differential across a tube of length L carrying a flow rate f? (Choose the expression.)

concepts.title: The Elasticity of Solids
concepts.content: When forces are applied to a solid they can stretch it (tension), squeeze it (compression), or bend it (shear). Stress is the applied force divided by the cross-sectional area, measured in pascals like pressure but without requiring the force to be perpendicular, and strain is the resulting fractional change in dimension (the change in length divided by the original length). By Hooke's law, as long as the material is not deformed past its elastic limit, stress is proportional to strain, with the proportionality constant being Young's modulus for tension or compression and the shear modulus for shear. A stiffer material has a larger modulus, and because stress is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area, thicker members deform less under the same load.

problems.prompt: A 10 m rope with Young's modulus E = 10^8 N/m^2 and cross-sectional area 5 cm^2 is run over a massless, frictionless pulley and attached at each end to a resting 100 kg mass. The pulley is steadily lifted until both masses just leave the ground. By how much will the rope stretch? (Use g = 10 m/s^2.)

A 20 m steel girder with a cross-sectional area of 0.1 m^2 is installed at 25 degrees C flush between rigid pylons. Steel has a thermal expansion coefficient alpha = 1.1 x 10^-5 per degree C and Young's modulus E = 2.0 x 10^11 N/m^2. If the temperature rises to 30 degrees C, how much force does the girder exert on an adjacent pylon (neglect expansion of the area)?

concepts.title: Electric Charge
concepts.content: Ordinary matter is built from atoms whose nuclei hold positively charged protons and neutral neutrons, surrounded by negatively charged electrons. Electric charge comes in two signs, and a proton and electron carry equal and opposite amounts of the elementary charge e, so charge is quantized in whole multiples of e. Like charges repel while opposite charges attract, and total charge is always conserved. Objects become charged by transferring electrons, and charge moves freely through conductors but not through insulators.

concepts.title: Electric Force and Coulomb's Law
concepts.content: Coulomb's law gives the electrostatic force between two point charges: its magnitude is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, F = k q1 q2 / r^2, directed along the line joining them. Coulomb's constant k is about 9 x 10^9 N m^2/C^2 in vacuum or air. The force is repulsive between like charges and attractive between opposite charges, and like gravitation it is an inverse-square law. When several charges are present, the net force on any one is the vector sum of the separate Coulomb forces.

problems.prompt: A muon is a particle with the same charge as an electron but a greater mass. An electron orbits a stationary proton in a circular path of radius r with kinetic energy K1, and a muon orbits a stationary proton at the same radius r with kinetic energy K2. Which of the following is true?
choices: The relationship between K1 and K2 cannot be determined without knowing the mass of the muon.

concepts.title: Electric Fields
concepts.content: An electric field is the alteration of space produced by a charge, such that any other charge placed in it feels a force; the field at a point is the force per unit positive test charge, E = F/q, in units of N/C. A point charge produces a field of magnitude kQ/r^2 that points away from a positive charge and toward a negative one, and field lines run from positive to negative charges. The force on a charge placed in a field is F = qE, along the field for positive charges and opposite the field for negative charges. Between the plates of a parallel-plate capacitor the field is uniform and equal to the voltage divided by the plate separation.

problems.prompt: Two isolated charges, one +2 nC and the other -3 nC, are separated by a distance of 2 m. Which of the following could be the magnitude of the electric field at a point that is an equal distance from the two charges? (k = 8.99 x 10^9 N m^2/C^2.) I. 30 N/C  II. 45 N/C  III. 60 N/C

An electron travels between two uniformly charged parallel capacitor plates separated by 3 cm, aligned so that the top plate is positively charged. If the voltage difference between the plates is 12 V, the electric force experienced by the electron will be:

concepts.title: Electric Potential and Potential Energy
concepts.content: Electric potential energy is the energy stored in a configuration of charges; moving a charge through an electric field changes this energy just as lifting a mass changes its gravitational potential energy. Electric potential, or voltage, is the potential energy per unit charge, V = PE/q, measured in volts, and only differences in potential are physically meaningful. The work done by the field on a charge equals the negative of its change in potential energy, W = -q(delta-V). Points at the same potential form equipotential surfaces, and no work is done moving a charge along one.

problems.prompt: Two negative charges are separated by a fixed distance of 4 cm, and the electric force between them is 1.6 x 10^-9 N. If the distance between the two particles is halved, what is the resulting electrical potential energy of the system?

concepts.title: Electric Circuits
concepts.content: An electric circuit drives charge around a closed loop; current is the rate of charge flow (in amperes), driven by the voltage of a source such as a battery. Ohm's law relates the voltage across a resistor to the current through it, V = IR. Resistors in series carry the same current and add directly, while resistors in parallel share the same voltage and combine reciprocally, so the equivalent parallel resistance is smaller than any single resistor. Power dissipated by a resistor is P = IV = I^2 R = V^2/R, and Kirchhoff's rules (charge conservation at junctions and energy conservation around loops) allow analysis of more complex networks.

problems.prompt: Four resistors with equal resistance are arranged in parallel and connected to a battery that provides a constant voltage. How do the total power dissipated over the resistors and the total current change if the resistance of each resistor is halved?
choices: Power is doubled and current is halved.
Power is doubled and current is doubled.
Power is halved and current is halved.
Power is halved and current is doubled.

problems.prompt: In the circuit shown, each resistor has the same resistance R. Switch S1 has been closed and switch S2 open for a long time, so the circuit is in steady state with the battery supplying constant power P1 and no current flowing into the capacitor. At a later time S2 is also closed (S1 stays closed). Compared to P1, what is P2, the battery's power output when the circuit reaches a new steady state?

In the circuit shown, a 15 V source is in series with a 3 ohm resistor in the outer loop, and a 12 V source is connected in parallel with a 6 ohm resistor. If the 15 V source were replaced with an 18 V source, which of the following is NOT true?
choices: The current through the (now 18 V) source would increase.
The current through the 3 ohm resistor would increase.
The current through the 12 V source would decrease.
The current through the 6 ohm resistor would increase.

concepts.title: Capacitors
concepts.content: A capacitor is a pair of conductors, often parallel plates, that store equal and opposite charge Q when connected to a voltage, with the charge proportional to the voltage, Q = CV, where C is the capacitance in farads. For a parallel-plate capacitor the capacitance increases with plate area and with the dielectric constant of the material between the plates, and decreases with plate separation. A charged capacitor stores energy equal to (1/2)QV = (1/2)CV^2. In circuits, capacitors in parallel add while capacitors in series combine reciprocally, and once fully charged in a steady-state DC circuit a capacitor passes no current.

problems.prompt: The inner and outer surfaces of a cell membrane act as the plates of a parallel-plate capacitor. Consider a 1 micrometer^2 section of an axon: the membrane's dielectric constant is 8 and it is 6 nm thick. If the voltage across the membrane is 70 mV, what is the approximate magnitude of charge that resides on each side of this 1 micrometer^2 section? (epsilon_0 = 8.85 x 10^-12 F/m.)

Capacitor C1 has a capacitance of 5 F and holds an initial charge of 40 C, and capacitor C2 has a capacitance of 15 F and holds an initial charge of 60 C. They are connected in parallel (like plates together) through an initially open switch S. A long time after the switch closes and the charges redistribute, what are the charges Q1,f and Q2,f on the two capacitors?
A 10-volt battery charges a capacitor, storing 20 microjoules of energy on it. What voltage battery would be required to double the energy stored on the same capacitor?

concepts.title: Alternating Current
concepts.content: In direct current the charge flows in one direction only, but in alternating current (AC) the voltage and current oscillate, periodically reversing direction as in household power. Because the instantaneous values continually change, AC quantities are described by their root-mean-square (rms) values, the effective averages that keep the power formulas identical to those for DC. Thus the average power dissipated by a resistor is P = I_rms^2 R and the average power delivered by the source is P = I_rms V_rms. For a sinusoidal source, the rms value equals the peak value divided by the square root of two.

concepts.title: Magnetic Fields and Forces
concepts.content: Magnetic fields are created by moving charges and electric currents, and they in turn exert forces on other moving charges. A charge q moving with speed v perpendicular to a magnetic field B feels a force of magnitude qvB directed perpendicular to both v and B, so a charged particle crossing a uniform field follows a circular arc of radius r = mv/(qB). Positive and negative charges curve in opposite directions, and the direction of the force is found with the right-hand rule (reversed for negative charges). Because the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, it does no work and changes only the direction of motion, not the speed.

problems.prompt: In a cloud chamber with a magnetic field pointing into the page, charged particles curve in circular paths of radius r = mv/(qB), and positive and negative charges curve in opposite directions; a lead plate slows particles so their radius of curvature decreases after they cross it. Positrons are lightweight like electrons (leaving long, thin tracks) but carry positive charge. In the figure, which of the tracks was most likely left by a positron?

In a cloud chamber, heavier particles interact more strongly with the vapor and come to a stop more quickly (leaving shorter tracks), and a particle's circular radius in the magnetic field is r = mv/(qB). If an electron and a proton have the same kinetic energy, the proton will:
choices: curve in a smaller circle and have a longer track length.
curve in a larger circle and have a shorter track length.
curve in a smaller circle and have a shorter track length.
curve in a larger circle and have a longer track length.

problems.prompt: The cloud chamber photograph (magnetic field into the page) shows tracks 1-4 left by charged particles. Suppose the magnetic field is turned off and replaced with an electric field pointing from left to right. Which track's particle would curve in the opposite direction from the way it curved in the magnetic field?

In a cloud chamber, a magnetic field points into the page. Suppose an electric field of strength E pointing from left to right is added in addition to the magnetic field of strength B. If a negatively charged particle is observed to move in a straight line, it would:
choices: be moving upward with speed E/B.
be moving upward with speed B/E.
be moving downward with speed E/B.
be moving downward with speed B/E.

problems.prompt: In a cloud chamber, a charged particle loses kinetic energy as it ionizes the vapor; particles with more charge interact more strongly, and a particle loses more energy the farther it travels. If q is the particle's charge, d is the distance traveled, and m is its mass, which formula most accurately describes the kinetic energy loss as the particle passes through the vapor?
choices: delta-KE proportional to q^2 * d / m
delta-KE proportional to m * d / q^2

problems.prompt: In a cloud chamber, a charged particle's radius of curvature is r = mv/(qB), and heavier, more highly charged particles leave thicker and shorter tracks. Compared to a proton with the same momentum, an alpha particle (2 protons and 2 neutrons) will leave: I. a track with a larger radius of curvature. II. a wider track. III. a shorter track.

concepts.title: Oscillations
concepts.content: Any motion that regularly repeats is periodic (harmonic) motion, described by its period, the time for one full cycle, and its frequency, the number of cycles per second; the two are reciprocals. Simple harmonic motion arises from a restoring force proportional to displacement, as in a mass on a spring obeying Hooke's law, F = -kx. The period of a mass on a spring is T = 2*pi*sqrt(m/k) and that of a simple pendulum is T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g), and both are independent of amplitude. For a mass on a vertical spring, gravity (and any buoyant force) shifts the equilibrium position but does not change the oscillation frequency.

problems.prompt: A cube of side length 10 cm and mass 2 kg hangs from a vertical spring, stretching it 12 cm beyond its rest length; pulled down and released, it oscillates vertically. The entire system is then immersed in water and the experiment is repeated (drag negligible). Which is true of the immersed system's equilibrium position and frequency? (Use g = 10 m/s^2, water density 1000 kg/m^3.)
choices: The equilibrium position is 6 cm beyond the spring's rest length, but the frequency is the same.
The equilibrium position is 6 cm beyond the spring's rest length, and the frequency has increased.
The equilibrium position is 6 cm less than the spring's rest length, but the frequency is the same.
The equilibrium position is 6 cm less than the spring's rest length, and the frequency has increased.

problems.prompt: The period of an oscillating mass on a spring is T = 2*pi*sqrt(m/k). A 1 kg mass attached to a spring with k = 64 N/m oscillates on a horizontal frictionless surface with an amplitude of 10 cm. As it passes through equilibrium, a hammer blow in its direction of motion increases its oscillation amplitude to 20 cm. What is the approximate frequency of the oscillations after the hammer blow?

concepts.title: Waves
concepts.content: A mechanical wave is a series of disturbances that travels through a medium, transporting energy without transporting the medium itself. In a transverse wave the medium oscillates perpendicular to the direction of travel, while in a longitudinal wave it oscillates along the direction of travel. A wave's speed, frequency, and wavelength are related by v = f*lambda, and the speed is set by the medium: for a wave on a string, v = sqrt(F_T/mu), so more tension speeds the wave up and more linear mass density slows it down. When a wave passes into a new medium its frequency stays the same while its speed and wavelength change, and its amplitude reflects the energy carried rather than its frequency or speed.

problems.prompt: A sound wave traveling initially through air passes into water. Which of the following quantities must be the same for the wave in air and the wave in water? I. The intensity  II. The frequency  III. The direction of motion

A mass hangs vertically from a heavy rope of uniform linear mass density, and a wave is generated at the top of the rope. As the wave travels downward toward the mass, which of the following is true? (The wave speed on a rope is v = sqrt(F_T/mu), where F_T is tension and mu is linear mass density.)
choices: The frequency and speed are constant.
The frequency is constant, but the speed decreases.
The frequency is constant, but the speed increases.
Both the frequency and the speed decrease.

concepts.title: Sound Waves
concepts.content: Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave made of alternating compressions and rarefactions of a medium, so it needs a material to travel through and cannot propagate in a vacuum. Because it is longitudinal rather than transverse, sound cannot be polarized. Sound generally travels faster in liquids and solids than in gases, and when it crosses into a new medium its frequency stays constant while its speed and wavelength adjust. The MHz-frequency sound used in medical ultrasound obeys the same v = f*lambda relation, so higher frequencies give shorter wavelengths and finer spatial precision.

problems.prompt: High-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) uses waves of 250 kHz to 2 MHz, and its wavelength sets a physical limit on the precision of treatment. Taking the speed of sound in tissue to be 1500 m/s, what is the minimum tissue size that can be targeted by these frequencies? (Assume the limit applies equally in all three dimensions, i.e., a cube of side x.)
Which of the following would NOT be a plausible reason why physical therapy patients receiving ultrasonic therapy for a muscle sprain experience short-term relief?
choices: The heating of tissue increases blood flow to the area, speeding healing.
The vibration of deep muscle tissue has an effect similar to a physical massage.
The placebo effect of having one's symptoms taken seriously and treated increases the patient's expectation of feeling better.
Polarized ultrasound waves realign scar tissue to its pre-injury condition.

problems.prompt: Cavitation is the formation and rapid collapse of gas bubbles in a fluid caused by large, rapid pressure changes, and the collapse generates tissue-disrupting shock waves. Which condition would most likely produce shock waves due to cavitation?
choices: A high intensity, high frequency ultrasound wave creates microbubbles in its rarefaction (low-pressure) region and then collapses them in its compression region.
A low intensity, high frequency ultrasound wave creates microbubbles in its rarefaction region and then collapses them in its compression region.
A high intensity, low frequency ultrasound wave creates microbubbles in its compression region and then collapses them in its rarefaction region.
A reflected ultrasound wave creates a standing wave whose pressure nodes create microbubbles that build up over time.

concepts.title: Interference of Waves and Beats
concepts.content: When two or more waves overlap, their displacements add by superposition, giving constructive interference where they reinforce (amplitudes add) and destructive interference where they cancel. The largest possible combined amplitude equals the sum of the individual amplitudes. When two waves of slightly different frequencies interfere, the loudness rises and falls periodically, producing beats heard at the beat frequency f_beat = |f1 - f2|. Because two waves of the same type in the same medium travel at the same speed, a difference in their wavelengths implies a difference in their frequencies.

problems.prompt: Two transverse waves travel toward one another along the same string. Wave 1 has amplitude 2 cm, wavelength 5 mm, and period 10 ms; Wave 2 has amplitude 3 cm, wavelength 4 mm, and period 8 ms. Observing the oscillation of a single point on the string as the two waves pass through it, which of the following is a possible observation?
choices: The point oscillates with a maximum displacement of 5 cm and a period of 40 ms.
The point oscillates with a maximum displacement of 5 cm and a period of 10 ms.
The point oscillates with a maximum displacement of 1 cm and a period of 40 ms.
The point oscillates with a maximum displacement of 1 cm and a period of 10 ms.

concepts.title: Standing Waves on Strings, Sound Waves in Pipes
concepts.content: A standing wave forms when a wave reflects and interferes with itself in a confined medium, creating fixed nodes with no motion and antinodes with maximum motion at particular resonant frequencies. A string fixed at both ends, or a pipe open at both ends, supports standing waves whose length is a whole number of half-wavelengths, giving resonant frequencies f_n = n*v/(2L) for n = 1, 2, 3, and so on. A pipe closed at one end instead fits odd numbers of quarter-wavelengths, giving f_n = n*v/(4L) with n odd only. As a result, an open pipe and an otherwise identical closed pipe have different, non-overlapping sets of resonant frequencies.

problems.prompt: How does a hollow cylindrical pipe that is open on both ends compare to the exact same pipe with one end closed off?
choices: Increasing the length of both pipes will increase the fundamental harmonic frequency of both pipes.
Sound propagates more quickly through the pipe with both ends open than through the pipe with one end closed.
The pipe with both ends open will never have any of the same resonant frequencies as the closed pipe.
Over a large but finite range of frequencies, the open pipe has more resonant frequencies than the closed pipe.

concepts.title: Intensity and Intensity Level
concepts.content: The intensity of a wave is the power it carries per unit area (W/m^2), and for a source of constant power the intensity decreases with distance as the energy spreads over a larger area. Sound intensity level is a logarithmic measure in decibels, beta = 10*log(I/I0), so each factor-of-ten change in intensity changes the level by 10 dB. A hundredfold drop in intensity is therefore a 20 dB decrease, and a change by a factor less than ten alters the level by less than 10 dB. Intensity itself, being power over area, has dimensions of mass per time cubed, which is distinct from the dimensionless decibel scale.

problems.prompt: A sound traveling from one medium to another loses 40% of its intensity. By approximately how much does the sound level decrease?
If M represents mass, T represents time, and L represents length, which of the following represents the dimensions of sound intensity?

Ultrasound intensity attenuates with depth, and each centimeter of bone attenuates a 1 MHz ultrasound signal by about 5 dB. Through approximately how many centimeters of bone would a 1 MHz ultrasound signal have to pass for its intensity to decrease by a factor of 100?

For ultrasound, attenuation constants increase linearly and proportionally with frequency. The minimum attenuation constant for muscle is about 1.3 dB/cm at 1 MHz. What minimum attenuation through muscle tissue would one expect for a 3 MHz ultrasound signal?

concepts.title: The Doppler Effect
concepts.content: The Doppler effect is the change in the frequency detected by an observer when the source and observer move relative to each other. When source and observer approach one another, the detected frequency is higher than the emitted frequency; when they move apart, it is lower. The shifted frequency is f' = f*(v +/- v_observer)/(v -/+ v_source), with the signs chosen so approaching motion raises the frequency and receding motion lowers it. Importantly, steady relative motion produces a constant shifted pitch, not a continuously rising one, unless the source is accelerating.

problems.prompt: A train sounding its whistle approaches waiting passengers at a constant speed that is substantially slower than the speed of sound in air. Which of the following best describes what the passengers notice about the sound?
choices: The loudness and the pitch are both increasing.
The loudness is increasing and the pitch is constant.
The loudness is constant and the pitch is increasing.
The loudness and the pitch are both constant.

problems.prompt: A motorcyclist is traveling at 10 m/s when an ambulance approaches from behind at 40 m/s. If the siren frequency detected by the ambulance driver is 700 Hz, which of the following is closest to the frequency detected by the motorcyclist? (The speed of sound in air is about 340 m/s.)

concepts.title: Electromagnetic Waves
concepts.content: An electromagnetic wave is produced by an oscillating electric charge and consists of oscillating electric and magnetic fields, mutually perpendicular and perpendicular to the direction of travel, requiring no medium. All electromagnetic waves travel through vacuum at the same speed, c = 3 x 10^8 m/s, with c = f*lambda. The electromagnetic spectrum runs from low-frequency radio waves through visible light to high-frequency X-rays and gamma rays, with photon energy increasing with frequency. Like other waves, light shows a Doppler shift: an approaching source is shifted to higher frequency (blueshift) and a receding source to lower frequency (redshift).

problems.prompt: A spectroscope splits incoming light into a pattern of spectral lines at frequencies characteristic of the elements in the source. If a distant galaxy is moving toward an astronomer studying it with a spectroscope, which of the following statements is true?
choices: Observed spectral lines from the galaxy are shifted toward the blue end of the visible spectrum.
Observed spectral lines from the galaxy are shifted toward the red end of the visible spectrum.
The observed spectral lines are the same as if the galaxy were stationary relative to Earth.
The observed spectral lines are brighter than if the galaxy were stationary relative to Earth.

problems.prompt: A beam of protons is accelerated to a kinetic energy of 0.7 MeV. What is the approximate speed of these protons in air? (Proton mass m_p = 1.67 x 10^-27 kg; 1 MeV = 1.60 x 10^-13 J; treat 0.7 MeV as the kinetic energy and use KE = (1/2)m v^2.)

In radiation therapy, X-rays (photons) reach their maximum dose shortly after entering the body, after which the dose decreases exponentially but does not fall to zero before the beam exits. Which of the following graphs best represents how the dose of an X-ray beam changes with depth in a patient's body? (Choose the graph.)

concepts.title: Reflection and Refraction
