concepts.content: When light strikes the boundary between two transparent media, part of it reflects and part passes through. In reflection, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal. In refraction, the transmitted ray bends because light changes speed between media, following Snell's law n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2); light bends toward the normal when entering a denser (higher-index) medium and away from the normal when entering a less dense one. This bending is why a submerged object appears displaced from its true position when viewed from above the water.

problems.prompt: A person spearfishing from a boat looks down into the water a few feet from the side of the boat, so that their line of sight makes an angle greater than zero with the vertical. What is the best strategy for aiming the spear so as to hit a fish they see in the water?
choices: Aim closer to the boat than where the fish appears to be.
Aim farther from the boat than where the fish appears to be.
No single strategy is possible without knowing how deep the fish is under the water.

problems.prompt: Which of the following is true regarding the X-ray and proton beams used in radiation therapy?
choices: Both X-ray beams and proton beams can be deflected within an external magnetic field.
The speed of an X-ray beam in tissue can be controlled by the radiation source.
An X-ray beam will refract in tissue if its angle of incidence is greater than 0 degrees.
An X-ray beam will have a lower exit dose compared to a beam of protons.

concepts.title: Wave Effects
concepts.content: Because light is a wave, it exhibits diffraction (bending and spreading around obstacles or through openings) and interference (constructive and destructive overlap), which set fundamental limits on imaging resolution. Total internal reflection occurs when light in a denser medium strikes the boundary with a less dense medium beyond the critical angle and reflects entirely, the basis of fiber optics and endoscopes. Light can also be polarized, its transverse electric-field oscillations confined to a single plane, which only transverse waves can do. These wave phenomena underlie many optical technologies and measurement techniques.

problems.prompt: Which of the following is/are likely concern(s) in medical imaging using light? I. Blurring of X-ray images due to refraction and diffraction. II. Burning of tissue due to endoscopic light intensity. III. Doppler shift of light frequencies due to movement of the endoscope.

concepts.title: Mirrors
concepts.content: A mirror forms an image by reflecting light. A plane mirror produces an upright, virtual image the same size as the object, while curved mirrors focus light: concave (converging) mirrors have a positive focal length and can form real, inverted images, whereas convex (diverging) mirrors have a negative focal length and always form upright, reduced, virtual images. The mirror equation 1/f = 1/o + 1/i relates focal length, object distance, and image distance, with the focal length equal in magnitude to half the radius of curvature. Magnification is m = -i/o, where a negative value indicates an inverted image and a magnitude less than one indicates the image is reduced.

problems.prompt: What is the magnification of the image formed of an object 20 cm from a mirrored sphere (a reflective convex sphere) with a diameter of 20 cm?

concepts.title: Lenses
concepts.content: A lens forms an image by refracting light. Converging lenses are thicker in the middle, bend parallel rays toward a real focal point, and have positive focal length and power, while diverging lenses are thinner in the middle, spread parallel rays as if from a virtual focal point, and have negative focal length and power. The thin-lens equation 1/f = 1/o + 1/i and the magnification m = -i/o work just as they do for mirrors. Lens power is the reciprocal of the focal length in meters, measured in diopters (D); a converging lens with positive power corrects farsightedness by bringing images forward onto the retina.

problems.prompt: A hyperopic (farsighted) individual has images of some objects coming into focus behind the retina rather than on it. Which of the following accurately describes the appropriate corrective lens for such an individual?
choices: A converging lens is appropriate, due to its positive power.
A converging lens is appropriate, due to its negative power.
A diverging lens is appropriate, due to its positive power.
A diverging lens is appropriate, due to its negative power.

problems.prompt: The human eye is typically about 1.7 cm from cornea to retina. Which of the following best describes the optics of the typical eye when viewing a distant object?
choices: The lensing system of the eye has a power of about +60 D, and it forms a real image on the retina.
The lensing system of the eye has a power of +60 D, and it forms a virtual image on the retina.
The lensing system of the eye has a power of -60 D, and it forms a real image on the retina.
The lensing system of the eye has a power of -60 D, and it forms a virtual image on the retina.

concepts.title: Photons and Quantization
concepts.content: Light energy is quantized into discrete packets called photons, each carrying energy proportional to its frequency, E = hf = hc/lambda, where h is Planck's constant. Higher-frequency light such as X-rays and gamma rays therefore delivers more energy per photon than lower-frequency light. Matter also shows wave-particle duality: a particle has a de Broglie wavelength lambda = h/p, so a higher-momentum particle has a shorter wavelength, which is why electron microscopes achieve far higher resolution than optical ones. A photon emitted or absorbed carries exactly the energy difference between two quantized states.

problems.prompt: Which photon would be most likely to knock an inner-shell electron out of a tungsten atom?
choices: A gamma ray, because it has the most energy
A gamma ray, because it can also rearrange the nucleus
An X-ray, because it has the most energy
A visible ray, because it is tuned to the resonant frequency

problems.prompt: The minimum size of an object visible through an optical microscope is approximately the shortest wavelength of light used for illumination. Electron microscopes have much higher resolution, and like photons an electron has a wavelength lambda = h/p, where p is momentum. Which of the following statements is true?
choices: The wavelength of an imaging electron is much greater than the wavelength of red light.
The momentum of an imaging electron is much less than the momentum of blue light.
The momentum of an imaging electron is much greater than the momentum of blue light.
The wavelength of an imaging electron is between the wavelengths of red and blue light.

problems.prompt: In radiation therapy, absorbed dose is the energy absorbed per unit mass, measured in grays (1 Gy = 1 J/kg), and destroying a tumor takes a dose of roughly 60 Gy. Approximately how much energy is required to destroy 99% of the mass of a tumor weighing 10 grams?

A proton beam deposits increasing energy with depth up to a maximum called the Bragg peak, beyond which the dose falls to zero within millimeters, and the depth of the Bragg peak increases with the beam's energy (see the figure of depth-dose curves). Which type of radiation would most likely be best for treating a tumor 17 cm within a patient's body?

concepts.title: The Bohr Model of the Atom
concepts.content: In the Bohr model, electrons occupy discrete, quantized energy levels around the nucleus rather than a continuous range of energies. An electron moves between levels only by absorbing a photon to jump up or emitting a photon to drop down, with the photon's energy exactly equal to the difference between the two levels, E = hf. Because the levels are fixed, each element emits and absorbs light only at characteristic frequencies, producing line spectra. The same idea explains light emission from other quantized systems, such as an electron dropping across the band gap of a semiconductor.

problems.prompt: In a light-emitting diode, an electron drops from a high-energy state (the conduction band) to a lower-energy state (the valence band), emitting a photon whose energy equals the band gap. For aluminum gallium arsenide, the band gap is 1.6 eV. What is the wavelength of the emitted light? (Planck's constant = 4.14 x 10^-15 eV*s; speed of light = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s.)

concepts.title: The Pauli Exclusion Principle
concepts.content: The Pauli exclusion principle states that no two electrons in an atom can share the same complete set of quantum numbers, so any single quantum state holds at most one electron. Because electrons also carry a spin quantum number with two possible values, a single spatial orbital (same n, l, and m) can hold two electrons as long as they have opposite spins. Two electrons with different quantum numbers can still have the same energy, since higher shells contain multiple states at the same energy. This principle governs how electrons fill atomic orbitals and underlies the structure of the periodic table.

problems.prompt: If a second electron binds to a hydrogen atom (forming H-) in the ground state, will both electrons have the same energy?
choices: No, because the Pauli exclusion principle forbids two electrons from having the same energy.
Yes, because the Pauli exclusion principle allows a maximum of two electrons with the same energy.
Yes, but the two electrons must have opposite spin to satisfy the Pauli exclusion principle.
No, the Pauli exclusion principle makes both energies uncertain, so they cannot be equal.

concepts.title: The Photoelectric Effect
concepts.content: The photoelectric effect is the ejection of electrons from a material when it absorbs sufficiently high-energy photons, and it provided key evidence that light behaves as particles. An electron is ejected only if a single photon's energy exceeds the material's work function (its binding energy), so below a threshold frequency no electrons are emitted no matter how intense the light. Above threshold, the ejected electron's kinetic energy equals the photon energy minus the work function, and brighter light ejects more electrons without increasing each one's energy. The effect involves photons ejecting electrons, not electrons ejecting other electrons.

problems.prompt: Which of the following could be a good reason a radiologist might decide to treat a tumor with beta radiation (electrons or positrons) instead of a proton beam?
choices: There is less risk of side scatter (deflection away from the original collimated beam) for beta particles than for a proton beam.
Negatively charged particles are more ionizing than positively charged particles, therefore requiring a smaller dose.
A beam of beta particles will ionize tumor tissue via the photoelectric effect, which is more finely tuned than the bulk ionization of proton therapy.
The tumor is close to the surface of the patient's skin, so the less penetrative beta particles are less likely to damage deep tissues along the beam's path.

concepts.title: The Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
concepts.content: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle is a consequence of wave-particle duality: it is impossible to know both a particle's position and its momentum with unlimited precision at the same time. Locating a particle's position more precisely requires shorter-wavelength, higher-energy probing light, which disturbs the particle's momentum more, and vice versa. The product of the uncertainties in position and momentum has a fundamental lower bound, so improving one measurement necessarily worsens the other. This limit is intrinsic to quantum systems, not merely a shortcoming of measuring instruments.
